A lamp in series with a capacitor glows brighter if C or the frequency is increased (XC falls, current rises).

ex.q: A 100 µF capacitor is connected to an AC supply with ω = 100 rad s⁻¹ and V = 50 V (RMS). Find XC and I.

topics.rl: Ceiling fans in India use a capacitor in series with one winding to create a phase shift between currents. That shift produces the rotating field that starts the fan.

topics.h: Radio sets, induction furnaces and the power-factor panels in Indian factories all contain resistors, inductors and capacitors in series. Phasors make them easy.
p: In series, the same current flows through R, L and C. VR is in phase with I, VL leads I by 90°, VC lags I by 90°.
Phasor sum: Vm² = VRm² + (VCm - VLm)², so the impedance is Z = √(R² + (XC - XL)²), with vm = imZ.
Impedance diagram: R along one axis and (XC - XL) at right angles; Z is the hypotenuse.
Phase angle: tanφ = (XC - XL)/R. If XL > XC the circuit is inductive (current lags); if XC > XL it is capacitive (current leads).
Individual voltages VR = IR, VL = IXL, VC = IXC can be larger than the supply voltage, because they are not in phase.

ex.q: R = 30 Ω, XL = 80 Ω, XC = 40 Ω in series across 100 V (RMS). Find Z, I and VR, VL, VC.
st: VR = 60 V, VL = 160 V, VC = 80 V
ex.a: Z = 50 Ω; I = 2 A; VR = 60 V, VL = 160 V, VC = 80 V

topics.rl: Induction furnaces in Indian steel foundries are big LCR circuits; engineers tune the capacitor banks so the circuit's impedance and phase are just right for efficient heating.

topics.h: Turn the tuning knob of an old FM radio and one station suddenly comes in loud and clear. You have just made an LCR circuit resonate.
p: Resonance occurs when XL = XC, i.e. ω₀L = 1/(ω₀C), so ω₀ = 1/√(LC) and ν₀ = 1/(2π√(LC)).
At resonance Z = R (minimum) and the current is maximum, im = vm/R. Current and voltage are in phase.
A graph of current against frequency peaks at ω₀. Smaller R gives a taller, sharper peak; larger R gives a flatter peak.
Resonance needs both L and C; an RL or RC circuit cannot resonate.
Radio tuning: changing C shifts ω₀ to match a station's frequency, so that station's signal produces the largest current.

ex.q: Find the resonant angular frequency for L = 0.5 H and C = 8 µF.

topics.rl: All India Radio and the many FM channels in Indian cities broadcast on different frequencies; your radio's tuning circuit picks one by resonance.

topics.t: Power in AC circuits and power factor
topics.h: Electricity boards in India charge factories a penalty if their power factor is low. A bank of capacitors can save lakhs of rupees a year.
p: Average power in an AC circuit: P = VI cosφ (V and I are RMS), where φ is the phase difference. cosφ is the power factor.
Pure resistor: φ = 0, cosφ = 1, P = VI. Pure inductor or capacitor: φ = ±90°, cosφ = 0, P = 0. Such current is called wattless current.
Series LCR: cosφ = R/Z. At resonance Z = R, so cosφ = 1 and power is maximum.
A low power factor means a large current for the same useful power, so I²R losses in the lines rise.
Industries add capacitors to cancel the lagging current drawn by motors (inductive loads), raising the power factor towards 1.

ex.q: A circuit with R = 60 Ω and Z = 100 Ω is connected to 200 V RMS. Find the power factor and the average power.

topics.rl: State electricity boards, from Maharashtra's MSEDCL to Tamil Nadu's TANGEDCO, set minimum power factor rules for industrial consumers, which is why factories install capacitor banks.

topics.h: A phone charger steps 230 V down to about 5 V. The power station steps it up to 400 kV. Both use the same simple device: two coils and an iron core.
p: Principle: mutual induction. An alternating current in the primary coil creates a changing flux in a soft iron core, which induces an emf in the secondary coil.
Ideal transformer: Vs/Vp = Ns/Np, and with no losses VpIp = VsIs, so Ip/Is = Ns/Np.
Step-up transformer: Ns > Np (voltage raised, current lowered). Step-down transformer: Ns < Np.

Energy losses: flux leakage (reduced by winding coils on top of each other), resistance of windings (thick copper wire), eddy currents in the core (laminated core) and hysteresis (soft iron with a narrow loop).
A transformer works only with AC (or changing current); steady DC gives no changing flux.

ex.q: A step-down transformer has 2000 primary turns and 100 secondary turns. With 220 V on the primary, find Vs. If the secondary delivers 10 A, find Ip (ideal).

topics.rl: The grey transformer on an electric pole in an Indian neighbourhood steps 11 kV down to about 415 V between phases (three-phase), which gives about 230-240 V between a phase and neutral for each home.

topics.t: Power transmission and AC problem solving
topics.h: Electricity from a hydro plant in Himachal reaches homes in Delhi hundreds of kilometres away. Transformers at both ends make that journey efficient.
p: Power is generated at about 11 to 25 kV, stepped up to hundreds of kV for long-distance lines, then stepped down at substations (to 33 kV, 11 kV and finally 230 V).
For a fixed power P = VI, raising V lowers I, and the line loss I²R falls as 1/V².
Problem example: an ideal step-up transformer from 11 kV to 220 kV has Ns/Np = 20; the line current is 1/20 of the generator current.
Toolkit: V = vm/√2; XL = ωL; XC = 1/(ωC); Z = √(R² + (XC - XL)²); ω₀ = 1/√(LC); P = VI cosφ; Vs/Vp = Ns/Np.
Always check whether values given are peak or RMS before using them in formulas.

ex.q: A plant generates 800 kW at 4 kV. It is stepped up to 40 kV for a line of resistance 10 Ω. Find the line current and loss.

topics.rl: POWERGRID's national grid links regional grids through 400 kV and 765 kV AC lines and HVDC links, carrying power from coal belts in the east to cities in the west and north.

topics.t: Maxwell's prediction and the first EM waves
topics.h: Long before Wi-Fi and 5G, a Scottish physicist doing algebra on paper predicted invisible waves that travel at the speed of light. A few decades later, they were found.
p: Faraday showed a changing magnetic field produces an electric field. Maxwell asked: does a changing electric field produce a magnetic field? He concluded it does.
Maxwell's equations then predicted electromagnetic (EM) waves of linked, changing E and B fields, travelling at about 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹: the speed of light. So light itself is an EM wave.
In 1887 Heinrich Hertz produced and detected EM waves in the laboratory, confirming Maxwell.
Jagadish Chandra Bose in Kolkata produced and studied EM waves of much shorter wavelength (about 25 mm to 5 mm).
Guglielmo Marconi transmitted EM waves over many kilometres, opening the era of radio communication.

ex.q: Why was Maxwell's calculated speed of EM waves such a big deal?
st: His theory gave the wave speed as 1/√(µ₀ε₀).
This came out equal to the measured speed of light.
So light must be an electromagnetic wave.
ex.a: It showed that light is an electromagnetic wave, uniting optics with electricity and magnetism

topics.rl: J.C. Bose's millimetre-wave work at Presidency College, Kolkata, in the 1890s anticipated technologies now used in 5G and car radar.

topics.h: While a capacitor charges, current flows in the wires but no charge crosses the gap. Yet a compass placed near the gap still feels a magnetic field. Maxwell found the missing current.
p: Ampere's law fails while a capacitor charges: a loop around the wire gives ∮B·dl = µ₀i through a flat surface, but zero through a surface passing between the plates. The results contradict each other.
Between the plates, the electric flux ΦE changes. Maxwell defined displacement current id = ε₀ dΦE/dt.
Ampere-Maxwell law: ∮B·dl = µ₀(ic + ε₀ dΦE/dt) = µ₀(ic + id).
The total current (conduction + displacement) is continuous: in the wires it is all ic, in the gap it is all id, and they are equal.
So a changing electric field produces a magnetic field, just as a changing magnetic field produces an electric field.

ex.q: A capacitor is being charged by a current of 2 A. What is the displacement current between its plates?
st: Charge on plate q = ε₀EA = ε₀ΦE

topics.rl: Electrical engineers designing high-frequency circuits for ISRO's satellites must account for displacement currents through capacitors and even through the air gaps between conductors.

topics.t: Maxwell's equations and how EM waves are made
topics.h: Four short equations describe every electric and magnetic phenomenon, from a static zap to a 5G signal. The fourth one makes waves possible.
p: Maxwell's equations: (1) Gauss's law ∮E·dA = Q/ε₀; (2) Gauss's law for magnetism ∮B·dA = 0; (3) Faraday's law ∮E·dl = -dΦB/dt; (4) Ampere-Maxwell law ∮B·dl = µ₀ic + µ₀ε₀ dΦE/dt. Plus the Lorentz force F = q(E + v × B).
Stationary charges make only E; charges in uniform motion (steady currents) make steady B; but accelerated charges radiate EM waves.
An oscillating charge (for example in an antenna) produces an oscillating E, which produces an oscillating B, and so on: the wave carries away energy at the charge's frequency.
In an EM wave, E and B oscillate perpendicular to each other and to the direction of travel: EM waves are transverse.
E, B and the direction of propagation follow the order E × B, giving the direction the wave travels.

ex.q: An electron oscillates in an antenna at 100 MHz. What frequency does the radiated wave have, and why?
st: The fields oscillate at the same frequency as the charge.
So the wave frequency is 100 MHz.
ex.a: 100 MHz, the frequency of the oscillating charge

topics.rl: The tall masts of Doordarshan and All India Radio have antennas in which electrons are made to oscillate; these accelerated charges launch the waves your TV or radio picks up.

topics.t: Nature and properties of EM waves
topics.h: Sunlight takes about 8 minutes to cross 150 million km of empty space, carrying enough energy to power the solar parks of Rajasthan and to push on solar sails.
p: For a wave travelling along z: Ex = E₀ sin(kz - ωt), By = B₀ sin(kz - ωt), with k = 2π/λ and ω = 2πν. E and B are in phase.
Speed in vacuum: c = ω/k = νλ = 1/√(µ₀ε₀) ≈ 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹. In a medium: v = 1/√(µε).
The amplitudes are related: E₀/B₀ = c (and E/B = c at every instant).
EM waves need no medium. They carry energy and momentum; on absorption they exert radiation pressure. Momentum delivered p = U/c for total absorption.
Example: a wave with B₀ = 2 × 10⁻⁸ T has E₀ = cB₀ = 6 V m⁻¹.

ex.q: A plane EM wave of frequency 30 MHz travels in vacuum along x. At some point E = 9 ĵ V m⁻¹. Find B there.
st: Direction: E × B must point along +x, and ĵ × k̂ = î, so B is along +z (k̂)

topics.rl: ISRO's solar panels on satellites and India's solar parks absorb sunlight energy; the same light also delivers a tiny momentum, which spacecraft designers must account for over long missions.

topics.t: EM spectrum: radio, microwave and infrared
topics.h: Your FM radio, the microwave oven warming leftover biryani and the TV remote are all using light that your eyes cannot see.
p: The EM spectrum is arranged by frequency or wavelength. The regions overlap; there are no sharp boundaries.
Radio waves (λ > 0.1 m): produced by accelerated charges in antennas. AM band 530 kHz to 1710 kHz; FM band 88 MHz to 108 MHz; TV bands from 54 MHz up to 890 MHz; mobile phones use UHF.

Microwaves (0.1 m to 1 mm): produced by special vacuum tubes such as klystrons and magnetrons, and Gunn diodes. Used in radar for aircraft navigation and in microwave ovens, where they heat food by agitating water molecules.

Infrared (1 mm to 700 nm): 'heat waves', given out by hot bodies and vibrating molecules. Used in TV remotes, night vision, physiotherapy heat lamps, and the greenhouse effect warms Earth by trapping IR.
Infrared is detected by thermopiles and bolometers, and many snakes can sense it.

ex.q: A station broadcasts at 98.3 MHz. Which band and roughly what wavelength?
st: So it is an FM radio station.

topics.rl: Doppler weather radars run by the India Meteorological Department use microwaves to track cyclones in the Bay of Bengal and monsoon rain bands.

topics.t: EM spectrum: visible, UV, X-rays and gamma rays
topics.h: Your eyes see only a thin slice of the spectrum, from about 400 nm to 700 nm. Beyond violet lie rays that can disinfect water, image bones and treat cancer.
p: Visible light: about 700 nm (red) to 400 nm (violet). The eye is most sensitive near the middle (yellow-green). Some animals see beyond: honeybees see into the ultraviolet, and snakes can sense infrared.

Ultraviolet (400 nm to 1 nm): produced by the Sun and special lamps. Most solar UV is absorbed by the ozone layer. UV lamps sterilise water and instruments; precise UV lasers are used in LASIK eye surgery. Welders wear special glass goggles to protect eyes from UV.
X-rays (1 nm to 10⁻³ nm): produced by bombarding a metal target with high-energy electrons. Used for medical diagnosis and cancer treatment; overexposure damages tissue.
Gamma rays (below about 10⁻³ nm): produced in nuclear reactions and emitted by radioactive nuclei. Used in medicine to destroy cancer cells.
Higher frequency means higher photon energy, and generally more harmful to living tissue.

ex.q: A radiation has wavelength 300 nm. Identify it and one use.
st: 300 nm is shorter than violet (400 nm).
It lies in 400 nm to 1 nm.
It is ultraviolet, used to sterilise water.

topics.rl: Water purifiers in many Indian homes use a UV lamp to kill bacteria, and cancer hospitals like Tata Memorial use high-energy X-rays and gamma rays in radiotherapy.

topics.t: EM spectrum: the full table and problem practice
topics.h: One table summarises it all: from radio waves longer than a cricket pitch to gamma rays smaller than an atomic nucleus.
p: Radio (> 0.1 m): produced by accelerated charges in aerials; detected by receiver aerials.

Microwave (0.1 m to 1 mm): klystrons, magnetrons, Gunn diodes; detected by point-contact diodes. Infrared (1 mm to 700 nm): vibrating atoms and molecules; detected by thermopiles, bolometers, IR film.
Light (700 nm to 400 nm): electrons in atoms dropping to lower energy levels; detected by the eye, photocells, photographic film.

Ultraviolet (400 nm to 1 nm): inner shell electrons in atoms; detected by photocells and photographic film. X-rays (1 nm to 10⁻³ nm): X-ray tubes or inner shell electrons; detected by photographic film, Geiger tubes, ionisation chambers.
Gamma rays (< 10⁻³ nm): radioactive decay of nuclei; detected the same way as X-rays. To identify a region, convert using c = νλ and compare with the ranges.

ex.q: Identify the radiation with frequency 3 × 10¹⁸ Hz.
st: 0.1 nm lies between 1 nm and 10⁻³ nm: X-rays

topics.rl: Airport security scanners at Indian airports use X-rays to see inside bags, while thermal cameras used during the COVID pandemic used infrared to measure skin temperature.

topics.t: Light rays and reflection by spherical mirrors
topics.h: The dentist's small concave mirror and the convex mirror at a hilly hairpin bend in Uttarakhand obey the same two simple laws.
p: Light is electromagnetic radiation; the eye detects wavelengths from about 400 nm to 750 nm. Its speed in vacuum, c ≈ 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, is a fundamental constant.
Ray optics (geometrical optics): when the wavelength is tiny compared with the objects involved, light can be treated as travelling in straight lines called rays. A bundle of rays is a beam.
Laws of reflection: the angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence, and the incident ray, reflected ray and normal lie in one plane.
For a spherical mirror, the normal at any point is along the radius through that point (towards the centre of curvature).

Terms: pole P (centre of the mirror's surface), centre of curvature C, principal axis (line through P and C), aperture (size of the mirror). Paraxial rays are rays close to and nearly parallel to the principal axis.

ex.q: A ray strikes a concave mirror at a point, making 25° with the radius drawn to that point. What is the angle of reflection?
st: The radius is the normal at that point.
Angle of reflection = angle of incidence

topics.rl: The convex mirrors fixed at sharp turns on mountain roads in Himachal Pradesh give drivers a wide view of oncoming traffic around the bend.

topics.t: Sign convention and the mirror equation
topics.h: Mirror problems become simple arithmetic once you agree on one rule for signs. Physicists use the Cartesian sign convention, like a number line placed on the mirror's axis.
p: Cartesian sign convention: all distances are measured from the pole; distances in the direction of incident light are positive, against it negative; heights above the axis are positive, below negative.
With light coming from the left, the object distance u is negative for real objects. Focal length of a concave mirror is negative; of a convex mirror, positive.
Focal length f = R/2 for spherical mirrors (paraxial rays).
Mirror equation: 1/v + 1/u = 1/f, derived from similar triangles in a ray diagram.
Magnification m = h'/h = -v/u. Negative m means a real, inverted image; positive m means a virtual, erect image.

ex.q: An object is 30 cm in front of a concave mirror of focal length 20 cm. Find the image position and magnification.
ex.a: v = -60 cm (real, in front); m = -2 (inverted, twice the size)

topics.rl: Shaving and make-up mirrors are concave: placed within f of your face, they give an enlarged, erect, virtual image, matching m positive and greater than 1.

topics.h: Where you place an object in front of a concave mirror decides whether you see a huge upright image, an upside-down one, or none at all.
p: Concave mirror, object beyond C: image between F and C, real, inverted, diminished.
Object at C: image at C, real, inverted, same size. Object between C and F: image beyond C, real, inverted, magnified.
Object at F: image at infinity. Object between F and P: image behind the mirror, virtual, erect, magnified.
A convex mirror always forms a virtual, erect, diminished image between P and F, whatever the object position.
Moving objects and rear-view mirrors: the image in a convex mirror moves much more slowly than the object; image speed ≈ (v/u)² × object speed.

ex.q: A car 9 m behind a truck is seen in the truck's convex mirror of focal length 1 m. The car approaches at 10 m s⁻¹. How fast does its image move?

topics.rl: The convex side-view mirrors on many cars and two-wheelers carry the warning 'objects in mirror are closer than they appear', because a convex mirror forms a diminished image.

topics.h: A straw in a glass of nimbu pani looks bent at the surface. Light changes speed as it crosses from water to air, and that bends its path.
p: Laws of refraction: the incident ray, refracted ray and normal lie in one plane; and Snell's law: sin i/sin r = n₂₁ (a constant for the pair of media and a given colour).
Refractive index of medium 2 relative to 1: n₂₁ = n₂/n₁ = v₁/v₂. Absolute refractive index n = c/v.
Going from rarer to denser (n₂₁ > 1), the ray bends towards the normal (r < i); from denser to rarer, it bends away from the normal.
Useful relations: n₁₂ = 1/n₂₁, and n₃₂ = n₃₁ × n₁₂.
Typical refractive indices: air 1.0003, water 1.33, crown glass 1.52, diamond 2.42.

ex.q: Light travels from air into glass of refractive index 1.5. Find its speed in glass.

topics.rl: Diamonds cut in Surat, India's diamond capital, sparkle partly because diamond's high refractive index (2.42) bends light strongly.

topics.t: Slabs, apparent depth and total internal reflection
topics.h: A swimming pool always looks shallower than it is, and on a hot road you see 'water' that is not there. Both tricks come from refraction near a boundary.
p: Glass slab: the emergent ray is parallel to the incident ray but shifted sideways (lateral shift), which grows with slab thickness and angle of incidence.
Apparent depth (for near-normal viewing) = real depth/n. A pool 2 m deep in water (n = 4/3) looks 1.5 m deep. The normal shift is d(1 - 1/n).
Going from a denser to a rarer medium, the refracted ray bends away from the normal. At the critical angle ic, the refraction angle is 90°.
Total internal reflection (TIR) happens when light goes from denser to rarer medium AND the angle of incidence exceeds ic. Then all light is reflected.
sin ic = 1/n₂₁ (n of denser relative to rarer). Critical angles: water 48.75°, crown glass about 41°, diamond about 24.4°.

ex.q: A coin lies at the bottom of a 12 cm deep beaker of water (n = 4/3). How deep does it appear, and by how much is it raised?
ex.a: Appears 9 cm deep; raised by 3 cm

topics.rl: Mirages on the Delhi-Jaipur highway in May are caused by refraction and total internal reflection of skylight in hot, less dense air near the road surface.

topics.t: Total internal reflection at work: prisms and optical fibres
topics.h: The broadband internet reaching Indian villages under BharatNet travels as light, bouncing through glass fibres thinner than a hair.
p: Activity: shine a laser pointer through slightly soapy or milky water in a glass and tilt it; beyond a certain angle the beam reflects completely at the surface. Safety: never look into or point a laser at anyone's eyes, and keep water away from electrical sockets.
Totally reflecting prisms (45°-90°-45° glass prisms, critical angle about 42°) turn rays through 90° (periscopes) or 180° (binoculars), and can invert images without changing size.
They reflect almost 100% of light, better than silvered mirrors.

Optical fibres: a glass or quartz core surrounded by cladding of lower refractive index. Light entering the core undergoes repeated TIR and travels long distances with little loss, even when the fibre bends.
Uses: telecommunication (huge data rates), endoscopy (light pipes to see inside the body), and decorative lamps.

ex.q: Why must the cladding of an optical fibre have a lower refractive index than the core?
st: TIR needs light to go from denser to rarer medium.
The core must be denser than the cladding.
Then rays hitting the boundary beyond ic are totally reflected.
ex.a: So that light in the core is totally internally reflected at the core-cladding boundary

topics.rl: Gastroenterologists in hospitals across India use endoscopes, bundles of optical fibres, to see inside a patient's stomach without surgery.

topics.t: Refraction at spherical surfaces and the lens maker's formula
topics.h: An air bubble in a glass paperweight looks bigger or smaller depending on where you look from. A single curved surface can act like a lens.
p: Refraction at a single spherical surface: n₂/v - n₁/u = (n₂ - n₁)/R, using the Cartesian sign convention (light from medium n₁ into n₂).
Applications: the apparent position of an object inside a glass sphere, or of an air bubble seen from outside.

A thin lens has two surfaces; combining the single-surface equation for both gives the lens maker's formula: 1/f = (n₂₁ - 1)(1/R₁ - 1/R₂), where n₂₁ is the lens material's index relative to the surroundings.
For a double convex lens, R₁ is positive and R₂ negative.
A lens in a different medium: its focal length changes because n₂₁ changes. A glass lens (n = 1.5) in water (n = 4/3) has f four times its value in air.

ex.q: A double convex lens has R₁ = 20 cm and R₂ = -20 cm, with n = 1.5. Find f.

topics.rl: Spectacle makers in Indian optical shops grind lens surfaces to specific radii; the lens maker's formula tells them which curvatures give the required power.

topics.t: Thin lens formula and power of a lens
topics.h: An optometrist writes '-1.5 D' on your prescription. That number is the power of a lens, and it tells you exactly how strongly it bends light.
p: Thin lens formula: 1/v - 1/u = 1/f. Magnification m = h'/h = v/u.
Convex (converging) lens: f > 0. Concave (diverging) lens: f < 0. Real images have v > 0 (on the other side); virtual images have v < 0.

Ray diagrams: a convex lens forms real, inverted images when the object is beyond F, and a virtual, erect, magnified image when the object is within F. A concave lens always gives virtual, erect, diminished images.
Power P = 1/f (f in metres). Unit: dioptre (D), 1 D = 1 m⁻¹.
Converging lenses have positive power; diverging lenses have negative power.

ex.q: An object is 30 cm in front of a convex lens of focal length 20 cm. Find v and m.

topics.rl: Millions of Indians wear spectacles. A short-sighted student might need a -2 D concave lens, and a reader over 45 a +1.5 D convex lens.

topics.t: Combinations of lenses and optics problem practice
topics.h: Camera and microscope objectives are not single lenses but stacks of them. Adding lenses is as easy as adding their powers.
p: Thin lenses in contact: 1/f = 1/f₁ + 1/f₂ + ...; equivalently P = P₁ + P₂ + ...
Total magnification of a combination: m = m₁m₂m₃...
Lenses at a separation: find the image by the first lens, then use it as the object for the second lens (measuring distances from the second lens).
Combining converging and diverging lenses of different glasses can reduce colour defects in cameras and microscopes.
Problem toolkit: mirror formula, lens formula, lens maker's formula, power, TIR condition, prism relations and instrument magnifications.

ex.q: Two lenses of +10 D and -4 D are placed in contact. Find the power and focal length of the combination.

topics.rl: Smartphone cameras made in Indian factories pack five or six tiny lenses into a few millimetres. Their combined power focuses the scene on the sensor.

topics.h: A prism bends light twice, once going in and once coming out. There is one special angle where the bending is the least, and it reveals the glass's refractive index.
p: For a triangular prism of angle A: r₁ + r₂ = A, where r₁ and r₂ are the refraction angles inside at the two faces.
Angle of deviation: δ = i + e - A, where i and e are the angles of incidence and emergence.
A graph of δ against i falls to a minimum Dm and then rises again.
At minimum deviation, i = e and r₁ = r₂ = A/2; the ray passes symmetrically. Then n₂₁ = sin[(A + Dm)/2]/sin(A/2).
For a thin prism (small A): δ = (n₂₁ - 1)A.

ex.q: A prism of angle 60° gives minimum deviation 30°. Find n.

topics.rl: Spectrometers in Indian research labs, like those at IIA Bengaluru, use prisms or gratings at minimum deviation to measure the refractive index and to split light into colours.

topics.h: With a simple lens you can read the tiny print on a medicine strip. With two lenses, a pathologist at a district hospital can see the malaria parasite in a drop of blood.
p: Simple microscope (magnifier): a converging lens with the object within its focal length gives an erect, magnified, virtual image.
Angular magnification: m = 1 + D/f when the image is at the near point (D = 25 cm), and m = D/f when the image is at infinity (relaxed eye).
Compound microscope: an objective of short focal length forms a real, inverted, magnified intermediate image; the eyepiece acts as a simple magnifier on it.
Magnifying power with the final image at infinity: m ≈ (L/fo)(D/fe), where L is the tube length (distance between the second focal point of the objective and the first focal point of the eyepiece).
To get high magnification, both fo and fe should be small.

ex.q: A magnifier has f = 5 cm. Find the magnification with the image at the near point (25 cm) and at infinity.
ex.a: 6 at the near point; 5 at infinity

topics.rl: Pathology labs across India use compound microscopes with 100× oil-immersion objectives and 10× eyepieces, giving a total magnification of about 1000×.

topics.h: The Giant Metrewave Radio Telescope near Pune collects faint radio waves from space, while the optical telescopes at Devasthal in Uttarakhand gather faint light from galaxies billions of light years away.
p: Refracting astronomical telescope: an objective of large focal length and large aperture, and an eyepiece of short focal length. The objective forms a real image of a distant object at its focus.
Magnifying power in normal adjustment (final image at infinity): m = fo/fe. Tube length = fo + fe.
A larger objective aperture gathers more light (light-gathering power ∝ area ∝ D²) and gives better resolving power, so fainter and finer details are seen.

Reflecting telescopes (such as the Cassegrain design) use a concave primary mirror and a small convex secondary mirror. Advantages: no chromatic aberration, the mirror can be supported across its back, and large mirrors are cheaper and lighter than large lenses.
The image of a distant object (like the Moon) formed by the objective has size = fo × angle subtended by the object.

ex.q: A telescope has fo = 100 cm and fe = 5 cm. Find the magnifying power and the tube length in normal adjustment.

topics.rl: The 3.6 m Devasthal Optical Telescope near Nainital, India's largest, is a reflecting telescope. Its huge mirror gathers enough light to study faint stars and galaxies.

topics.h: For over a century, Newton's particle picture of light ruled. Then a thin film of soap and two tiny slits showed that light behaves like waves.
p: Newton favoured a corpuscular (particle) model of light. Huygens (1678) proposed a wave model.

Young's interference experiment (1801) and later Maxwell's electromagnetic theory established the wave nature of light. The wave model also correctly predicts that light travels slower in water than in air.
Ray optics is the limit of wave optics when the wavelength is very small compared with the size of obstacles and apertures.
A wavefront is a surface of constant phase. A point source gives spherical wavefronts; a line source gives cylindrical ones; far from any source, small portions are plane wavefronts.
Rays are perpendicular to wavefronts, and energy travels along the rays, perpendicular to the wavefront.

ex.q: What shape of wavefront reaches Earth from a distant star, and why?
st: A star is a point source, so its wavefronts are spherical.
Its distance is enormous, so the sphere's radius is huge.
A small part of a huge sphere is practically flat.

topics.rl: The rainbow colours you see in a soap bubble or an oil film on a wet Mumbai road during the monsoon are evidence of light's wave nature through interference.

topics.h: Drop pebbles in a still pond: each ripple spreads in circles. Huygens imagined every point on a wave doing exactly that.
p: Huygens principle: every point on a wavefront acts as a source of secondary wavelets that spread out at the wave speed. The new wavefront is the forward envelope (common tangent) of these wavelets.
The backward wave is ignored; a fuller theory shows that the amplitude of the backwave is zero, so the wave only goes forward.
Reflection by Huygens construction: comparing two triangles formed by the incident and reflected wavefronts proves that i = r.

Wavefronts through optical elements: a plane wave through a thin prism is tilted; through a convex lens it becomes a converging spherical wave; after reflection from a concave mirror it becomes a spherical wave converging to the focus.
Optical paths: all rays from a point to its image take the same time (equal optical path), which is why lenses work.

ex.q: Explain using Huygens principle why a plane wave stays plane as it travels in a uniform medium.
st: Each point on the plane wavefront sends out spherical wavelets.
After time t, all have radius vt.
Their forward common tangent is a plane parallel to the original.
ex.a: The envelope of equal wavelets is a parallel plane, so the wave stays plane

topics.rl: Ultrasound scanners in Indian hospitals shape their beams using arrays of tiny sources, an engineering application of Huygens' idea that a wavefront is built from many secondary wavelets.

topics.h: Imagine a marching band walking from a road onto sand at an angle. The band members who hit the sand first slow down, and the whole row turns. Light does the same.
p: Huygens construction for refraction: while one end of the wavefront travels v₁τ in medium 1, the wavelet from the other end travels v₂τ in medium 2. Comparing triangles gives sin i/sin r = v₁/v₂ = n₂/n₁ (Snell's law).
Entering a denser medium (v₂ < v₁): the ray bends towards the normal.
Frequency stays the same across the boundary; speed and wavelength change: λ₂/λ₁ = v₂/v₁, so λ in medium = λ₀/n.
Going into a rarer medium (v₂ > v₁): the ray bends away from the normal. When sin i = v₁/v₂, r = 90°; beyond this critical angle, no refracted wavefront forms, giving total internal reflection.
Example: in glass of n = 1.5, light of vacuum wavelength 600 nm has λ = 400 nm and speed 2 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹.

ex.q: Yellow light of wavelength 589 nm in air enters water (n = 1.33). Find its frequency, speed and wavelength in water.

topics.rl: Fishermen in Kerala aim their spears below where a fish appears, because light from the fish refracts at the water surface, bending as its speed changes.

topics.h: Two speakers playing the same note can make spots of silence in a room. Light waves can do the same, if their sources are perfectly in step.
p: Coherent sources keep a constant phase difference; incoherent sources have a phase difference that changes randomly and rapidly.
Two coherent waves of equal intensity I₀ meeting with phase difference φ give resultant intensity I = 4I₀ cos²(φ/2).
Constructive interference (bright, I = 4I₀) for path difference nλ (φ = 2nπ); destructive (dark, I = 0) for path difference (n + ½)λ (φ = (2n + 1)π).
For incoherent sources, the cos² term averages to ½, so the intensities simply add: I = 2I₀. No fringes are seen.
Interference can be demonstrated with water waves: two dippers moving up and down together in a ripple tank produce lines of calm and agitated water.

ex.q: Two coherent waves of intensity I₀ each meet with a path difference of λ/3. Find the resultant intensity.

topics.rl: Noise-cancelling headphones sold across India work by destructive interference: they produce sound waves that cancel incoming noise.

topics.h: Thomas Young needed two light sources perfectly in step. His trick was simple and brilliant: split the light from one source using two pinholes.
p: Two independent sources are incoherent. Young used light from a single source passing through two narrow slits S₁ and S₂, which then act as coherent sources.
For slits separated by d, screen at distance D (D ≫ d), the path difference at a point at height x on the screen is S₂P - S₁P ≈ xd/D.
Bright fringes at x = nλD/d (n = 0, ±1, ±2...); dark fringes at x = (n + ½)λD/d.
Fringe width (distance between consecutive bright or dark fringes): β = λD/d. The fringes are equally spaced.
The central fringe (x = 0, zero path difference) is always bright.

ex.q: In a YDSE, d = 1 mm, D = 1 m and λ = 600 nm. Find the fringe width and the position of the third bright fringe.
ex.a: β = 0.6 mm; third bright fringe at 1.8 mm

topics.rl: Physics students in Indian colleges measure the wavelength of sodium light using double-slit or biprism set-ups, with fringe widths measured to a hundredth of a millimetre.

topics.h: Swap red light for blue, dunk the apparatus in water, or move the screen back: each tweak stretches or squeezes the fringes in a predictable way.
p: β = λD/d: β increases with λ and D, and decreases with d.
Immersing the apparatus in a liquid of refractive index n reduces λ to λ/n, so β becomes β/n.
With white light, the central fringe is white, and the others are coloured: violet (shorter λ) fringes lie nearer the centre, red ones farther out. Only a few fringes are visible.
Energy is redistributed in interference: it is not destroyed at dark fringes but moved to bright ones.
Fringe shift problems: λ can be found from measured fringe width or from the change in position of a given fringe when D or λ changes.

ex.q: Fringes of width 0.6 mm are formed in air. Find the fringe width when the whole apparatus is immersed in water (n = 4/3).

topics.rl: Engineers at ISRO use interferometers, which measure tiny distances by counting fringe shifts, to test the flatness of mirrors and lenses for satellite cameras.

topics.h: Look at a street light through a narrow gap between two fingers on a dark night. You will see faint bright and dark bands: light bending round the edges.
p: Diffraction is the bending of light around the edges of obstacles or apertures whose size is comparable to the wavelength.
A single slit of width a gives a broad central maximum with weaker secondary maxima and minima on either side.
Minima occur at a sinθ = nλ (n = ±1, ±2, ...); secondary maxima lie roughly at θ ≈ (n + ½)λ/a, with intensity falling quickly.
Angular width of the central maximum = 2λ/a; on a screen at distance D its linear width = 2λD/a. The central maximum is twice as wide as each secondary maximum.
Narrower slits give wider diffraction patterns.

ex.q: Light of 600 nm falls on a slit of width 0.2 mm. Find the width of the central maximum on a screen 1 m away.

topics.rl: The coloured patterns you see in the tiny tracks of a CD or DVD lying in an Indian home, or in a peacock's feathers, involve diffraction and interference of light.

topics.h: Both interference and diffraction give bright and dark bands. A careful look at the band widths and brightness tells you which one you are seeing.
p: Interference (two slits): fringes of equal width β = λD/d and (ideally) equal intensity.
Diffraction (single slit): a central maximum twice as wide as the others, with intensity falling rapidly for higher orders.
Interference comes from superposition of waves from two separate (coherent) sources; diffraction from superposition of wavelets from different parts of one wavefront.

Activity: hold two razor blades edge to edge to form a narrow slit and look at a distant frosted bulb with a straight filament; you see a diffraction pattern. Safety: handle blades carefully, with edges away from fingers, and never look at the Sun.
In a real double-slit experiment, each slit's diffraction pattern acts as an envelope over the interference fringes.

ex.q: A pattern shows bands of equal width and equal brightness. Is it interference or single-slit diffraction?
st: Single-slit diffraction has a central band twice as wide as the rest.
Diffraction bands fade quickly away from the centre.
Equal widths and brightness match two-source interference.

topics.rl: The colourful bands you see when looking at a bright street lamp through a fine cotton dupatta or umbrella fabric are diffraction patterns from the tiny gaps between threads.

topics.h: Tilt your head while wearing polarising sunglasses and look at an LCD screen: it can go dark. Light has a hidden direction, and polaroids can reveal it.
p: Polarisation shows that light is a transverse wave. Analogy: a wave on a string passes through a vertical slit only if the string vibrates vertically.
Unpolarised light (sunlight, bulbs) has its electric field vibrating in all directions perpendicular to the direction of travel, changing randomly.
Plane (linearly) polarised light has its electric field vibrating in one direction only.
A polaroid transmits only the component of E along its pass axis. Unpolarised light of intensity I₀ through one polaroid becomes polarised with intensity I₀/2, whatever the polaroid's orientation.
A second polaroid (the analyser) rotated in front of the first changes the intensity: maximum when the axes are parallel, zero when crossed.

ex.q: Unpolarised light of intensity 80 W m⁻² passes through a polaroid. What is the transmitted intensity, and does it change if the polaroid is rotated?
st: A polaroid transmits half of unpolarised light.
Rotating it does not change this, because unpolarised light has no preferred direction.

topics.rl: Polarising sunglasses popular with drivers on Indian highways cut glare from wet roads and car bonnets, because the reflected glare is partly polarised.

topics.t: Malus' law and uses of polaroids
topics.h: 3D movies in Indian multiplexes send two polarised images at once, one for each eye. Your 3D glasses use polaroids to separate them.
p: Malus' law: when plane polarised light of intensity I₀ falls on an analyser whose axis makes angle θ with the polarisation, the transmitted intensity is I = I₀ cos²θ.
θ = 0: full transmission; θ = 90°: zero; θ = 45°: I₀/2; θ = 60°: I₀/4.
Three polaroids: unpolarised I₀ → first polaroid → I₀/2, then multiply by cos² of each successive angle between axes.
Two crossed polaroids block all light, but inserting a third polaroid at 45° between them lets I₀/8 through.
Uses: sunglasses (cut glare), camera filters, LCD screens of phones and calculators, and 3D movie glasses.

ex.q: Unpolarised light of intensity I₀ passes through three polaroids. The second is at 45° to the first, and the third is at 90° to the first. Find the final intensity.
st: After P₃ (45° to P₂): I₀/4 × cos²45° = I₀/8

topics.rl: Calculator and digital watch displays made for Indian classrooms use liquid crystals between polarisers; applying a voltage rotates the light's polarisation and darkens the digits.

topics.ch: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
topics.t: Electrons and how they escape metals
topics.h: The solar panels on rooftops from Gujarat to Tamil Nadu rely on light knocking electrons free. To understand them, we start with the electron itself.
p: J.J. Thomson (1897), studying cathode rays in discharge tubes, showed they are streams of negatively charged particles, electrons, and measured their charge-to-mass ratio e/m. Millikan's oil-drop experiment measured the charge e (about 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C).
This raised a deep question: do light and matter have both wave and particle character?
Free electrons in a metal cannot normally leave its surface; they are held by the attraction of the positive ions. Extra energy is needed to pull them out.

Work function φ₀: the minimum energy needed to free an electron from a metal surface, usually given in eV (1 eV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J). It depends on the metal and its surface; caesium has a low value (about 2.14 eV) and platinum a high one (about 5.65 eV).
Ways to supply this energy: thermionic emission (heating), field emission (very strong electric field, about 10⁸ V m⁻¹), and photoelectric emission (light of suitable frequency).

ex.q: A metal has a work function of 2.3 eV. Express it in joules.

topics.rl: Old television picture tubes and the X-ray tubes at Indian diagnostic centres use thermionic emission: a heated filament boils off electrons.

topics.ch: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
topics.h: In 1887, Heinrich Hertz noticed that sparks jumped more easily when ultraviolet light shone on his metal electrodes. He had stumbled on the photoelectric effect.
p: Hertz (1887): ultraviolet light falling on the spark gap made high-voltage sparks pass more easily.
Hallwachs and Lenard (1886–1902): UV light on a zinc plate releases negatively charged particles (electrons). A negatively charged zinc plate loses its charge, while a neutral one becomes positive.
There is a threshold frequency ν₀: below it no electrons are emitted, however intense the light.
Alkali metals (lithium, sodium, potassium, caesium, rubidium) emit electrons even with visible light; zinc, cadmium and magnesium need ultraviolet. Such materials are called photosensitive.

Experimental set-up: an evacuated glass tube with a photosensitive plate (emitter, cathode C) and a collector (anode A), a variable potential difference between them, a microammeter, and a monochromatic light source through a quartz window.

ex.q: A neutral zinc plate on an electroscope is exposed to UV light. What happens to the leaves and why?
st: UV ejects electrons from the zinc.
The plate is left with positive charge.
ex.a: The leaves diverge because the plate becomes positively charged

topics.rl: The automatic doors at Indian metro stations and malls once used photocells: light falling on a photosensitive surface gave a current, and blocking the beam changed it.

topics.ch: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
topics.h: Turn up the brightness of the light in a photocell and the current rises. But the fastest electrons do not get any faster. That surprised everyone.
p: For a frequency above threshold, the photocurrent (and number of electrons emitted per second) is directly proportional to the intensity of light.
As the anode's positive potential increases, the photocurrent rises and then levels off: the saturation current, when all emitted electrons are collected.
Making the anode negative reduces the current; at the stopping potential V₀ (cut-off), even the fastest electrons are stopped and the current becomes zero. Then Kmax = eV₀.
For a given frequency, the stopping potential is the same for all intensities; only the saturation current changes.
Emission is instantaneous: electrons come out within about 10⁻⁹ s of the light being switched on, even for very dim light.

ex.q: The stopping potential for a metal is 1.5 V. Find the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons in eV and J.

topics.rl: Light meters in cameras and the automatic street lights switched on at dusk in many Indian towns use the fact that photocurrent grows with light intensity.

topics.ch: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
topics.t: Effect of frequency, and why wave theory failed
topics.h: Classical physics said: make the light bright enough and electrons will fly out at any colour. Experiments said no. Something had to give.
p: For a given metal, the stopping potential V₀ increases linearly with the frequency ν of the incident light.
A graph of V₀ against ν is a straight line cutting the ν-axis at the threshold frequency ν₀. Below ν₀, no emission.
For different metals, the lines are parallel (the same slope, h/e), but they have different threshold frequencies.
Wave theory predicted that Kmax should increase with intensity, since a brighter wave carries more energy. Experiment shows Kmax depends only on frequency.
Wave theory also could not explain the existence of a threshold frequency or why emission is instantaneous (it predicted a long delay for dim light while energy builds up).

ex.q: For a metal, V₀ = 0 at ν = 5 × 10¹⁴ Hz and V₀ = 2 V at ν = 10 × 10¹⁴ Hz. Find the slope h/e.
ex.a: 4 × 10⁻¹⁵ V s (so h = slope × e ≈ 6.4 × 10⁻³⁴ J s from these data, close to the accepted 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s)

topics.rl: Physicists at India's Raman Research Institute in Bengaluru and elsewhere still teach this experiment as the moment classical physics broke and quantum physics was born.

topics.ch: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
topics.h: In 1905 Einstein proposed that light comes in packets of energy. One equation then explained everything the wave theory could not, and won him the Nobel Prize.
p: Light consists of quanta (photons), each of energy E = hν, where h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s (Planck's constant). One photon is absorbed by one electron.
Einstein's equation: Kmax = hν - φ₀ = eV₀.
Threshold frequency ν₀ = φ₀/h; threshold wavelength λ₀ = c/ν₀ = hc/φ₀. No emission if ν < ν₀ (or λ > λ₀).

This explains: threshold (photon energy must exceed φ₀); Kmax rising linearly with ν; intensity affecting only the number of photons (and so the current); instantaneous emission (one photon, one electron, no waiting).
Millikan's careful experiments verified the equation; the slope h/e of the V₀-ν graph gave a value of h close to Planck's.

ex.q: Light of frequency 1.2 × 10¹⁵ Hz falls on a metal with φ₀ = 3 eV. Find Kmax and V₀. (h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s)

topics.rl: Solar cells on ISRO's satellites and on Indian rooftops work on the photon idea: each absorbed photon with enough energy frees one electron to drive a current.

topics.ch: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
topics.h: Is a photon a particle? It has energy and momentum, travels at c, but has no rest mass. Here is the photon's identity card.
p: Typical problem 1: given λ and φ₀, find Kmax = hc/λ - φ₀ and V₀ = Kmax/e. Handy value: hc ≈ 1240 eV nm.
Typical problem 2: given V₀ at two frequencies, find h/e from the slope, then φ₀ and ν₀.
Photon properties: energy E = hν = hc/λ; momentum p = hν/c = h/λ; speed c in vacuum; zero rest mass.
The intensity of light at a given frequency is proportional to the number of photons crossing unit area per second, not to the energy of each photon.
Bright red light has many low-energy photons; dim violet light can have fewer but more energetic photons.

ex.q: Light of wavelength 310 nm falls on a metal and V₀ = 1.5 V. Find φ₀. (hc = 1240 eV nm)

topics.rl: LED lights promoted under India's UJALA scheme emit photons whose energies are set by the semiconductor material, giving different colours at very high efficiency.

topics.ch: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
topics.t: Photons in collisions and photon counting
topics.h: A 1 W LED glows with billions of billions of photons every second. Counting them is as simple as dividing power by the energy of one photon.
p: Photons are electrically neutral, so they are not deflected by electric or magnetic fields.
In photon-particle collisions (such as photon-electron collisions), total energy and total momentum are conserved, but the number of photons need not be: photons can be absorbed or created.
Number of photons emitted per second by a source of power P at wavelength λ: n = P/(hν) = Pλ/(hc).
Photon energy E = hν = hc/λ; photon momentum p = h/λ.
For a fixed power, shorter-wavelength (higher-energy) light means fewer photons per second.

ex.q: A 3 mW laser emits light of wavelength 663 nm. How many photons does it emit per second? (h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, c = 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹)

topics.rl: Fibre-optic receivers in Indian telecom networks are so sensitive that they detect signals carrying just a few thousand photons per bit.

topics.ch: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
topics.h: If light waves can act like particles, can particles act like waves? A young Louis de Broglie said yes in 1924, and electrons proved him right.
p: de Broglie hypothesis: a moving particle of momentum p has an associated wavelength λ = h/p = h/(mv).
For everyday objects λ is unimaginably tiny (a cricket ball's is about 10⁻³⁴ m), so no wave effects are seen. For electrons, λ is comparable to atomic spacings, so wave effects are clear.
In terms of kinetic energy K: λ = h/√(2mK). For an electron accelerated through V volts: λ = h/√(2meV) ≈ 1.227/√V nm.
Wave-particle duality: both radiation and matter show wave and particle aspects, but not both in the same measurement.
Electron microscopes use the very short de Broglie wavelength of fast electrons to resolve details far smaller than optical microscopes can.

ex.q: Find the de Broglie wavelength of an electron accelerated through 100 V.

topics.rl: Electron microscopes at IISc Bengaluru and other Indian research centres image viruses and nanomaterials using electrons whose de Broglie wavelength is far shorter than visible light's.

topics.ch: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
topics.h: Electrons, neutrons and photons: each has a wavelength, and quantum problems often ask you to compare them. A few formulas cover them all.
p: Particle with speed v: λ = h/(mv). With kinetic energy K: λ = h/√(2mK).
Electron accelerated through V volts: λ = 1.227/√V nm. Doubling V divides λ by √2.
Photon: E = hc/λ and p = h/λ. For a photon and an electron of the same wavelength, their momenta are equal, but their energies differ.
Slow (thermal) neutrons from reactors have de Broglie wavelengths of the order of 0.1 nm, comparable to atomic spacings, so they are used to study crystals.
Comparing particles: at the same speed, λ ∝ 1/m; at the same kinetic energy, λ ∝ 1/√m; for the same accelerating voltage V and charge q, λ ∝ 1/√(mq).

ex.q: An electron and a photon both have λ = 1 nm. Compare their momenta, and find the photon's energy. (hc = 1240 eV nm)
st: p = h/λ is the same for both

topics.rl: Neutron beams from the Dhruva research reactor at BARC, Mumbai, are used for neutron diffraction, exploiting the de Broglie wavelength of slow neutrons to study materials.

topics.t: Thomson's model and the gold foil experiment
topics.h: Imagine firing cannon shells at a sheet of tissue paper and seeing a few bounce straight back. That was Rutherford's astonishment at the gold foil results.
p: Atoms are electrically neutral, and each element gives a characteristic spectrum. A good atomic model must explain both structure and spectra.
Thomson's 'plum pudding' model (1898): positive charge spread uniformly through the atom, with electrons embedded like seeds in a watermelon. It could not explain large-angle scattering.

Geiger-Marsden experiment (1911, suggested by Rutherford): a beam of alpha particles was aimed at a very thin gold foil; scattered particles were detected by flashes on a zinc sulphide (ZnS) screen viewed through a microscope.
Observations: most alpha particles passed straight through; a few were deflected through large angles; a very few (about 1 in 8000) were turned back by more than 90°.
Conclusion: the atom's positive charge and nearly all its mass are concentrated in a tiny central nucleus, about 10⁴ to 10⁵ times smaller than the atom; most of the atom is empty space.

ex.q: Why did most alpha particles pass undeflected through the gold foil?
st: The nucleus occupies a tiny fraction of the atom's volume.
Most of the atom is empty space.
Most alpha particles never come close to a nucleus.
ex.a: Because most of the atom is empty space

topics.rl: Students at Indian science festivals often recreate the Rutherford experiment with marbles rolled at a hidden central block: most roll past, a few bounce sharply off.

topics.t: Impact parameter and distance of closest approach
topics.h: How close can an alpha particle get to a gold nucleus before it is turned back? Energy conservation gives a surprisingly simple estimate of nuclear size.
p: The path of an alpha particle near a nucleus depends on its impact parameter b: the perpendicular distance of its initial line of motion from the nucleus.
Small b (nearly head-on) gives large scattering angles; b = 0 means the particle turns back (scattering through 180°). Large b gives little deflection.
In a head-on approach, the alpha particle stops momentarily at the distance of closest approach d, where all its kinetic energy has become electric potential energy.
K = (1/4πε₀)(2e)(Ze)/d, so d = (1/4πε₀)(2Ze²)/K.
d gives an upper limit for the nuclear size; for gold and alpha energies of a few MeV, d is a few × 10⁻¹⁴ m.

ex.q: An alpha particle of 7.2 MeV heads straight for a tin nucleus (Z = 50). Find the distance of closest approach. (1/4πε₀ = 9 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻², e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)

topics.rl: Particle accelerators like the Pelletron at TIFR Mumbai fire nuclei at targets; physicists use closest-approach estimates to judge whether nuclei will touch and react.

topics.t: Electron orbits and the trouble with Rutherford's model
topics.h: Rutherford's atom was a mini solar system. But classical physics predicted that it should collapse in a split second. Clearly, something was missing.
p: In Rutherford's planetary model, the electron orbits the nucleus with the Coulomb attraction providing centripetal force: mv²/r = e²/(4πε₀r²).
Kinetic energy K = e²/(8πε₀r), potential energy U = -e²/(4πε₀r), total energy E = K + U = -e²/(8πε₀r).
The total energy is negative, meaning the electron is bound to the nucleus. Energy must be supplied to free it.
Limitation 1: an orbiting electron accelerates, and by classical EM theory it should radiate energy continuously, spiralling into the nucleus. Atoms would be unstable.
Limitation 2: a spiralling electron would emit a continuous range of frequencies, but atoms emit sharp line spectra.

ex.q: For a hydrogen electron orbit, K = 13.6 eV. Find U and the total energy E.

topics.rl: Fluorescent tube lights and sodium-vapour street lamps along Indian highways glow in definite colours, line spectra that Rutherford's model could not explain.

topics.h: Astronomers know what distant stars are made of without ever visiting them. Each element leaves a unique barcode of light.
p: When a gas or vapour is excited (for example by an electric discharge or heating), it emits light only at certain wavelengths: an emission line spectrum of bright lines on a dark background.
Each element has its own characteristic set of lines.
When white light passes through a cool gas, the gas absorbs light at the same wavelengths it would emit, giving dark lines on a continuous background: an absorption spectrum.
The emission and absorption lines of an element appear at the same wavelengths.
Because spectra are unique, they act as fingerprints for identifying elements in labs, in industry and in stars (helium was first discovered in the Sun's spectrum).

ex.q: Sodium vapour gives a bright yellow emission line near 589 nm. Where will a dark line appear if white light passes through cool sodium vapour?
st: Absorption lines lie at the same wavelengths as emission lines.

topics.rl: Forensic and food-testing labs in India, including those under FSSAI, use atomic absorption spectroscopy to detect metals like lead in food and water.

topics.h: In 1913 Niels Bohr rescued the nuclear atom by making three bold rules. They broke classical physics but matched the hydrogen spectrum beautifully.
p: Postulate 1: electrons revolve in certain stable orbits (stationary states) without radiating energy.
Postulate 2: in these orbits, angular momentum is quantised: L = mvr = nh/2π, where n = 1, 2, 3, ... is the principal quantum number.
Postulate 3: an electron emits or absorbs a photon only when it jumps between orbits: hν = Ei - Ef.
Radius of the nth orbit: rn = n²h²ε₀/(πme²), so rn ∝ n². The smallest, the Bohr radius, is a₀ ≈ 5.3 × 10⁻¹¹ m (0.53 Å).
Speed of the electron in the nth orbit vn ∝ 1/n; in the first orbit v₁ ≈ 2.2 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹ (about c/137).

ex.q: Find the radius of the third orbit of hydrogen and the electron's speed there, compared with the first orbit.
ex.a: r₃ = 4.77 Å; speed is one third of the first orbit's

topics.rl: Astronomers at Indian observatories such as Hanle and Devasthal still label hydrogen lines by Bohr's quantum numbers (for example the n = 3 to n = 2 line), and his model is the first quantum atom taught in every CBSE Class 12 classroom.

topics.h: An electron in hydrogen lives on an energy staircase. The bottom step is at -13.6 eV, and the steps crowd together as they climb towards zero.
p: Energy of the nth level of hydrogen: En = -13.6/n² eV. E₁ = -13.6 eV, E₂ = -3.4 eV, E₃ = -1.51 eV, E₄ = -0.85 eV, ... up to E∞ = 0.
n = 1 is the ground state; n ≥ 2 are excited states. The energy level diagram shows levels getting closer together as n increases.
Ionisation energy of hydrogen from the ground state = 13.6 eV. Excitation energy from n = 1 to n = 2 = 10.2 eV.
Energy needed to ionise from level n is 13.6/n² eV. Above E = 0 the electron is free and can have any (continuous) energy.
The Franck-Hertz experiment (1914) gave direct evidence for discrete energy levels: electrons colliding with mercury atoms lost energy only in definite amounts.

ex.q: How much energy is needed to ionise a hydrogen atom from the n = 3 state?

topics.rl: The plasma physicists at the Institute for Plasma Research, Gandhinagar, study hydrogen at temperatures where atoms are ionised, i.e. electrons have been pushed above the E = 0 level.

topics.h: Every line in the hydrogen spectrum is an electron jumping down the energy staircase and throwing off a photon whose energy matches the drop.
p: A spectral line arises when an electron jumps from a higher level ni to a lower level nf, emitting a photon of energy hν = Ei - Ef.
ν = (13.6 eV/h)(1/nf² - 1/ni²), or 1/λ = R(1/nf² - 1/ni²), where R ≈ 1.097 × 10⁷ m⁻¹ is the Rydberg constant.
Absorption lines correspond to the same energy differences in reverse (nf → ni upward).
A transition from n = 3 to n = 2 gives a red line near 656 nm; transitions ending on n = 1 give ultraviolet lines.
Handy shortcut: λ (in nm) = 1240/ΔE (in eV).

ex.q: Find the wavelength of the photon emitted when hydrogen's electron falls from n = 3 to n = 2. (hc = 1240 eV nm)

topics.rl: The pink-red glow of hydrogen in nebulae photographed by Indian astronomers at Hanle, Ladakh, comes from the n = 3 to n = 2 transition.

topics.t: Bohr's orbits as matter waves, and limits of the model
topics.h: Why should angular momentum come in multiples of h/2π? A decade after Bohr, de Broglie's matter waves gave a beautiful answer.
p: de Broglie's explanation: an electron in a Bohr orbit is a standing wave, like a vibrating string closed into a circle.
For a stable standing wave, the circumference must hold a whole number of wavelengths: 2πr = nλ.
With λ = h/(mv): 2πr = nh/(mv), so mvr = nh/2π, exactly Bohr's quantisation condition.

Limitations of Bohr's model: it works only for hydrogen-like atoms (one electron, such as He⁺ and Li²⁺); it cannot explain the relative intensities of spectral lines or the spectra of many-electron atoms.
Problem toolkit: rn ∝ n², vn ∝ 1/n, En ∝ -1/n²; number of spectral lines from level n down to ground state = n(n - 1)/2.

ex.q: An electron in hydrogen is excited to n = 4. How many different spectral lines can be emitted as it returns to the ground state?

topics.rl: Guitar and sitar strings vibrate only at frequencies that fit whole numbers of half-wavelengths on them; de Broglie pictured electrons in atoms the same way.

topics.h: If an atom were the size of a cricket stadium, its nucleus would be a small marble at the centre spot, yet the marble would hold almost all of the stadium's mass.
p: The nucleus is about 10⁴ times smaller than the atom (radius ~10⁻¹⁴ m versus ~10⁻¹⁰ m), but contains more than 99.9% of the atom's mass.
Questions for this chapter: what is a nucleus made of, how big and heavy is it, what holds it together, and how can nuclear energy be released?
Atomic mass unit: 1 u = 1/12 of the mass of one carbon-12 atom = 1.660539 × 10⁻²⁷ kg (≈ 1.66 × 10⁻²⁷ kg).
Atomic masses are measured precisely with a mass spectrometer.
Non-integral atomic masses arise from isotopes. Chlorine is about 75.4% ³⁵Cl and 24.6% ³⁷Cl, so its average atomic mass is about 35.47 u.

ex.q: Find the average atomic mass of chlorine from 75.4% of mass 34.98 u and 24.6% of mass 36.98 u.

topics.rl: Nuclear scientists at the Bhabha Atomic Research Centre (BARC), Mumbai, use mass spectrometers to measure isotope ratios in uranium fuel for India's reactors.

topics.h: For years, physicists puzzled over why nuclei were heavier than their protons alone. In 1932, James Chadwick found the missing piece: the neutron.
p: The proton is the nucleus of a hydrogen atom, with charge +e and mass about 1.00728 u.

The neutron was discovered by James Chadwick (1932) when beryllium was bombarded with alpha particles and gave out neutral, penetrating radiation. Its mass is about 1.00866 u, slightly more than the proton's.
A nucleus has Z protons (atomic number) and N neutrons; the mass number A = Z + N is the total number of nucleons. It is written ᴬ_Z X (for example ¹⁹⁷₇₉Au).
Isotopes: same Z, different A (¹H, ²H, ³H). Isobars: same A, different Z (³H and ³He). Isotones: same N, different Z (¹⁹⁸₈₀Hg and ¹⁹⁷₇₉Au, both N = 118).
A free neutron is unstable (it decays into a proton, an electron and an antineutrino), but it is stable inside many nuclei.

ex.q: How many protons, neutrons and nucleons does ²³⁸₉₂U have?

topics.rl: India's three-stage nuclear programme, planned by Homi Bhabha, uses isotopes of uranium and thorium: natural uranium first, then plutonium, and finally thorium-232, which India has in large reserves.

topics.t: Size of the nucleus and nuclear density
topics.h: A teaspoon of nuclear matter would weigh about a billion tonnes. That is the density of a nucleus, and of a neutron star.
p: From scattering experiments: nuclear radius R = R₀A^(1/3), with R₀ ≈ 1.2 fm (1 fm = 10⁻¹⁵ m).
So nuclear volume (4/3)πR³ ∝ A: each nucleon occupies about the same volume.
Nuclear density = mass/volume ≈ (A × 1.66 × 10⁻²⁷)/((4/3)πR₀³A) is independent of A, about 2.3 × 10¹⁷ kg m⁻³.
This is roughly 10¹⁴ times the density of ordinary matter (water is 10³ kg m⁻³).
Neutron stars are giant 'nuclei' with roughly this density.

ex.q: Find the ratio of the radius of a nucleus with A = 125 to that of a nucleus with A = 8.

topics.rl: Astrophysicists at India's Inter-University Centre for Astronomy and Astrophysics in Pune study neutron stars, whose density matches that of nuclear matter.

topics.h: Weigh a helium nucleus precisely and you find it lighter than the two protons and two neutrons that make it. The 'missing' mass became binding energy.
p: Einstein's mass-energy equivalence: E = mc². Mass and energy can be converted into each other.
1 u of mass is equivalent to 931.5 MeV of energy. One gram of matter is equivalent to 10⁻³ × (3 × 10⁸)² = 9 × 10¹³ J.
Mass defect: ΔM = [Zmp + (A - Z)mn] - M, the difference between the total mass of free nucleons and the mass M of the nucleus.
Binding energy Eb = ΔMc²: the energy needed to break the nucleus completely into separate protons and neutrons (or the energy released when they come together).
With atomic masses: ΔM = Z m(¹H) + N mn - m(atom), since electron masses cancel.

ex.q: Find the binding energy of a deuteron. m(¹H) = 1.007825 u, mn = 1.008665 u, m(²H) = 2.014102 u. (1 u = 931.5 MeV)

topics.rl: At the Kudankulam nuclear plant in Tamil Nadu, a tiny loss of mass in each uranium fission becomes the energy that generates electricity for millions of homes.

topics.t: Binding energy per nucleon and nuclear stability
topics.h: Plot how tightly each nucleon is held across the periodic table and you get a hill with iron at the summit. Both nuclear power and the Sun's power slide towards that summit.
p: Binding energy per nucleon Ebn = Eb/A measures how tightly a nucleus is bound; larger Ebn means a more stable nucleus.
Ebn versus A curve: it rises steeply for light nuclei, is nearly constant around 8 MeV for 30 < A < 170, peaks near A = 56 (about 8.75 MeV, iron), and falls to about 7.6 MeV for A = 238 (uranium).
The nearly constant Ebn shows the nuclear force is short-range and saturates: each nucleon binds only to its close neighbours.
Heavy nuclei (A > 170) can release energy by splitting into medium nuclei (fission); light nuclei (A < 30) by combining (fusion). In both, Ebn increases.
Example: ¹⁶O with ΔM = 0.13708 u has Eb ≈ 127.7 MeV and Ebn ≈ 7.98 MeV.

ex.q: ⁵⁶Fe has a binding energy of about 492 MeV. Find its binding energy per nucleon.

topics.rl: India's long-term fusion research at the Institute for Plasma Research and its role in ITER aim to harness the steep rise of the binding energy curve for light nuclei.

topics.h: Protons in a nucleus are pushed apart by enormous electrical repulsion. Something far stronger glues them together, but only over incredibly tiny distances.
p: The nuclear force binds nucleons together; within its range it is much stronger than the Coulomb repulsion between protons (and vastly stronger than gravity).

It is short-range: strongly attractive at separations of a few femtometres, falling rapidly to zero beyond that. It becomes strongly repulsive when nucleons come closer than about 0.8 fm, which stops the nucleus from collapsing.
It is nearly charge independent: the n-n, n-p and p-p nuclear forces are almost equal.
The potential energy versus separation graph has a minimum near 0.8 fm; to the right the force is attractive, to the left repulsive.
It has no simple formula like Coulomb's law.

ex.q: Two protons are 1 fm apart. Which forces act between them, and which wins?
st: Nuclear force at 1 fm: strongly attractive
The nuclear force is much stronger at this distance
ex.a: The nuclear attraction wins over the Coulomb repulsion

topics.rl: Kamini, a small research reactor at Kalpakkam, uses uranium-233 made from thorium. Its operation depends on the short-range nuclear force that binds and splits nuclei.

topics.h: Burning a kilogram of coal gives about 3 × 10⁷ J. Fissioning a kilogram of uranium-235 gives about 8 × 10¹³ J, millions of times more.
p: Energy is released whenever nuclei rearrange into products with higher binding energy per nucleon.
Chemical reactions release a few eV per reaction (electrons rearranging); nuclear reactions release MeV per reaction, about a million times more.
Fission: a slow neutron is absorbed by ²³⁵U, forming unstable ²³⁶U, which splits into two medium-mass nuclei plus 2 or 3 neutrons, for example ²³⁵U + n → ¹⁴⁴Ba + ⁸⁹Kr + 3n.
Each fission releases about 200 MeV, mostly as kinetic energy of the fragments.
Chain reaction: neutrons from one fission can cause more fissions. Controlled in reactors (power), uncontrolled in a bomb.

ex.q: Estimate the energy released per nucleon in fission. Heavy nucleus Ebn ≈ 7.6 MeV, products Ebn ≈ 8.5 MeV.

topics.rl: Tarapur in Maharashtra, India's first nuclear power station (1969), and later plants like Kaiga and Rawatbhata use controlled chain reactions of uranium fission to produce electricity.

topics.h: Every second, the Sun turns about 600 million tonnes of hydrogen into helium. The 'missing' mass becomes the sunlight that warms the Indian monsoon.
p: Fusion: light nuclei combine into a heavier nucleus, releasing energy (for example ²H + ²H → ³He + n + 3.27 MeV).
Nuclei must come very close despite Coulomb repulsion, which needs extremely high temperatures (millions of kelvin). Hence 'thermonuclear' fusion.
In stars like the Sun, the proton-proton cycle converts four protons into one helium-4 nucleus (plus positrons, neutrinos and energy), releasing about 26.7 MeV in total.

Controlled fusion on Earth needs a very hot plasma confined (for example by magnetic fields) long enough; this is very hard. ITER, an international project in France in which India is a partner, is developing a fusion reactor.
Q-value of a reaction: Q = (total initial mass - total final mass) × c² (using 931.5 MeV per u). Q > 0 means energy is released.

ex.q: Find the Q-value of ²H + ²H → ³He + n. m(²H) = 2.014102 u, m(³He) = 3.016029 u, mn = 1.008665 u.

topics.rl: India is a full member of ITER and supplies major in-kind components, such as the giant cryostat (the huge steel vessel around the reactor), whose sections were made in India and then assembled at the ITER site in France.

topics.ch: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
topics.h: The first computers filled whole rooms with glowing vacuum tubes. Today, a phone made in Noida packs billions of semiconductor devices into a chip smaller than a fingernail.
p: Early electronics used vacuum tubes (valves) such as the vacuum diode and triode, in which electrons flowed through vacuum from a heated cathode.
Semiconductor (solid-state) devices replaced them: they are small, use little power, run at low voltages, are reliable and long-lived, and need no heated filament.
Classification by resistivity ρ: metals (10⁻² to 10⁻⁸ Ω m), semiconductors (10⁻⁵ to 10⁶ Ω m) and insulators (10¹¹ to 10¹⁹ Ω m).
Elemental semiconductors: silicon (Si) and germanium (Ge).
Compound semiconductors: inorganic ones like GaAs, CdS, CdSe, InP, and organic ones like anthracene and conducting polymers.

ex.q: A material has a resistivity of 10² Ω m. Classify it.
st: 10² Ω m lies in the semiconductor range (10⁻⁵ to 10⁶ Ω m)

topics.rl: India's Semiconductor Mission is setting up chip fabrication and assembly units in Gujarat and Assam, building on the solid-state revolution that began with the transistor.

topics.ch: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
topics.h: A single atom has sharp energy levels. Pack billions of atoms into a crystal and those levels smear into bands. The gap between bands decides whether a solid conducts.
p: In a crystal, the energy levels of neighbouring atoms overlap and split into many closely spaced levels, forming energy bands.
The valence band holds the valence electrons; the conduction band above it is where electrons can move freely. Between them is the forbidden energy gap Eg.
Metals: the conduction band is partly filled, or the valence and conduction bands overlap, so electrons move easily.
Insulators: Eg is large (more than about 3 eV), so almost no electrons reach the conduction band.
Semiconductors: Eg is small (Si about 1.1 eV, Ge about 0.7 eV), so at room temperature some electrons jump across and conduct.

ex.q: Silicon has Eg ≈ 1.1 eV and diamond Eg ≈ 6 eV (much more than 3 eV). Which conducts at room temperature?
st: Room-temperature thermal energy can lift a few electrons across a 1.1 eV gap.
It cannot bridge a 6 eV gap.
So silicon conducts a little; diamond acts as an insulator.
ex.a: Silicon (a semiconductor); diamond is an insulator

topics.rl: Solar cells on rooftops in Rajasthan use silicon because its band gap of about 1.1 eV lets sunlight photons lift electrons into the conduction band.

topics.ch: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
topics.h: A perfect, pure silicon crystal is nearly an insulator when cold. Warm it up and it starts conducting with two kinds of charge carriers, one of which is just an empty space.
p: In Si and Ge, each atom forms four covalent bonds with its four neighbours, sharing electron pairs in a tetrahedral lattice.
Thermal energy breaks some bonds: each freed electron leaves behind a vacancy called a hole, which behaves like a positive charge +e. Electrons and holes are created in pairs.
In a pure (intrinsic) semiconductor, the number density of free electrons equals that of holes: ne = nh = ni.
Under an applied field, electrons move one way and holes the other; the total current I = Ie + Ih.
At 0 K all bonds are intact and the semiconductor is an insulator. As temperature rises, more pairs form and conductivity increases.

ex.q: A pure germanium sample has ni = 2.4 × 10¹⁹ m⁻³ at room temperature. What are ne and nh?
st: In an intrinsic semiconductor, ne = nh = ni

topics.rl: Silicon wafers for chips are refined to extreme purity, better than 99.9999999%, so that their electrical behaviour starts from the intrinsic state before controlled doping.

topics.ch: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
topics.h: Add just one impurity atom per million silicon atoms and the conductivity jumps enormously. This deliberate 'impurity' is called doping.
p: Doping: adding a tiny, controlled amount of impurity to a pure semiconductor to increase its conductivity. The dopant atoms replace some Si or Ge atoms.

n-type: doping with a pentavalent element (arsenic As, phosphorus P, antimony Sb). Four electrons bond; the fifth is loosely held and easily freed. These donors give extra electrons, which are majority carriers; holes are minority carriers.
p-type: doping with a trivalent element (indium In, boron B, aluminium Al). One bond is incomplete, creating a hole. These acceptors give holes as majority carriers; electrons are minority carriers.

Band picture: donor levels lie just below the conduction band, so donated electrons easily jump up. Acceptor levels lie just above the valence band, so valence electrons easily jump into them, leaving holes.
A doped semiconductor as a whole remains electrically neutral.

ex.q: Silicon is doped with phosphorus. What type of semiconductor results, and what are its majority carriers?
st: Its fifth electron becomes free: a donor.
n-type, with electrons as majority carriers.

topics.rl: The solar cells being made by Indian manufacturers in Gujarat and Tamil Nadu use phosphorus-doped (n-type) and boron-doped (p-type) silicon layers.

topics.ch: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
topics.t: Carrier concentrations and the mass action law
topics.h: Doping silicon with donors floods it with electrons, and something surprising happens: the number of holes drops dramatically.
p: Law of mass action: in thermal equilibrium, ne × nh = ni², for intrinsic and doped semiconductors alike.
In n-type material with donor density ND (all ionised): ne ≈ ND and nh = ni²/ND, which is far smaller.
In p-type material with acceptor density NA: nh ≈ NA and ne = ni²/NA.
Adding donors increases electrons and reduces holes, because extra electrons recombine with holes.

Problem tips: identify majority carriers from the dopant, use mass action for minority carriers, recall band gaps (Si 1.1 eV, Ge 0.7 eV), and remember a full-wave rectifier doubles the output frequency.

ex.q: Silicon (ni = 1.5 × 10¹⁶ m⁻³) is doped with 9 × 10²² m⁻³ arsenic atoms. Find ne and nh.
st: Arsenic is a donor, so ne ≈ ND = 9 × 10²² m⁻³

topics.rl: Chip designers in Bengaluru's semiconductor design centres use the mass action law in simulation tools to set doping levels for transistors with billions of copies on a chip.

topics.ch: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
topics.h: Join p-type and n-type silicon and, in a microsecond, a thin barrier builds itself at the boundary. That barrier is what makes diodes, LEDs and solar cells work.
p: Formation: at the junction, electrons diffuse from the n-side (high concentration) to the p-side, and holes diffuse from p to n. This diffusion current flows from p to n.
Electrons leaving the n-side expose positive donor ions; holes leaving the p-side expose negative acceptor ions. These immobile ions form the depletion region, which has no free carriers.
The ions create an electric field (from n to p) that drives minority carriers across the junction: the drift current, opposite to diffusion current.
In equilibrium, diffusion current = drift current, so there is no net current.
The potential difference across the depletion region is the barrier potential: about 0.7 V for Si and 0.2 V for Ge (ignoring small variations).

ex.q: Why is there no net current across an unbiased p-n junction?
st: Diffusion of majority carriers gives a current from p to n.
The junction field drives a drift current of minority carriers from n to p.
In equilibrium the two are equal and opposite.
ex.a: Diffusion and drift currents balance each other

topics.rl: Every LED street light installed under India's Street Lighting National Programme has a p-n junction at its heart.

topics.ch: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
topics.h: A diode is a one-way street for current. Push it the right way and current flows easily; push the wrong way and almost nothing gets through.
p: Diode symbol: an arrow (triangle) with a bar. The p-side is the anode, the n-side the cathode; the arrow shows the direction of conventional current in forward bias.

Forward bias: p connected to the positive terminal. The applied voltage opposes the barrier, the depletion layer narrows, and once V exceeds the threshold (cut-in or knee) voltage, about 0.7 V for Si and 0.2 V for Ge, current rises sharply (milliamperes).

Reverse bias: p connected to the negative terminal. The barrier rises, the depletion layer widens, and only a tiny reverse saturation current (microamperes) flows, due to minority carriers. It hardly changes with voltage.
Reverse breakdown: at a large reverse voltage the reverse current suddenly increases sharply.
So a diode conducts well in one direction only.

ex.q: A silicon diode is connected with its p-side to the positive terminal of a 3 V battery through a resistor. Is it forward or reverse biased, and does it conduct?
st: p-side to positive means forward bias.
3 V exceeds the cut-in voltage (~0.7 V).

topics.rl: Phone chargers sold across India contain diodes that let current through only one way; that is how they turn the AC from the wall socket into the DC a battery needs.

topics.ch: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
topics.h: Plot current against voltage for a diode and you get a curve that hugs zero, then shoots up like a hockey stick. Its slope tells you the diode's resistance.
p: Experiment: the diode is connected to a variable DC supply with a milliammeter and voltmeter for forward bias; for reverse bias, a microammeter is used and the supply reversed. Use a series resistor to protect the diode.
