Forward characteristic: very small current up to the threshold voltage, then a steep, non-linear rise.
Reverse characteristic: a tiny, nearly constant current (µA) until breakdown.
Dynamic resistance rd = ΔV/ΔI, the inverse slope of the V-I curve at a point. It is small in forward bias above threshold and very large in reverse bias.
Lab safety: never exceed the diode's rated current; a small series resistor prevents overheating, and switch off before rewiring.

ex.q: On a diode's forward curve, current rises from 10 mA to 30 mA when voltage rises from 0.7 V to 0.8 V. Find rd.

topics.rl: Electronics labs in Indian polytechnics and engineering colleges still have students trace diode V-I curves by hand, a rite of passage for future engineers.

topics.ch: Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits
topics.h: Your phone battery needs DC, but the socket gives AC. Inside the charger, diodes chop and flip the AC into one-way pulses, then a capacitor smooths them out.
p: Rectification: converting AC into DC using the one-way conduction of diodes.

Half-wave rectifier: one diode in series with the load. It conducts only in the half-cycles when it is forward biased, so the output is pulsating DC with alternate half-cycles missing. Output frequency = input frequency.
Full-wave rectifier: a centre-tap transformer with two diodes. Each diode conducts in alternate half-cycles, sending current through the load in the same direction both times.
The full-wave output has twice the input frequency (100 Hz for 50 Hz mains) and is more efficient.

Filter: a capacitor across the load (capacitor-input filter) charges during each peak and discharges slowly between peaks, smoothing the output. A larger C and larger load resistance RL give smaller ripple.

ex.q: A full-wave rectifier works on 50 Hz mains. What is the output frequency, and why?
st: Each half-cycle produces one output pulse.
So the output frequency is 100 Hz.

topics.rl: The adaptors that power Wi-Fi routers and set-top boxes in Indian homes contain full-wave rectifiers with capacitor filters, turning 230 V, 50 Hz AC into steady low-voltage DC.

qa.q: A glass rod rubbed with silk acquires a positive charge. What happened at the microscopic level?
qa.a: Electrons moved from the glass to the silk
qa.e: In charging by friction, only electrons are transferred. Glass loses electrons and is left with a net positive charge.

qa.q: Which statement about the two kinds of charge is correct?
qa.a: Like charges repel and unlike charges attract
qa.e: This is the basic experimental fact behind the two-charge model.

qa.q: A plastic rod rubbed with fur becomes negatively charged. The fur becomes
qa.a: positively charged, with the same magnitude of charge
qa.e: Electrons transferred to the rod come from the fur, so the fur is left with an equal positive charge.

qa.q: Electrostatics is the branch of physics that studies
qa.a: forces, fields and potentials of charges at rest
qa.e: Static means at rest; electrostatics deals with stationary charges.

qa.q: A rubbed balloon sticks to a wall. Which everyday effect is of the same kind?
qa.a: A comb run through dry hair attracting bits of paper
qa.e: Both are static electricity effects from charges produced by friction.

qa.q: Assertion (A): A body becomes negatively charged when it gains electrons. Reason (R): An electron carries a negative charge. Choose the correct option.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
qa.e: Gaining extra negatively charged electrons gives the body a net negative charge, so R directly explains A.

qa.q: Two charged bodies X and Y repel each other. X attracts a third body Z, which is positively charged. What is the charge on Y?
qa.e: X attracts positive Z, so X is negative. Y repels X, so Y has the same sign as X: negative.

qa.q: Why do you get a small shock when touching a metal door handle after walking on a nylon carpet in dry weather?
qa.a: Your body gathers charge by friction and discharges through the handle
qa.e: Friction between shoes and carpet transfers electrons; touching a conductor lets the charge rush out as a small spark. Dry air lets charge build up instead of leaking away.

qa.q: Which of these allows electric charge to move through it most easily?
qa.e: Metals have many free electrons, so they are good conductors.

qa.q: A charged gold-leaf electroscope has diverged leaves. What happens if you touch its cap with your finger?
qa.e: Your body is a conductor, so the charge flows to the earth and the leaves close.

qa.q: Why do the leaves of a gold-leaf electroscope diverge when a charged rod touches the cap?
qa.a: Both leaves get the same kind of charge and repel
qa.e: The charge spreads to both leaves, giving them like charges, so they repel.

qa.q: A metal sphere and a glass sphere are both given some charge at one spot. Which statement is correct?
qa.a: Charge spreads over the metal surface but stays at the spot on the glass
qa.e: In a conductor charges move freely and spread over the surface; in an insulator they cannot move.

qa.q: Which material is a semiconductor?
qa.e: Germanium, like silicon, conducts better than insulators but much worse than metals.

qa.q: When is it reasonable to treat a charged body as a point charge?
qa.a: When its size is very small compared with the distances being considered
qa.e: A point charge is an idealisation; it works when the body's size is negligible compared with separations.

qa.q: Assertion (A): A metal rod held in the hand cannot be charged by rubbing. Reason (R): The human body and the earth are conductors. Choose the correct option.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
qa.e: Charge produced on the metal leaks through the conducting body to earth, so the rod does not stay charged.

qa.q: A gold-leaf electroscope is mainly used to
qa.a: detect the presence of charge on a body
qa.e: Divergence of the leaves shows the presence of charge.

qa.q: Three charges +4 µC, -7 µC and +1 µC are placed in a box. What is the total charge in the box (in µC)?
qa.e: Charge is additive and scalar, so add with signs: 4 - 7 + 1 = -2 µC.

qa.q: How many electrons make up a charge of -8 × 10⁻¹⁸ C? (e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)
Which of these cannot be the charge on an isolated body? (e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)
qa.e: 2.4 × 10⁻¹⁹ C is 1.5e, not a whole-number multiple of e, so it breaks quantisation.

qa.q: A current of electrons removes 10¹² electrons per second from a neutral body. How long (in seconds) will it take for the body to gain a charge of +1.6 µC? (e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)
qa.e: Charge gained per second = 10¹² × 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 1.6 × 10⁻⁷ C. Time = 1.6 × 10⁻⁶ / 1.6 × 10⁻⁷ = 10 s.

qa.q: In the decay of a free neutron, it changes into a proton, an electron and an antineutrino. Which property of charge does this obey?
qa.e: The total charge before (zero) equals the total after: +e - e + 0 = 0.

qa.q: Why is quantisation of charge ignored when we deal with charges of a few microcoulombs?
qa.a: Each microcoulomb contains about 10¹³ electronic charges, so charge looks continuous
qa.e: Steps of 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C are far too small to notice in a total of 10⁻⁶ C.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Charge is a scalar quantity. Reason (R): Charges add algebraically, taking their signs into account, not by direction. Choose the correct option.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
qa.e: Signs on charge mean positive or negative, not direction; addition is algebraic, so charge is a scalar.

qa.q: A neutral comb gains 5 × 10¹² electrons when it is run through hair. What is its charge, in µC? (e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)
qa.e: q = -ne = -5 × 10¹² × 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ = -8 × 10⁻⁷ C = -0.8 µC. It is negative because electrons were gained.

qa.q: Two point charges of +4 µC and +5 µC are placed 20 cm apart in air. What is the force between them (in N)? (k = 9 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻²)
The force between two point charges is F. If the distance between them is tripled, the new force is
qa.e: F ∝ 1/r². Tripling r divides F by 3² = 9.

qa.q: The force between two charges is 12 N. Each charge is doubled and the distance is also doubled. What is the new force (in N)?
qa.e: F ∝ q₁q₂/r²: (2 × 2)/2² = 1, so the force is unchanged.

qa.q: Two equal charges q placed 1 m apart in vacuum repel with a force of 9 × 10⁹ N. What is q (in C)?
qa.e: F = kq²/r² gives 9 × 10⁹ = 9 × 10⁹ q²/1, so q = 1 C. This is how 1 coulomb is defined from Coulomb's law.

qa.q: In the vector form F₂₁ = k q₁q₂ r̂₂₁/r², what does a negative value of q₁q₂ mean?
qa.a: The force on q₂ points towards q₁ (attraction)
qa.e: r̂₂₁ points from q₁ to q₂. A negative product reverses it, so q₂ is pulled towards q₁.

qa.q: Two small charged spheres attract with a force of 0.8 N. They are moved so the separation becomes half. What is the new force (in N)?
qa.e: Halving r makes F four times larger: 4 × 0.8 = 3.2 N.

qa.q: What is the SI unit of ε₀, the permittivity of free space?
qa.e: From F = q₁q₂/(4πε₀r²), ε₀ = q₁q₂/(4πFr²), giving C²/(N m²).

qa.q: Point charges +2 µC and -8 µC are 3 m apart in air. What is the magnitude of the force between them (in mN)?
qa.e: F = 9 × 10⁹ × 2 × 10⁻⁶ × 8 × 10⁻⁶ / 9 = 1.6 × 10⁻² N = 16 mN, and it is attractive.

qa.q: Roughly how many times stronger is the electric force than the gravitational force between an electron and a proton?
qa.e: Fe/Fg = ke²/(Gmₑmₚ) ≈ 2.4 × 10³⁹.

qa.q: Why does the ratio of electric to gravitational force between an electron and a proton not depend on their separation?
qa.a: Both forces vary as 1/r², so r cancels in the ratio
qa.e: The two inverse-square laws have the same r² factor, which cancels.

qa.q: Equal charges of +2 µC sit at the corners of a regular hexagon. What is the net force on a charge of 1 µC at its centre (in N)?
qa.e: Charges at opposite corners are equidistant and push in opposite directions, so all forces cancel in pairs.

qa.q: Charges of +1 µC each sit at two corners of an equilateral triangle of side 30 cm. What is the magnitude of the net force on a +1 µC charge at the third corner (in N)? (k = 9 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻²; take √3 = 1.73)
qa.e: Each force is F = 9 × 10⁹ × 10⁻¹²/0.09 = 0.1 N. The angle between them is 60°, so the resultant is 2F cos 30° = √3F = 0.173 N.

qa.q: The superposition principle states that the force on a charge due to a group of charges is
qa.a: the vector sum of the individual forces from each charge
qa.e: Each charge acts independently, and forces add as vectors.

qa.q: Charges +q are at all four corners of a square, and a charge Q is at the centre. One corner charge is now replaced by -q. The net force on Q is due effectively to
qa.a: two charges of +q and -q at the same diagonal, so it points along that diagonal
qa.e: The two untouched corners on the other diagonal still cancel. On the changed diagonal, +q and -q both push Q (if positive) towards the -q corner, so the force is along that diagonal.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Gravitational force dominates the motion of planets even though electric force is much stronger. Reason (R): Planets are almost electrically neutral. Choose the correct option.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
qa.e: With nearly equal positive and negative charge, electric forces cancel on large bodies, while gravity always adds up.

qa.q: Three charges +q, +q and +q are placed at the corners of an equilateral triangle. The force on each charge is directed
qa.a: along the line from the centroid through that charge, away from the centre
qa.e: Two equal repulsive forces 60° apart add along their bisector, which points outward from the centroid through that corner.

qa.q: What is the magnitude of the electric field 30 cm from a point charge of 2 µC in air (in N C⁻¹)? (k = 9 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻²)
A charge of 5 µC placed at a point experiences a force of 0.02 N. What is the electric field there (in N C⁻¹)?
The test charge used to measure E at a point is doubled. The measured electric field
qa.e: Force doubles but E = F/q₀ does not change; the field is a property of the source.

qa.q: An electron and a proton are released from rest in the same uniform electric field and travel the same distance. Which statement is correct?
qa.a: The electron takes much less time because its acceleration eE/m is much larger
qa.e: Equal force eE acts on both, but the electron's mass is about 1/1836 of the proton's, so its acceleration is far greater and t = √(2d/a) is smaller.

qa.q: An electron is released from rest in a uniform field of 2 × 10⁴ N C⁻¹. What is the magnitude of its acceleration (in units of 10¹⁵ m s⁻²)? (e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, mₑ = 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg; give to 2 decimal places)
Which statement best describes the physical significance of the electric field?
qa.a: It conveys the interaction between charges and, for changing charges, travels at finite speed carrying energy
qa.e: For time-dependent sources the field changes propagate at the speed of light and carry energy, so the field is physically real.

qa.q: The direction of the electric field due to an isolated negative point charge is
qa.e: E points along the force on a positive test charge, which is attracted toward a negative charge.

qa.q: At a distance r from a point charge the field is 800 N C⁻¹. What is the field at 2r (in N C⁻¹)?
qa.e: E ∝ 1/r², so doubling r divides E by 4: 800/4 = 200 N C⁻¹.

qa.q: Charges +9 µC and +1 µC are placed 4 m apart. At what distance from the 9 µC charge (in m) is the net electric field zero?
qa.e: 9/x² = 1/(4 - x)² gives 3/x = 1/(4 - x), so 12 - 3x = x and x = 3 m.

qa.q: Why can two electric field lines never intersect?
qa.a: At the crossing point the field would have two directions, which is impossible
qa.e: E has a single definite direction at each point, given by the tangent to the line.

qa.q: Electrostatic field lines
qa.a: begin on positive charges and end on negative charges
qa.e: They are continuous curves from + to - (or to and from infinity); no closed loops in electrostatics.

qa.q: Charges +2 µC and -2 µC are 2 m apart. What is the magnitude of the electric field at the midpoint (in N C⁻¹)? (k = 9 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻²)
qa.e: Each field at 1 m is 9 × 10⁹ × 2 × 10⁻⁶ = 18000 N C⁻¹, and both point towards the negative charge, so they add to 36000 N C⁻¹.

qa.q: In a field line diagram, the field is weaker where the lines are
qa.e: Density of lines is proportional to field strength.

qa.q: For two equal positive charges, the field lines near the midpoint between them
qa.a: bend away so that no line passes through the midpoint, which is a neutral point
qa.e: Lines from like charges repel each other's pattern; the fields cancel at the midpoint.

qa.q: Charges +q and +4q are a distance d apart. Where is the neutral point?
qa.a: At d/3 from +q, between the charges
qa.e: q/x² = 4q/(d - x)² gives d - x = 2x, so x = d/3 from the smaller charge.

qa.q: The electric field due to a system of point charges at a point is found by
qa.a: adding the fields of each charge as vectors
qa.e: Superposition applies to fields just as to forces.

qa.q: A uniform field of 300 N C⁻¹ passes through a flat surface of area 0.2 m² whose normal is along the field. What is the flux (in N m² C⁻¹)?
The same surface is turned so that its plane is parallel to the field. The flux is now (in N m² C⁻¹)
qa.e: If the plane is parallel to E, the normal is at 90° to E and cos 90° = 0.

qa.q: A field E = 100 N C⁻¹ makes an angle of 60° with the normal of a 0.4 m² surface. What is the flux (in N m² C⁻¹)?
Which is a correct SI unit of electric flux?
qa.e: φ = E × area, so units are (N C⁻¹)(m²).

qa.q: Why do the field lines of a point charge thin out as 1/r²?
qa.a: A fixed number of lines spreads over sphere areas that grow as 4πr²
qa.e: The total number of lines through any sphere around the charge is the same, but the area grows as r².

qa.q: For a closed surface, an electric field line entering the surface contributes
qa.a: negative flux, since the outward normal is opposite to the field
qa.e: Outward normals are positive by convention, so incoming field gives cos θ < 0.

qa.q: A square sheet of side 10 cm is held in a uniform field of 500 N C⁻¹ with its normal at 0° to the field. What is the flux through it (in N m² C⁻¹)?
Flux through a flat surface in a uniform field is maximum when
qa.a: the field is perpendicular to the surface (along its normal)
qa.e: cos θ is largest (1) when E is along the normal, i.e. perpendicular to the surface plane.

qa.q: Charges of ±4 µC are separated by 5 mm. What is the dipole moment (in units of 10⁻⁸ C m)?
A short dipole of moment 10⁻⁹ C m: what is the field on its axis at 0.1 m from the centre (in N C⁻¹)? (k = 9 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻²)
For the same dipole (p = 10⁻⁹ C m), what is the field at 0.1 m on the equatorial line (in N C⁻¹)?
qa.e: E = kp/r³ = 9 × 10⁹ × 10⁻⁹/10⁻³ = 9000 N C⁻¹, pointing opposite to p.

qa.q: The axial field of a short dipole at distance r is E. What is the axial field at distance 2r?
qa.e: Dipole field varies as 1/r³: (1/2)³ = 1/8.

qa.q: The direction of the electric dipole moment is
qa.a: from the negative charge to the positive charge
qa.e: This is the standard NCERT convention.

qa.q: Why does a dipole field fall off faster (1/r³) than a point-charge field (1/r²)?
qa.a: Far away, the fields of +q and -q nearly cancel, leaving a small difference
qa.e: The two charges are almost at the same place from far away; only their small separation leaves a net field.

qa.q: At a point on the equatorial plane of a dipole, the electric field is
qa.e: The components perpendicular to the axis cancel, and the remaining components point from + to - side, i.e. along -p.

qa.q: At the same large distance r, what is the ratio of axial field to equatorial field magnitude for a short dipole?
qa.e: 2kp/r³ ÷ kp/r³ = 2.

qa.q: A dipole with p = 2 × 10⁻⁸ C m is placed at 90° to a uniform field of 10⁵ N C⁻¹. What is the torque (in mN m)?
What is the net force on an electric dipole placed in a uniform electric field?
qa.e: The charges feel qE and -qE, which are equal and opposite.

qa.q: A dipole of moment 3 × 10⁻⁹ C m is at 30° to a field of 2 × 10⁴ N C⁻¹. What is the torque (in units of 10⁻⁵ N m)?
Which of these molecules has a permanent electric dipole moment?
qa.e: Water's bent shape puts its charge centres apart, so it is polar. CO₂ is linear and symmetric, so its moments cancel.

qa.q: Why does a charged comb attract small bits of neutral paper?
qa.a: It polarises the paper and the non-uniform field pulls the induced dipoles towards it
qa.e: Induced dipoles in a non-uniform field feel a net force towards the stronger field near the comb.

qa.q: The torque on a dipole in a uniform field is maximum when the angle between p and E is
qa.e: sin θ is largest at 90°.

qa.q: An ideal electric dipole is one in which
qa.a: the charges become infinite and the separation tends to zero, keeping p finite
qa.e: This limit gives a point dipole whose field formulas are exact at all r.

qa.q: Assertion (A): A dipole in a uniform field may rotate but does not move bodily. Reason (R): The two forces on it are equal and opposite but do not act along the same line. Choose the correct option.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
qa.e: Equal and opposite forces with different lines of action form a couple: zero net force but non-zero torque.

qa.q: A thin rod 50 cm long carries a uniform charge of 2 µC. What is its linear charge density (in µC m⁻¹)?
qa.e: λ = q/L = 2 µC/0.5 m = 4 µC m⁻¹.

qa.q: A charge of 17.708 nC lies inside a closed surface. What is the total flux through the surface (in N m² C⁻¹)? (ε₀ = 8.854 × 10⁻¹² C² N⁻¹ m⁻²)
A point charge sits at the centre of a sphere. If the radius of the sphere is doubled, the total flux through it
qa.e: Flux = q/ε₀ depends only on the enclosed charge.

qa.q: Gauss's law states that the total flux through a closed surface equals
qa.a: the net charge enclosed divided by ε₀
qa.e: φ = q_enc/ε₀ for any closed surface.

qa.q: A metal sheet of area 2 m² carries a uniform charge of 6 µC. What is its surface charge density (in µC m⁻²)?
qa.e: σ = q/A = 6/2 = 3 µC m⁻².

qa.q: In the proof of Gauss's law for a point charge at the centre of a sphere, why is E·dS simply E dS everywhere?
qa.a: The field is radial, so it is along the outward normal at every point of the sphere
qa.e: By symmetry E is radial and the sphere's normal is radial, so the angle between them is zero.

qa.q: Why can we use smooth charge densities even though charge is quantised?
qa.a: Small elements still contain huge numbers of charges, so averaging gives a smooth density
qa.e: Macroscopic averaging over regions large compared with atomic sizes hides the graininess.

qa.q: The field of a continuous charge distribution is found by
qa.a: dividing it into small elements dq and adding their fields as vectors (integration)
qa.e: Superposition extends to continuous charge by integration.

qa.q: A point charge of 6 µC is at the centre of a cube. What is the flux through one face, in terms of 1/ε₀ (in µC)?
qa.e: Total flux 6 µC/ε₀ divides equally among 6 faces: 1 µC/ε₀ each.

qa.q: A closed cylinder lies with its axis along a uniform electric field. The net flux through it is
qa.e: Flux enters one end and leaves the other; the curved surface has no flux; no charge is enclosed.

qa.q: The net outward flux through a closed box is 8000 N m² C⁻¹. What charge (in nC) is inside? (ε₀ = 8.854 × 10⁻¹² C² N⁻¹ m⁻²; give to 2 decimal places)
Charges +3 µC, -5 µC are inside a closed surface and +10 µC is outside. The net flux is (in µC/ε₀)
qa.e: Only enclosed charges count: 3 - 5 = -2 µC, so φ = -2 µC/ε₀.

qa.q: The net flux through a closed surface is zero. What can we conclude?
qa.a: The net charge enclosed is zero
qa.e: Zero flux means q_enc = 0; there may still be charges inside summing to zero, or charges outside.

qa.q: Why do we choose a cylindrical Gaussian surface for an infinitely long charged wire?
qa.a: The field is radial and has the same magnitude at equal distances, matching a cylinder's symmetry
qa.e: On the curved surface E is constant and along the normal; on the flat ends E is parallel to the surface, giving zero flux.

qa.q: A charge q is placed at one corner of a cube. What is the flux through the whole cube?
qa.e: Eight such cubes would surround the corner completely, so this cube gets one eighth of q/ε₀.

qa.q: A field E = 3x î N C⁻¹ (x in m) exists. A cube of side 1 m has faces at x = 1 m and x = 2 m. What is the net flux through it (in N m² C⁻¹)?
qa.e: Out through x = 2: 6 × 1 = 6; in through x = 1: 3 × 1 = 3. Net = 6 - 3 = 3 N m² C⁻¹. Other faces are parallel to E.

qa.q: A long straight wire has λ = 2 × 10⁻⁶ C m⁻¹. What is the field 10 cm from it (in N C⁻¹)? (1/4πε₀ = 9 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻²)
The field of an infinite line charge at 4 cm is 600 N C⁻¹. What is it at 12 cm (in N C⁻¹)?
qa.e: E ∝ 1/r for a line charge, so tripling r gives 600/3 = 200 N C⁻¹.

qa.q: An infinite plane sheet has σ = 17.708 × 10⁻¹² C m⁻². What is the field near it (in N C⁻¹)? (ε₀ = 8.854 × 10⁻¹² C² N⁻¹ m⁻²)
How does the field of an infinite plane sheet of charge change as you move away from it?
qa.e: E = σ/(2ε₀) has no r in it: the field lines are parallel.

qa.q: Two large parallel plates carry σ = +8.854 × 10⁻¹² C m⁻² and -8.854 × 10⁻¹² C m⁻². What is the field between them (in N C⁻¹)?
qa.e: Between the plates E = σ/ε₀ = 1 N C⁻¹.

qa.q: For the same pair of oppositely charged plates, what is the field outside them?
qa.e: Outside, the two sheet fields are equal and opposite, so they cancel.

qa.q: In deriving E for an infinite line charge, why is there no flux through the flat ends of the Gaussian cylinder?
qa.a: The radial field is parallel to the end faces, so E·dS = 0 there
qa.e: E is radial (perpendicular to the wire) and the end faces' normals are along the wire.

qa.q: Two infinite parallel sheets both carry the same positive σ. What is the field between them?
qa.e: Each sheet gives σ/2ε₀ pointing away from itself. Between them these point in opposite directions and cancel.

qa.q: A thin shell of radius 20 cm carries 4 nC. What is the field at 10 cm from its centre (in N C⁻¹)?
qa.e: 10 cm is inside the shell, where q_enc = 0, so E = 0.

qa.q: For the same shell (4 nC, radius 20 cm), what is the field at 60 cm from the centre (in N C⁻¹)?
The field just outside a charged conductor is 8.854 × 10⁵ N C⁻¹. What is the surface charge density (in µC m⁻²)? (ε₀ = 8.854 × 10⁻¹² C² N⁻¹ m⁻²)
A spherical conductor of radius 0.3 m has σ = 10⁻⁶ C m⁻². What is the field just outside it (in units of 10⁵ N C⁻¹)? (ε₀ = 8.854 × 10⁻¹² C² N⁻¹ m⁻²; give to 2 decimal places)
qa.e: E = σ/ε₀ = 10⁻⁶/8.854 × 10⁻¹² ≈ 1.13 × 10⁵ N C⁻¹. The radius is not needed.

qa.q: Which graph best describes E versus r for a charged thin spherical shell of radius R?
qa.a: Zero up to R, then a jump to a maximum at R, falling as 1/r² outside
qa.e: Inside E = 0; at R it jumps to kq/R²; outside it falls as 1/r².

qa.q: Why is the field outside a uniformly charged shell the same as that of a point charge at its centre?
qa.a: A concentric Gaussian sphere outside encloses the full charge q and has the same symmetry as a point charge
qa.e: Gauss's law with spherical symmetry gives E·4πr² = q/ε₀ exactly as for a point charge.

qa.q: A charged shell's field at its outer surface is E₀. What is the field at a distance 2R from the centre?
qa.e: E ∝ 1/r² outside; going from R to 2R divides by 4.

qa.q: A thin plastic (insulating) spherical shell carries charge spread uniformly over it. A small charged bead is held at rest inside it, not touching. The force on the bead due to the shell's charge is
qa.a: zero, because the field inside the shell is zero
qa.e: The uniformly spread charge on the shell produces no field anywhere inside it, so the bead feels no force from the shell.

qa.q: An external force does 4 × 10⁻⁴ J of work to bring a 2 µC charge slowly from infinity to a point. What is the potential there (in V)?
Why can electric potential energy be defined for electrostatic forces?
qa.a: Because the electrostatic force is conservative
qa.e: A conservative force does path-independent work, so U depends only on position.

qa.q: A charge is moved from A to B along three different paths. The work done by the electrostatic force is
qa.e: For a conservative force the work depends only on the end points.

qa.q: Why do we bring the test charge 'slowly' when defining potential?
qa.a: So that no kinetic energy is gained and all work goes into potential energy
qa.e: Moving it without acceleration means the external force just balances the electric force.

qa.q: The potential difference between two points is 12 V. How much work is done by an external agent in moving 3 C slowly from the lower to the higher potential (in J)?
Which of these is physically meaningful in electrostatics?
qa.a: The potential difference between two points
qa.e: Adding a constant to all potentials changes nothing physical; only differences matter.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The work done by an electrostatic field in moving a charge around a closed loop is zero. Reason (R): The electrostatic force is conservative. Choose the correct option.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
qa.e: For a conservative force, returning to the start means no net work.

qa.q: A charge of -2 µC is brought slowly from infinity to a point where V = 500 V. What work is done by the external agent (in mJ)?
qa.e: W = qV = -2 × 10⁻⁶ × 500 = -10⁻³ J = -1 mJ. The negative sign means the field pulls the charge in.

qa.q: What is the potential 30 cm from a point charge of 5 nC (in V)? (k = 9 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻²)
The potential at a distance r from a point charge is 60 V. What is it at 3r (in V)?
qa.e: V ∝ 1/r, so tripling r divides V by 3.

qa.q: How much work is needed to bring a charge of 3 µC from infinity to a point where V = 200 V (in mJ)?
Charges +4 nC and -2 nC are placed 6 cm apart. At what distance from the +4 nC charge, between them, is the potential zero (in cm)?
qa.e: 4/x = 2/(6 - x) gives 24 - 4x = 2x, so x = 4 cm.

qa.q: For the same pair (+4 nC and -2 nC, 6 cm apart), where is the second zero-potential point on the line?
qa.a: 12 cm from +4 nC, beyond the -2 nC charge
qa.e: Outside, beyond the smaller charge: 4/x = 2/(x - 6) gives x = 12 cm.

qa.q: Which statement about the potential due to a negative point charge is correct?
qa.a: It is negative and rises towards zero as r increases
qa.e: V = kQ/r with Q < 0 is negative and approaches 0 at infinity.

qa.q: The potential at the surface of a nucleus-like sphere of charge 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁸ C at r = 1.44 × 10⁻¹⁵ m is (in MV)? (k = 9 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻²)
1 volt is equivalent to
qa.e: V = W/q, so 1 V = 1 J C⁻¹.

qa.q: A short dipole has p = 2 × 10⁻⁹ C m. What is the potential on its axis 0.3 m away (in V)? (k = 9 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻²)
For the same dipole, what is the potential at the same distance on the equatorial plane (in V)?
Six charges of +1 nC each sit at the corners of a regular hexagon of side 0.1 m. What is the potential at the centre (in V)? (k = 9 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻²)
qa.e: Each corner is 0.1 m from the centre (hexagon side = circumradius). V = 6 × 9 × 10⁹ × 10⁻⁹/0.1 = 540 V.

qa.q: At the same large distance, how does the dipole potential at θ = 60° compare with that on the axis (θ = 0°)?
qa.e: V ∝ cos θ: cos 60° = 0.5 compared with cos 0° = 1.

qa.q: The potential of a dipole at an axial distance r is V. What is it at 2r on the axis?
qa.e: Dipole potential ∝ 1/r²: (1/2)² = 1/4.

qa.q: Charges +3 nC, -5 nC and +8 nC sit at the corners of an equilateral triangle; the centroid is 0.15 m from each. What is V at the centroid (in V)?
Why is it often easier to find the potential than the field due to several charges?
qa.a: Potential is a scalar, so contributions add algebraically
qa.e: No directions or components are needed for a scalar sum.

qa.q: Assertion (A): At points on the equatorial plane of a dipole, the potential is zero but the field is not. Reason (R): Potential is a scalar sum, while the field is a vector sum. Choose the correct option.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
qa.e: Equal and opposite potentials cancel as numbers; the fields' components along the axis add instead of cancelling.

qa.q: Equipotentials are 2 cm apart and differ by 4 V each in a uniform field. What is the field strength (in V m⁻¹)?
How much work is done in moving a 5 µC charge 3 m along an equipotential surface at 100 V (in J)?
qa.e: ΔV = 0 along an equipotential, so W = 0.

qa.q: The equipotential surfaces of an isolated point charge are
qa.a: concentric spheres centred on the charge
qa.e: V = kQ/r is constant where r is constant.

qa.q: In a region, V changes from 30 V to 10 V over 4 mm along x. What is the field along x (in V m⁻¹)?
qa.e: Ex = -dV/dx = -(10 - 30)/0.004 = +5000 V m⁻¹. The field points towards lower potential (+x).

qa.q: Why must the electric field be perpendicular to an equipotential surface?
qa.a: If E had a component along the surface, moving a charge along it would need work, contradicting constant V
qa.e: Zero work along the surface means zero field component along it.

qa.q: In the region where equipotentials are drawn closer together, the field is
qa.e: E = ΔV/Δl; smaller Δl for the same ΔV gives larger E.

qa.q: For a uniform field along +x, the equipotential surfaces are
qa.a: planes parallel to the y-z plane
qa.e: They must be perpendicular to E, i.e., perpendicular to x.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Two equipotential surfaces never intersect. Reason (R): At an intersection point, the potential would have two different values. Choose the correct option.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
qa.e: Potential at a point has a single value, so two different equipotentials cannot share a point.

qa.q: What is the potential energy of two charges of +2 µC and +3 µC placed 0.6 m apart (in J)? (k = 9 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻²)
A proton and an electron are 0.53 × 10⁻¹⁰ m apart. What is the sign of their electrostatic potential energy?
qa.e: q₁q₂ = (+e)(-e) < 0, so U < 0: the system is bound.

qa.q: Four charges of +1 µC each are at the corners of a square of side 0.3 m. How many pairs must be counted in the total potential energy?
qa.e: 4C2 = 6 pairs: four sides and two diagonals.

qa.q: Charges +4 µC and -2 µC are 0.2 m apart. How much work is needed to separate them to infinity (in J)?
Two equal charges of 1 µC are moved from 0.3 m apart to 0.1 m apart. What work is done by the external agent (in J)? (k = 9 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻²)
qa.e: U changes from 0.03 J to 0.09 J, so W = 0.09 - 0.03 = 0.06 J.

qa.q: Charges +q, +q and -q sit at the corners of an equilateral triangle of side a. What is the total potential energy?
qa.e: Pairs: (+q,+q) gives +kq²/a; two (+q,-q) pairs give -2kq²/a. Total = -kq²/a.

qa.q: The potential energy of a pair of charges is independent of
qa.a: the path and order in which they were brought together
qa.e: U is a state function of the final configuration because the force is conservative.

qa.q: Three charges of 2 µC each are placed at the corners of an equilateral triangle of side 0.3 m. What is the total potential energy (in J)? (k = 9 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻²)
qa.e: Each pair: 9 × 10⁹ × 4 × 10⁻¹²/0.3 = 0.12 J. Three pairs: 0.36 J.

qa.q: An electron is accelerated from rest through a potential difference of 500 V. What kinetic energy does it gain (in eV)?
qa.e: K = eΔV = 500 eV.

qa.q: What is 5 MeV in joules (in units of 10⁻¹³ J)? (1 eV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J)
An alpha particle (charge 2e) is accelerated through 2 kV. What kinetic energy does it gain (in keV)?
qa.e: K = qΔV = 2e × 2000 V = 4000 eV = 4 keV.

qa.q: A charge of 3 µC is at a point where the external potential is 400 V. What is its potential energy (in mJ)?
For two charges q₁ and q₂ in an external field, the total potential energy contains
qa.e: Each charge interacts with the external field, and the two also interact with each other.

qa.q: Which statement is correct about an electron released from rest in an electric field?
qa.a: It moves towards higher potential and gains kinetic energy
qa.e: For negative charge U = -eV falls as V rises, so it moves to higher V.

qa.q: Two charges 5 µC and -3 µC are placed 15 cm apart, both on the V = 0 equipotential of an external field. What is the system's potential energy (in J)? (k = 9 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻²)
qa.e: Both charges sit where the external V = 0, so only the mutual term remains: kq₁q₂/r = 9 × 10⁹ × (5 × 10⁻⁶)(-3 × 10⁻⁶)/0.15 = -0.9 J.

qa.q: An electron volt is
qa.a: the energy gained by an electron moving through a potential difference of 1 V
qa.e: eV is energy: charge e times 1 V.

qa.q: A dipole p = 5 × 10⁻⁹ C m is at θ = 0° in a field of 2 × 10⁴ N C⁻¹. What is its potential energy (in units of 10⁻⁴ J)?
How much work is needed to rotate a dipole of p = 10⁻⁸ C m from θ = 0° to 180° in a field of 5 × 10³ N C⁻¹ (in units of 10⁻⁵ J)?
In which orientation is an electric dipole in unstable equilibrium in a uniform field?
qa.e: At 180° torque is zero but U is maximum, so any tilt makes it rotate away.

qa.q: A molecule with p = 10⁻²⁹ C m is turned from θ = 0° to θ = 60° in a field of 10⁶ N C⁻¹. What work is needed (in units of 10⁻²⁴ J)?
The expression U = -p·E for a dipole assumes U = 0 when
qa.e: -pE cos 90° = 0, so the reference is θ = 90°.

qa.q: At which angle are both the torque and the potential energy of the dipole zero?
qa.a: No angle: U = 0 at 90°, where the torque is maximum
qa.e: U = 0 at 90°, where τ = pE is maximum; τ = 0 at 0° and 180°, where U = ∓pE ≠ 0.

qa.q: A dipole in a field of 10⁴ N C⁻¹ has a potential energy of -3 × 10⁻⁵ J when aligned with the field. What is p (in nC m)?
qa.e: U = -pE, so p = 3 × 10⁻⁵/10⁴ = 3 × 10⁻⁹ C m = 3 nC m.

qa.q: Assertion (A): A dipole placed in a uniform field tends to align with the field. Reason (R): Its potential energy is minimum when p is along E. Choose the correct option.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
qa.e: Systems move towards minimum potential energy; the torque rotates p into line with E.

qa.q: What is the electric field inside a solid metal sphere carrying 5 µC, in electrostatic equilibrium (in N C⁻¹)?
qa.e: In equilibrium the field inside any conductor is zero.

qa.q: Where does excess charge given to an isolated conductor reside?
qa.e: Gauss's law with E = 0 inside shows no charge in the interior.

qa.q: A charged conductor has potential 200 V at its surface. What is the potential at its centre (in V)?
qa.e: E = 0 inside, so V does not change from surface to centre.

qa.q: A conductor has σ = 8.85 × 10⁻⁸ C m⁻². What is the field just outside (in kN C⁻¹)? (ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² C² N⁻¹ m⁻²)
Why is the electrostatic field at the surface of a conductor normal to it?
qa.a: Any tangential component would move surface charges, so equilibrium needs it to vanish
qa.e: In equilibrium charges are at rest, so no force along the surface.

qa.q: Assertion (A): A conductor in electrostatic equilibrium is an equipotential. Reason (R): The field inside and the tangential field on its surface are zero. Choose the correct option.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
qa.e: With no field along any path within or on the conductor, no work is done, so V is the same everywhere.

qa.q: The surface charge density at a point on a conductor is doubled. The field just outside that point
qa.e: E = σ/ε₀ is proportional to σ.

qa.q: A neutral metal slab is placed in a uniform external field. Which statement is correct?
qa.a: Negative charge appears on the face where the field enters and positive on the face where it leaves
qa.e: Electrons drift against the field to the entry face; the other face is left positive. Their field cancels the external field inside.

qa.q: A thin shell of radius 0.2 m carries 4 nC. What is the potential at a point 0.1 m from its centre (in V)? (k = 9 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻²)
qa.e: Inside the shell V is constant and equal to kq/R = 36/0.2 = 180 V.

qa.q: For the same shell (4 nC, R = 0.2 m), what is the potential at 0.4 m from the centre (in V)?
qa.e: Outside V = kq/r = 36/0.4 = 90 V.

qa.q: Why does a lightning conductor have pointed tips?
qa.a: Charge density and field are very high at sharp points, so charge leaks away into the air
qa.e: High σ at points gives strong fields that ionise air, enabling discharge.

qa.q: A charge +q is placed at the centre of a cavity in a neutral conducting sphere. What charges appear on the inner and outer surfaces?
qa.a: -q on the inner surface, +q on the outer surface
qa.e: The inner wall gets -q so that E = 0 in the metal; the outer surface gets +q since the conductor is neutral overall.

qa.q: Which is the best example of electrostatic shielding?
qa.a: Keeping a sensitive instrument inside a closed metal box
qa.e: The field inside a closed conducting enclosure is zero.

qa.q: A conducting sphere of radius 9 cm has a potential of 200 V at its surface. What is the charge on it (in nC)? (k = 9 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻²)
A hollow conducting sphere carries charge Q₁. A small charge Q₂ is placed at its centre. The field outside the sphere at distance r from the centre is
qa.e: The outer surface ends up with Q₁ + Q₂ (the original Q₁ plus the induced +Q₂), so Gauss's law gives k(Q₁ + Q₂)/r².

qa.q: Assertion (A): Corona discharge is seen near sharp points of high-voltage conductors. Reason (R): Surface charge density is larger at points of smaller radius of curvature. Choose the correct option.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
qa.e: Large σ means large field σ/ε₀, which ionises the surrounding air.

qa.q: What is the main difference between a conductor and a dielectric placed in an electric field?
qa.a: The field inside a conductor becomes zero, but inside a dielectric it is only reduced
qa.e: Free charges in a conductor cancel the field; bound charges in a dielectric only partly oppose it.

qa.q: Polarisation P of a dielectric is defined as
qa.e: P = total dipole moment / volume.

qa.q: In the relation P = χe E, the quantity χe is called the
qa.e: χe measures how strongly a material polarises in response to the field.

qa.q: A non-polar molecule placed in an electric field
qa.a: develops an induced dipole moment along the field
qa.e: The field pushes the nucleus and electron cloud apart, inducing a dipole along E.

qa.q: Why do polar molecules not show any net polarisation without an external field?
qa.a: Their permanent dipoles point in random directions due to thermal motion
qa.e: Random orientations average out; an applied field partly aligns them.

qa.q: A dielectric slab in an applied field E₀ has a net internal field of 0.2E₀. What field do its bound charges produce (in terms of E₀, opposing)?
qa.e: Net = E₀ - E_bound, so E_bound = E₀ - 0.2E₀ = 0.8E₀.

qa.q: Where do the bound charges of a uniformly polarised dielectric slab appear?
qa.a: On its two faces perpendicular to the field
qa.e: Inside, neighbouring dipole charges cancel; only the end faces have uncancelled bound charge.

qa.q: Assertion (A): A dielectric reduces the field between capacitor plates. Reason (R): Bound charges on its surfaces produce a field opposing the applied field. Choose the correct option.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
qa.e: The opposing field of the induced surface charges reduces the net field.

qa.q: A capacitor holds 40 µC at 8 V. What is its capacitance (in µF)?
A 10 µF capacitor is connected to a 9 V battery. What charge does it store (in µC)?
qa.e: Q = CV = 10 µF × 9 V = 90 µC.

qa.q: The potential difference across a capacitor is doubled. Its capacitance
qa.e: C depends on geometry and medium only; Q doubles instead.

qa.q: A parallel plate capacitor's plates have σ = 17.7 × 10⁻⁹ C m⁻². What is the field between them (in V m⁻¹)? (ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² C² N⁻¹ m⁻²)
Why is there a maximum safe voltage rating printed on a capacitor?
qa.a: Above it, the field in the dielectric exceeds its dielectric strength and the dielectric breaks down
qa.e: Breakdown ionises the insulator and lets charge leak across.

qa.q: Air breaks down at about 3 × 10⁶ V m⁻¹. What is the largest voltage that can be applied across an air gap of 1 mm (in kV)?
The field outside an ideal parallel plate capacitor (away from the edges) is
qa.e: Fields of the +σ and -σ plates cancel outside.

qa.q: A capacitor consists of
qa.a: two conductors separated by an insulator
qa.e: The insulator keeps the charges ±Q apart on the two conductors.

qa.q: A parallel plate capacitor has plates of area 0.1 m² separated by 0.885 mm in air. What is its capacitance (in nF)? (ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² C² N⁻¹ m⁻²)
The gap of a 20 pF air capacitor is completely filled with a dielectric of K = 5. What is the new capacitance (in pF)?
The plate separation of a parallel plate capacitor is tripled and its plate area is doubled. The capacitance becomes
A charged capacitor is disconnected from the battery and a dielectric of K = 4 is inserted. The potential difference becomes
qa.e: Q is fixed and C becomes 4C, so V = Q/C becomes V/4.

qa.q: What area (in units of 10⁹ m²) would a 1 F air-filled parallel plate capacitor with a 1 cm gap need? (ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² C² N⁻¹ m⁻²; give to 2 decimal places)
qa.e: A = Cd/ε₀ = 1 × 0.01/8.85 × 10⁻¹² ≈ 1.13 × 10⁹ m². This shows the farad is a huge unit.

qa.q: The dielectric constant K of a medium is defined as
qa.a: the ratio ε/ε₀ of its permittivity to that of free space
qa.e: K = ε/ε₀ is dimensionless and greater than 1.

qa.q: With charge held fixed, inserting a dielectric of constant K into a capacitor makes the field between the plates
qa.e: Polarisation reduces the field by a factor K.

qa.q: Which material listed would give the largest capacitance when filling the same capacitor?
qa.e: Water has K ≈ 80, much larger than mica (≈ 6) and air (≈ 1).

qa.q: Capacitors of 4 µF and 12 µF are connected in series. What is the equivalent capacitance (in µF)?
qa.e: C = C₁C₂/(C₁ + C₂) = 48/16 = 3 µF.

qa.q: Three capacitors of 2 µF, 3 µF and 5 µF are connected in parallel across 10 V. What total charge is drawn (in µC)?
A 2 µF and a 3 µF capacitor are in series across 100 V. What is the voltage across the 2 µF capacitor (in V)?
qa.e: C = 6/5 = 1.2 µF; Q = 120 µC; V = 120/2 = 60 V. The smaller capacitor takes the larger voltage.

qa.q: A parallel plate capacitor has C₀ = 9 pF with an air gap d. A dielectric slab of K = 3 and thickness d/2 is inserted. What is the new capacitance (in pF)?
What is the minimum number of 1 µF capacitors, each rated 300 V, needed to make a 2 µF combination that can safely take 1000 V?
qa.e: Each row needs 4 in series so that each takes 250 V (3 would take about 333 V each, above the rating). A row of 4 gives 1/4 µF, so 8 parallel rows give 2 µF: 4 × 8 = 32 capacitors.

qa.q: Three equal capacitors of C each are connected in series. The equivalent capacitance is
qa.e: 1/Ceq = 3/C, so Ceq = C/3.

qa.q: A metal slab of thickness d/2 is inserted into the gap of an air capacitor C₀ (gap d). What is the new capacitance?
qa.e: For a conducting slab C = ε₀A/(d - t) = ε₀A/(d/2) = 2C₀.

qa.q: In a series combination of capacitors, which quantity is the same for each capacitor?
qa.e: Charge induced on facing plates passes the same Q along the chain.

qa.q: A 20 µF capacitor is charged to 100 V. What energy does it store (in J)?
A capacitor stores 300 µC at 50 V. What energy does it hold (in mJ)?
The field between capacitor plates is 10⁵ V m⁻¹ in air. What is the energy density (in J m⁻³)? (ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² C² N⁻¹ m⁻²; give to 3 decimal places)
A 4 µF capacitor at 100 V is connected across an uncharged 4 µF capacitor. What is the common potential (in V)?
qa.e: V = C₁V₁/(C₁ + C₂) = 400/8 = 50 V.

qa.q: For the same case (4 µF at 100 V connected to an uncharged 4 µF), how much energy is lost (in mJ)?
A capacitor stays connected to a battery while a dielectric of K = 3 is inserted. The stored energy
qa.e: V fixed, C → 3C, U = ½CV² → 3U.

qa.q: An isolated charged capacitor (disconnected) has a dielectric of K = 4 inserted. The stored energy
qa.e: Q fixed, C → 4C, U = Q²/2C → U/4. The field pulls the slab in, doing work.

qa.q: A capacitor of 5 µF must store 0.4 J. What voltage is needed (in V)?
A wire carries 0.5 A for 2 minutes. How much charge passes through it (in C)?
How many electrons pass a point each second in a wire carrying 1.6 A? (e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C; answer in units of 10¹⁹)
qa.e: n = I/e = 1.6/1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 10¹⁹ electrons per second.

qa.q: In a metal wire, electrons drift from end A to end B. The conventional current flows
qa.e: Conventional current is the direction positive charge would move, opposite to electron flow.

qa.q: The charge through a cross-section varies as q = 4t² + 2t (q in C, t in s). What is the current at t = 2 s (in A)?
qa.e: I = dq/dt = 8t + 2 = 18 A at t = 2 s.

qa.q: Which of these is an example of current carried by ions rather than electrons?
qa.a: Current through salt water in an electrolytic cell
qa.e: In electrolytes, positive and negative ions are the charge carriers.

qa.q: The SI unit of current is the ampere. Which statement is correct?
qa.a: The ampere is a base SI unit, and 1 A = 1 C s⁻¹
qa.e: The ampere is one of the seven SI base units.

qa.q: A lightning stroke transfers 20 C in 1 ms. What is the average current (in kA)?
Which quantity is a measure of current?
qa.e: I = dq/dt.

qa.q: A potential difference of 6 V drives 0.3 A through a wire. What is its resistance (in Ω)?
Why is the current zero in a metal wire not connected to any cell, even though electrons move fast?
qa.a: Their velocities are random, so as many cross any section one way as the other
qa.e: Random thermal motion gives no net transport of charge.

qa.q: Why can a charged capacitor's discharge through a wire not give a steady current for long?
qa.a: The field disappears as the charges neutralise, so a source is needed to maintain it
qa.e: A steady current needs a continuously maintained field, which a cell provides.

qa.q: For an ohmic resistor, the graph of V against I is
qa.a: a straight line through the origin whose slope is R
qa.e: V = IR is linear with slope R.

qa.q: The current through a resistor of 25 Ω is 0.2 A. What is the potential difference across it (in V)?
The voltage across an ohmic resistor is tripled at the same temperature. The current
qa.e: I = V/R with constant R.

qa.q: What are the charge carriers in a metallic conductor?
qa.e: The lattice ions are fixed; only free electrons move.

qa.q: Assertion (A): A steady current in a wire needs a source such as a cell. Reason (R): The source maintains the electric field inside the conductor. Choose the correct option.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
qa.e: Without the source, charges would pile up at the ends and cancel the field, stopping the current.

qa.q: A wire 2 m long with cross-section 10⁻⁶ m² has a resistivity of 1.7 × 10⁻⁸ Ω m. What is its resistance (in Ω)?
A wire of resistance 9 Ω is stretched uniformly until its length is tripled. What is its new resistance (in Ω)?
qa.e: R ∝ l² at constant volume: 9 × 3² = 81 Ω.

qa.q: Two wires of the same material and length have diameters in the ratio 1:2. What is the ratio of their resistances R₁:R₂?
A wire of cross-section 2 mm² carries 3 A. What is the current density (in A mm⁻²)?
A copper wire is cut into two equal halves. The resistivity of each half
qa.e: Resistivity is a material property; only R changes.

qa.q: Ohm's law in its vector (microscopic) form is
qa.e: Current density equals conductivity times field.

qa.q: A material has ρ = 2 × 10⁻⁸ Ω m. What is its conductivity (in units of 10⁷ S m⁻¹)?
Assertion (A): The resistance of a wire changes when it is stretched, but its resistivity does not. Reason (R): Resistivity depends only on the material and temperature. Choose the correct option.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
qa.e: Stretching changes l and A (so R) but not the material, so ρ stays the same.

qa.q: A wire with n = 8 × 10²⁸ m⁻³ and A = 2 × 10⁻⁶ m² carries 2.56 A. What is the drift speed (in mm s⁻¹)? (e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)
The current in a wire is doubled while its cross-section is unchanged. The drift velocity
qa.e: I = neAvd, so vd ∝ I for fixed n and A.

qa.q: Two wires of the same material carry the same current; wire B has twice the cross-section of wire A. Compare the drift speeds vA : vB.
qa.e: vd = I/(neA): halving the area doubles vd, so vA = 2vB.

qa.q: Why does a bulb light almost at once although drift speed is only about 0.1 mm s⁻¹?
qa.a: The electric field is set up throughout the circuit almost at the speed of light, so electrons everywhere start drifting together
qa.e: The signal is the field, which travels very fast; every electron in the wire responds immediately.

qa.q: The resistivity of a metal can be written as
qa.e: From j = (ne²τ/m)E, conductivity σ = ne²τ/m, so ρ = m/(ne²τ).

qa.q: The relaxation time τ of electrons in a metal is
qa.a: the average time between successive collisions
qa.e: τ is a statistical average of collision intervals.

qa.q: If the potential difference across a wire is doubled, with temperature constant, the drift velocity
qa.e: E = V/l doubles and vd = eEτ/m, so vd doubles.

qa.q: In terms of the field, the drift velocity of electrons is
qa.e: Average acceleration -eE/m over average time τ gives -eEτ/m.

qa.q: Electrons drift at 3 × 10⁻⁴ m s⁻¹ in a field of 0.1 V m⁻¹. What is their mobility (in units of 10⁻³ m² V⁻¹ s⁻¹)?
The SI unit of mobility is
qa.e: µ = (m s⁻¹)/(V m⁻¹) = m² V⁻¹ s⁻¹.

qa.q: Mobility of an electron in terms of e, τ and m is
qa.e: From vd = eEτ/m, dividing by E gives µ = eτ/m.

qa.q: A bulb's filament shows a V-I graph that bends towards the V-axis at high currents. This is because
qa.a: its resistance rises as it heats up
qa.e: Higher temperature increases resistivity of the metal, so V/I grows.

qa.q: Which device conducts very differently when the voltage across it is reversed?
qa.e: A diode's V-I relation depends on the sign of V.

qa.q: What feature distinguishes GaAs-type non-ohmic behaviour?
qa.a: The same current can occur at more than one voltage
qa.e: Its V-I graph folds back, so one I value matches more than one V.

qa.q: A material's carriers have mobility 0.2 m² V⁻¹ s⁻¹ in a field of 50 V m⁻¹. What is their drift speed (in m s⁻¹)?
Assertion (A): Ohm's law is not a universal law. Reason (R): Devices like diodes have V-I relations that depend on the sign of V. Choose the correct option.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
qa.e: Ohm's law holds only for certain materials under certain conditions; diodes are a clear counterexample.

qa.q: A copper coil has R = 50 Ω at 20 °C. What is its resistance at 120 °C (in Ω)? (α = 4 × 10⁻³ °C⁻¹)
Why are manganin and constantan used for making standard resistors?
qa.a: Their resistivity changes very little with temperature
qa.e: A tiny α keeps the resistance stable as the room temperature varies.

qa.q: Roughly how many orders of magnitude separate the resistivity of good conductors from that of good insulators?
qa.e: From about 10⁻⁸ Ω m for metals to over 10¹⁴ Ω m for insulators: more than 22 orders.

qa.q: A wire's resistance rises from 10 Ω to 12 Ω when heated by 50 °C. What is α (in units of 10⁻³ °C⁻¹)?
Going by its resistivity, which of these materials is a semiconductor?
qa.e: Silicon's resistivity lies between metals and insulators.

qa.q: The temperature coefficient of resistivity of a typical metal is
qa.e: Resistivity of metals increases with temperature.

qa.q: In ρT = ρ₀[1 + α(T - T₀)], what does ρ₀ represent?
qa.a: Resistivity at the reference temperature T₀
qa.e: It is the value at the reference temperature, often 20 °C or 0 °C.

qa.q: Why is nichrome preferred for the heating coil of an electric iron?
qa.a: It has high resistivity and its resistance changes little when hot
qa.e: High ρ gives large R in a short coil; small α keeps the heating steady.

qa.q: Why does the resistivity of a metal increase with temperature?
qa.a: Collisions become more frequent, so the relaxation time τ decreases
qa.e: In ρ = m/(ne²τ), n stays almost constant while τ falls.

qa.q: Why does the resistivity of a semiconductor decrease with temperature?
qa.a: The number density of charge carriers increases rapidly
qa.e: More bonds break, freeing carriers; this beats the drop in τ.

qa.q: A heater coil has R = 100 Ω at 20 °C and 120 Ω when hot, with α = 2 × 10⁻⁴ °C⁻¹. What is its hot temperature (in °C)?
The temperature coefficient of resistivity of a semiconductor is
qa.e: Its resistivity falls as temperature rises.

qa.q: In the expression ρ = m/(ne²τ), which quantity changes most with temperature in a metal?
qa.e: n is fixed by the metal's structure; τ falls as lattice vibrations grow.

qa.q: A platinum resistance thermometer reads 5 Ω at 0 °C and 6 Ω at an unknown temperature. If α = 4 × 10⁻³ °C⁻¹, what is the temperature (in °C)?
Assertion (A): An insulator's resistivity decreases with increasing temperature. Reason (R): More charge carriers become available as temperature rises. Choose the correct option.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
qa.e: Like semiconductors, heating frees a few carriers in insulators, lowering resistivity.

qa.q: Which statement correctly compares heating a copper wire and a silicon crystal?
qa.a: Copper's resistance rises while silicon's falls
qa.e: Metals have positive α; semiconductors have negative α.

qa.q: A resistor of 10 Ω carries 3 A. What power does it dissipate (in W)?
A 60 W bulb is designed for 240 V. What is its resistance (in Ω)?
A 2 kW geyser runs for 30 minutes a day. How many kWh does it use in 30 days?
qa.e: Daily: 2 kW × 0.5 h = 1 kWh. In 30 days: 30 kWh.

qa.q: A power of 100 kW is sent through a line of resistance 0.5 Ω at 10 kV. What is the power lost in the line (in W)?
If the same 100 kW is sent through the same 0.5 Ω line at 100 kV instead, what is the loss (in W)?
qa.e: I = 1 A, loss = 1 × 0.5 = 0.5 W, a hundredth of the earlier loss.

qa.q: Why is electric power transmitted at very high voltage?
qa.a: For a given power, higher V means lower current and much smaller I²R loss
qa.e: Loss = P²Rc/V² falls as 1/V².

qa.q: Two bulbs of 40 W and 100 W, both rated for 220 V, are connected in series across 220 V. Which glows brighter?
qa.e: In series the same current flows, so P = I²R is larger for the larger R. The 40 W bulb has the higher resistance (R = V²/P).

qa.q: A 5 Ω resistor is connected across 10 V. How much heat is produced in 1 minute (in J)?
A cell of emf 1.5 V and internal resistance 0.3 Ω is connected to a 1.2 Ω resistor. What is the current (in A)?
A 12 V battery with r = 0.4 Ω supplies 5 A. What is its terminal voltage (in V)?
The terminal voltage of a cell is 2.2 V on open circuit and 1.8 V when a current of 2 A flows. What is the internal resistance (in Ω)?
What is the maximum current that can be drawn from a cell of emf 9 V and internal resistance 0.5 Ω (in A)?
qa.e: Short circuit: I = ε/r = 9/0.5 = 18 A.

qa.q: Why is the terminal voltage of a cell less than its emf when it supplies current?
qa.a: Part of the emf is used to drive current through the internal resistance (Ir drop)
qa.e: V = ε - Ir.

qa.q: Emf of a cell is best described as
qa.a: the energy supplied per unit charge by the cell, equal to the terminal p.d. on open circuit
qa.e: Despite its name, emf is not a force; it is measured in volts.

qa.q: A cell gives 0.5 A through a 4 Ω resistor and 0.25 A through a 9 Ω resistor. What is its emf (in V)?
A cell with ε = 2 V, r = 1 Ω is connected to R = 1 Ω. What is the power delivered to R (in W)?
Two cells of 1.5 V (r = 0.5 Ω each) are in series with a 2 Ω resistor. What is the current (in A)?
Cells of emf 6 V (r = 1 Ω) and 2 V (r = 1 Ω) are connected in series with opposite polarity across a 2 Ω resistor. What is the current (in A)?
Two cells of 4 V and 2 V with internal resistances 2 Ω and 2 Ω are connected in parallel. What is the equivalent emf (in V)?
Six identical cells, each of emf 2 V and internal resistance 0.6 Ω, are arranged as 2 parallel rows of 3 cells in series. What is the internal resistance of the combination (in Ω)?
For the same arrangement (2 rows of 3 cells of 2 V, 0.6 Ω each) connected to a 5.1 Ω resistor, what is the current (in A)?
Four identical cells (ε, r) are connected in parallel. The equivalent emf and internal resistance are
qa.e: Identical cells in parallel keep emf ε and divide r by the number of cells.

qa.q: Why are cells connected in parallel when a large current is needed at low voltage?
qa.a: Parallel grouping reduces the internal resistance, so more current can flow
qa.e: r_eq = r/m drops, raising the maximum current.

qa.q: Two cells of emf 2 V and 2 V with internal resistances 1 Ω and 3 Ω are in parallel. What is the equivalent internal resistance (in Ω)?
qa.e: r_eq = r₁r₂/(r₁ + r₂) = 3/4 = 0.75 Ω.

qa.q: At a junction, currents of 4 A and 3 A enter and a current of 5 A leaves along one wire. What current leaves through the only other wire (in A)?
qa.e: In = out: 4 + 3 = 5 + I, so I = 2 A.

qa.q: Kirchhoff's loop rule is a consequence of
qa.e: A charge that goes round a loop returns to the same potential, so no net energy is gained or lost.

qa.q: In a loop, you go across a 4 Ω resistor in the direction opposite to its current of 2 A. The change in potential is (in V)
qa.e: Going against the current, potential rises by IR = +8 V.

qa.q: A single loop has a 10 V cell (negligible r) and resistors of 2 Ω and 3 Ω in series. Using the loop rule, what is the current (in A)?
A loop contains a 12 V cell and a 4 V cell connected to oppose each other, with a total resistance of 4 Ω (including internal resistances). What is the current (in A)?
qa.e: Net emf = 12 - 4 = 8 V. I = 8/4 = 2 A, in the direction driven by the 12 V cell.

qa.q: While solving a network, a current comes out as -0.5 A. This means
qa.a: the current is 0.5 A but flows opposite to the direction assumed
qa.e: The assumed direction was just a guess; the sign corrects it.

qa.q: Twelve equal resistors of 6 Ω form the edges of a cube. What is the equivalent resistance between two diagonally opposite corners (in Ω)?
qa.e: R_eq = 5R/6 = 5 × 6/6 = 5 Ω (by symmetry: current I splits into 3, then 6, then 3 parts).

qa.q: Kirchhoff's junction rule is based on
qa.e: Charge cannot pile up at a junction in steady state.

qa.q: A Wheatstone bridge balances with P = 8 Ω, Q = 2 Ω and R = 12 Ω. What is S (in Ω)?
qa.e: P/Q = R/S gives S = RQ/P = 24/8 = 3 Ω.

qa.q: In a balanced bridge, why does no current flow through the galvanometer?
qa.a: The two ends of the galvanometer are at the same potential
qa.e: Current flows only if there is a potential difference across the galvanometer.

qa.q: Four resistors P = 2 Ω, Q = 4 Ω, R = 6 Ω and S = 12 Ω form a bridge. Is it balanced?
qa.e: 2/4 = 6/12 = 0.5, so the bridge is balanced whatever the cell.

qa.q: In a balanced bridge, the galvanometer and the cell are interchanged. The bridge
qa.e: The condition P/Q = R/S is symmetric; swapping cell and galvanometer keeps balance.

qa.q: A bridge has P = Q = R = 10 Ω and S = 10 Ω with a galvanometer of 20 Ω. If S is changed to 20 Ω, will a galvanometer current flow?
qa.e: Balance needs P/Q = R/S; now 1 ≠ 1/2, so the bridge is unbalanced.

qa.q: In bridge ABCD, P = 1 Ω (A to B), Q = 2 Ω (B to C), R = 2 Ω (A to D) and S = 1 Ω (D to C). A 10 V cell of negligible internal resistance is connected across A and C, and a galvanometer of resistance 2 Ω across B and D. What current flows through the galvanometer (in A)?
qa.e: P/Q = 1/2 but R/S = 2, so the bridge is unbalanced. Taking V_C = 0 and V_A = 10 V, the junction rule at B and D gives V_B = 6 V and V_D = 4 V, so Ig = (6 - 4)/2 = 1 A, from B to D.

qa.q: When a bridge is balanced, the galvanometer can be removed without changing any current. Why?
qa.a: It carries zero current, so removing it changes nothing
qa.e: A branch with zero current can be removed (or replaced by any resistor) without effect.

qa.q: In a balanced bridge P = 4 Ω, Q = 6 Ω and S = 9 Ω. What is R (in Ω)?
A wire of resistance 8 Ω is used as S in a balanced bridge with P = 2 Ω and Q = 4 Ω. What is R (in Ω)?
Who first observed that an electric current deflects a magnetic compass needle?
qa.e: Oersted noticed this in 1820, linking electricity and magnetism.

qa.q: In a diagram, a magnetic field pointing straight towards the reader is shown by
qa.e: A dot is like the tip of an arrow coming at you.

qa.q: A compass placed near a straight wire with current tends to align
qa.a: along circles centred on the wire
qa.e: The field of a straight wire forms concentric circles around it.

qa.q: Which of these produces a magnetic field?
qa.e: Moving charges make magnetic fields; static charges make only electric fields.

qa.q: Two wires each produce a field of 3 µT at a point, in the same direction. What is the net field there (in µT)?
qa.e: Superposition: same direction, so the fields add: 3 + 3 = 6 µT.

qa.q: Two wires produce fields of 3 µT (east) and 4 µT (north) at a point. What is the magnitude of the net field (in µT)?
qa.e: Fields add as vectors: √(3² + 4²) = 5 µT.

qa.q: Maxwell's work showed that
qa.a: electricity and magnetism are unified, and light is an electromagnetic wave
qa.e: Maxwell's equations predicted EM waves moving at the speed of light.

qa.q: Assertion (A): A compass needle deflects near a wire only while current flows. Reason (R): Only moving charges produce magnetic fields. Choose the correct option.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
qa.e: When the current stops, the charges no longer drift, so there is no magnetic field to turn the needle.

qa.q: An electron moves at 3 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹ at right angles to a field of 0.2 T. What is the magnitude of the force on it (in units of 10⁻¹⁴ N)? (e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)
A charge of 2 µC moves at 10⁴ m s⁻¹ at 30° to a field of 0.5 T. What is the magnetic force (in mN)?
A proton moves along +x in a field along +y. What is the direction of the magnetic force on it?
qa.e: F = q(v × B) = e(x̂ × ŷ) = +eẑ.

qa.q: An electron moves along +x in a field along +y. The magnetic force on it points along
qa.e: x̂ × ŷ = ẑ, and the negative charge flips it to -z.

qa.q: A charged particle moves through a region with no deflection. Which conclusion is certain?
qa.a: It cannot be concluded that B = 0, since the particle may be moving along B
qa.e: A charge moving parallel to B feels no magnetic force, so the field could be non-zero.

qa.q: Why does the magnetic force not change the speed of a charge?
qa.a: It is always perpendicular to the velocity, so it does no work
qa.e: A force perpendicular to motion changes direction but not kinetic energy.

qa.q: Which is the SI unit of magnetic field?
qa.e: The tesla (T) is the SI unit; the gauss is a smaller non-SI unit.

qa.q: The Lorentz force on a charge q in combined fields is
qa.e: Electric force qE plus magnetic force q(v × B).

qa.q: A wire 0.5 m long carries 4 A at right angles to a field of 0.3 T. What force acts on it (in N)?
A 10 cm wire carries 5 A at 30° to a 0.8 T field. What is the force on it (in N)?
A horizontal rod of mass 0.1 kg and length 0.5 m is suspended in a horizontal field of 0.49 T perpendicular to it. What current makes the tension in the support threads zero (in A)? (g = 9.8 m s⁻²)
A horizontal wire carries current towards the north in a magnetic field pointing vertically upward. In which direction is the force on the wire?
qa.e: F = I l × B. Taking x = east, y = north and z = up: ŷ × ẑ = x̂, so the force points east.

qa.q: Why does a magnetic field do no work on the charges in a wire, even though the wire itself can be pushed?
qa.a: The force on each charge is perpendicular to its velocity
qa.e: Each charge's magnetic force is perpendicular to its motion, so no work is done on it directly.

qa.q: The force on a straight conductor in a uniform field is given by
qa.e: F = I l × B, with l along the current.

qa.q: The current in a wire is doubled and the field is halved. The force on the wire

qa.a: Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
qa.e: The beams do have a magnetic attraction (R is true), but the electrostatic repulsion between the electrons is much larger, so they repel overall. R does not explain A.

qa.e: A self-reinforcing change would grow without any work input, which is impossible.

qa.q: A magnet dropped through a vertical copper tube falls slowly because

qa.e: As the magnet falls, the flux through each ring of the tube changes, inducing currents whose magnetic field opposes the magnet's motion (Lenz's law).

qa.q: The field through a loop points upward and is increasing. The induced current produces a field that, inside the loop, points
qa.e: To oppose the increase of upward flux, the induced field points down.

qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R explains A

qa.q: A metal ring is placed around the top of a vertical solenoid. When the current in the solenoid is switched on, the ring
qa.a: jumps up, repelled by the solenoid
qa.e: The increasing flux induces a current in the ring that opposes it, so the ring is repelled (the jumping ring experiment).

qa.q: A rod of length 0.3 m moves at 5 m s⁻¹ perpendicular to a field of 0.4 T. What emf is induced (in V)?

qa.q: In terms of the Lorentz force, the emf in a moving rod arises because

qa.e: This force pushes charges to the ends and does work vBl per unit charge.

qa.e: v × B = 0 when v is parallel to B.

qa.q: A 0.5 m rod rotates about one end at 200 rad s⁻¹ in a perpendicular field of 0.4 T. What is the emf between its ends (in V)?
A metal wheel of radius 0.2 m spins at 50 rad s⁻¹ in an axial field of 0.1 T. What is the emf between the axle and the rim (in V)?

qa.e: The wings move horizontally, so only the vertical component is perpendicular to both v and the wing.

qa.e: From ε = M dI/dt, M = ε/(dI/dt) has units V/(A s⁻¹) = V s A⁻¹.

qa.q: Inductance of a pair of coils depends on

qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
qa.e: This reciprocity holds generally, so the induced emf per unit rate of change is the same both ways.

qa.q: The current in a 0.3 H coil changes at 50 A s⁻¹. What is the magnitude of the self-induced emf (in V)?

qa.q: A coil's current rises from 0 to 2 A in 0.05 s, and the average back emf is 8 V. What is L (in H)?

qa.q: An inductor's role in a circuit is analogous to which quantity in mechanics?

qa.e: U ∝ I²: doubling I gives 4 × 8 = 32 J.

qa.q: A coil of 50 turns and area 0.2 m² rotates at ω = 100 rad s⁻¹ in a field of 0.05 T. What is the peak emf (in V)?

qa.a: Its voltage can be changed easily and efficiently using transformers
