qa.q: For a spherical mirror, the normal at the point of incidence is
qa.a: along the radius through that point
qa.e: A radius of a sphere is perpendicular to its surface.

qa.q: Ray optics is a good approximation when
qa.a: the wavelength of light is very small compared with the size of objects
qa.e: Then diffraction is negligible and rays travel straight.

qa.q: What are paraxial rays?
qa.a: Rays close to the principal axis and making small angles with it
qa.e: Mirror formulas are derived for paraxial rays.

qa.q: The speed of light in vacuum is about
The incident ray, the reflected ray and the normal at the point of incidence
qa.a: all lie in the same plane
qa.e: This is the second law of reflection.

qa.q: A ray travels along the radius towards the centre of curvature of a concave mirror. After reflection it
qa.e: It hits along the normal (angle of incidence 0), so it reflects straight back.

qa.q: The visible range of light for the human eye is about
qa.e: Violet to red covers about 400 to 750 nm.

qa.q: An object is 15 cm in front of a concave mirror of focal length 10 cm. Where is the image (v, in cm)?
For that case (u = -15 cm, v = -30 cm), what is the magnification?
qa.e: m = -v/u = -(-30)/(-15) = -2: real, inverted, magnified.

qa.q: An object is 20 cm in front of a convex mirror of focal length 20 cm. What is the image distance (in cm)?
qa.e: f = +20, u = -20: 1/v = 1/20 + 1/20 = 1/10, v = +10 cm (virtual, behind the mirror).

qa.q: A concave mirror has a radius of curvature of 36 cm. What is its focal length under the Cartesian convention (in cm)?
An object 4 cm tall is placed 10 cm in front of a concave mirror of focal length 15 cm. What is the image height (in cm)?
In the Cartesian sign convention, the image formed behind a mirror has
qa.e: Behind the mirror is in the direction of incident light, so v > 0.

qa.q: A negative magnification means the image is
qa.e: m = -v/u < 0 for images on the same side as the object (real).

qa.q: Why is f = R/2 only approximately true for a spherical mirror?
qa.a: It holds exactly only for paraxial rays; rays far from the axis focus at different points
qa.e: Wide-angle rays are brought to focus nearer the mirror (spherical aberration).

qa.q: An object is placed between F and C of a concave mirror. The image is
qa.a: real, inverted and magnified, beyond C
qa.e: This is the case used in projectors.

qa.q: An object is at 40 cm from a concave mirror of focal length 20 cm (u = -40, f = -20). Where is the image (in cm)?
qa.e: The object is at C (R = 40 cm), so the image is also at C: v = -40 cm.

qa.q: For any position of a real object, a convex mirror forms an image that is
qa.e: Rays diverge after reflection from a convex mirror.

qa.q: A 2 cm tall object is placed 30 cm from a convex mirror of focal length 15 cm. What is the image height (in cm)?
A truck's convex mirror has f = 2 m. A car is 18 m behind it, approaching at 20 m s⁻¹. What is the speed of the image (in m s⁻¹)?
Where should an object be placed in front of a concave mirror to get an image of the same size?
qa.e: u = 2f gives v = 2f and m = -1.

qa.q: Why does a dentist use a concave mirror?
qa.a: With the tooth within the focal length, it gives an erect, magnified, virtual image
qa.e: Object between F and P gives an enlarged, upright image.

qa.q: An object is moved from infinity towards the focus of a concave mirror. The real image moves
qa.e: As u goes from ∞ to F, v goes from F to ∞.

qa.q: The speed of light in a medium is 2.25 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹. What is its refractive index? (c = 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹)
qa.e: n = c/v = 3/2.25 ≈ 1.33 (like water).

qa.q: If the refractive index of glass relative to air is 1.5, what is the refractive index of air relative to glass?
Light goes from water (n = 1.33) into glass (n = 1.6). What is the refractive index of glass relative to water? (give to 2 decimal places)
A ray passes from glass into air. It
qa.e: Going from denser to rarer, the ray speeds up and bends away.

qa.q: A ray in air meets glass (n = √3) at i = 60°. What is the angle of refraction (in degrees)?
Which statement is correct about refraction?
qa.a: Frequency is unchanged; speed and wavelength change
qa.e: The source sets the frequency; v = νλ falls in a denser medium.

qa.q: Given n of glass relative to air is 1.5 and n of water relative to air is 1.33, what is n of glass relative to water? (give to 2 decimal places)
Snell's law of refraction is
qa.e: The ratio of sines is constant for a given pair of media.

qa.q: A pool is 3 m deep. How deep does it appear when viewed from directly above? (n of water = 4/3)
qa.e: Apparent depth = 3/(4/3) = 2.25 m.

qa.q: A mark under a glass slab of thickness 6 cm appears raised by 2 cm. What is the refractive index of the glass?
qa.e: Apparent depth = 6 - 2 = 4 cm. n = real/apparent = 6/4 = 1.5.

qa.q: What is the critical angle for a glass-air surface if n of glass is √2 (in degrees)?
qa.e: sin ic = 1/√2, so ic = 45°.

qa.q: Total internal reflection can occur when light travels
qa.a: from a denser medium to a rarer medium at an angle greater than the critical angle
qa.e: Both conditions are needed.

qa.q: The critical angle for diamond is about 24.4°, and for crown glass about 41°. Why does diamond sparkle more?
qa.a: Its small critical angle traps light by many total internal reflections before it escapes
qa.e: Light is reflected many times inside a well-cut diamond.

qa.q: A glass slab produces a lateral shift of a ray. The emergent ray is
qa.e: Refraction at the two parallel faces cancels the deviation, leaving only a sideways shift.

qa.q: Light in water (n = 4/3) strikes the water-air surface. What is sin ic?
A fish sees the outside world through a circular window at the water surface. This happens because
qa.a: rays from outside are bent into a cone of half-angle equal to the critical angle
qa.e: All rays from above enter within ic of the normal; outside that cone the fish sees reflections.

qa.q: Optical fibres guide light by
qa.e: Light reflects at the core-cladding boundary again and again.

qa.q: In an optical fibre, the refractive index of the core compared with the cladding is
qa.e: TIR requires the inner medium to be denser.

qa.q: A 45°-90°-45° glass prism is used to turn a ray through 90°. Why does the ray reflect at the hypotenuse face?
qa.a: It strikes at 45°, which exceeds the critical angle of glass (about 42°)
qa.e: 45° > 42°, so TIR occurs.

qa.q: A glass has n = 1.5. Is a 45°-90°-45° prism of this glass able to reflect a ray totally at 45° incidence? (sin 45° ≈ 0.707)
qa.a: Yes, since sin 45° = 0.707 is more than 1/1.5 = 0.667

qa.q: How can a totally reflecting prism turn a ray through 180°?
qa.a: By two total internal reflections at the two shorter faces
qa.e: Light enters the hypotenuse face, reflects twice, and comes back parallel.

qa.q: Which of these is a medical use of optical fibres?
qa.e: Fibre bundles carry light into the body and the image back out.

qa.q: Why are totally reflecting prisms often preferred to plane mirrors in periscopes?
qa.a: Total internal reflection reflects nearly all the light, without a silver coating that tarnishes
qa.e: TIR is near 100% efficient and does not degrade.

qa.q: In a demonstration of TIR with a laser beam and water, which precaution is most important?
qa.a: Never shine the laser into anyone's eyes
qa.e: Laser light can permanently damage the retina.

qa.q: A double convex lens of glass (n = 1.5) has both radii 30 cm. What is its focal length in air (in cm)?
A plano-convex lens (n = 1.5) has its curved surface of radius 10 cm. What is its focal length (in cm)?
qa.e: For a plane surface 1/R = 0, so 1/f = 0.5 × 1/10, f = 20 cm.

qa.q: A glass lens (n = 1.5) has f = 20 cm in air. What is its focal length in water (n = 4/3) (in cm)?
An object in air is 30 cm from a convex spherical glass surface (n = 1.5, R = 10 cm). Where is the image (v, in cm)?
A small air bubble is at the centre of a glass sphere (n = 1.5) of radius 5 cm. Viewed from outside, where does it appear?
qa.a: At the centre, 5 cm inside the surface
qa.e: Rays from the centre travel along radii, hitting the surface normally, so they are not bent.

qa.q: A lens of n = 1.5 is immersed in a liquid of n = 1.5. Its focal length becomes
qa.a: infinite (it acts like a plane glass plate)
qa.e: n₂₁ = 1, so 1/f = 0.

qa.q: The refraction equation for a single spherical surface is
qa.e: Derived from Snell's law with paraxial approximations.

qa.q: A double concave lens (n = 1.5) has radii 20 cm each. What is its focal length (in cm)?
An object is 15 cm from a convex lens of focal length 10 cm. Where is the image (v, in cm)?
For that lens (u = -15 cm, v = +30 cm), what is the magnification?
An object is 20 cm from a concave lens of focal length 20 cm. Where is the image (in cm)?
What is the power of a convex lens of focal length 25 cm (in D)?
A lens has a power of -2.5 D. What is its focal length (in cm)?
qa.e: f = 1/P = -0.4 m = -40 cm; it is diverging.

qa.q: An object is placed 5 cm from a convex lens of focal length 10 cm. The image is
An object 2 cm tall is 30 cm from a convex lens of focal length 10 cm. What is the image height (in cm)?
The unit of power of a lens, the dioptre, is equal to
qa.e: P = 1/f with f in metres.

qa.q: Two thin lenses of focal lengths +20 cm and -40 cm are in contact. What is the focal length of the combination (in cm)?
A +4 D lens is in contact with a -1.5 D lens. What is the power of the combination (in D)?
Two convex lenses, each of focal length 10 cm, are 40 cm apart on a common axis. An object is 20 cm in front of the first. How far beyond the second lens is the final image (in cm)?
qa.e: Lens 1: 1/v₁ = 1/10 - 1/20 = 1/20, so v₁ = 20 cm. This image is 40 - 20 = 20 cm in front of lens 2, so u₂ = -20 cm and v₂ = +20 cm: a real image 20 cm beyond the second lens.

qa.q: For a combination of lenses, the total magnification equals
qa.a: the product of the individual magnifications
qa.e: Each lens magnifies the image formed by the previous one.

qa.q: A convex lens of focal length 30 cm is in contact with a concave lens of focal length 20 cm. The combination is
An object 2 cm high is 40 cm from a concave mirror of radius 40 cm. What is the image height (in cm)?
qa.e: f = -20, u = -40 is at C, so v = -40 and m = -1: h' = -2 cm (inverted, same size).

qa.q: A thin lens of power +2 D is placed in contact with another to give a total power of +5 D. What is the focal length of the second lens (in cm)?
Why are camera objectives made of several lenses rather than one?
qa.a: Combinations can correct defects (like colour fringes) and give the required overall power
qa.e: Lenses of different glasses and powers cancel aberrations.

qa.q: A prism has A = 60°. A ray inside has r₁ = 35°. What is r₂ (in degrees)?
A ray enters a prism of angle 60° at i = 50° and leaves at e = 40°. What is the deviation (in degrees)?
A thin prism of angle 5° has n = 1.6. What deviation does it produce (in degrees)?
A 60° prism shows minimum deviation of 30°. What is its refractive index? (√2 = 1.414)
At minimum deviation in an equilateral prism (A = 60°), the angle of refraction r₁ is (in degrees)
For a prism of n = √3 and A = 60°, what is the angle of minimum deviation (in degrees)?
How does the angle of deviation vary as the angle of incidence increases from small values?
qa.a: It decreases to a minimum and then increases
qa.e: The δ-i graph is a U-shaped curve with minimum Dm.

qa.q: Which condition holds at the minimum deviation position?
qa.e: The ray passes symmetrically through the prism.

qa.q: A simple microscope has a focal length of 2.5 cm. What is its magnifying power when the image is at the near point (25 cm)?
The same magnifier (f = 2.5 cm) used with the image at infinity gives magnification
A compound microscope has fo = 1 cm, fe = 5 cm and tube length L = 20 cm. What is its magnifying power with the final image at infinity?
In a compound microscope, the image formed by the objective is
qa.e: The object is placed just beyond fo, giving a large real image.

qa.q: Which lenses give the highest magnifying power for a compound microscope?
qa.a: Objective and eyepiece both of short focal length
qa.e: m ≈ (L/fo)(D/fe), which increases as fo and fe fall.

qa.q: A simple magnifier works because
qa.a: it lets the object be brought closer than the near point while forming an image at a comfortable distance
qa.e: A larger angle at the eye means a bigger retinal image.

qa.q: A microscope objective is labelled 40× and the eyepiece 15×. What is the total magnification?
qa.e: Total m = mo × me = 40 × 15 = 600.

qa.q: The final image in a compound microscope, as seen by the eye, is
qa.a: virtual and inverted relative to the object
qa.e: The objective inverts; the eyepiece magnifies without re-inverting.

qa.q: A telescope has an objective of focal length 150 cm and an eyepiece of 5 cm. What is its magnifying power in normal adjustment?
For that telescope (fo = 150 cm, fe = 5 cm), what is the tube length in normal adjustment (in cm)?
qa.e: L = fo + fe = 155 cm.

qa.q: The objective of a telescope has a focal length of 10 m. The Moon (diameter 3.48 × 10⁶ m) is 3.8 × 10⁸ m away. What is the diameter of its image formed by the objective (in cm)?
Why do astronomical telescopes have objectives of large aperture?
qa.a: To gather more light and improve resolving power
qa.e: Light-gathering ∝ D² and resolution improves with D.

qa.q: Which is an advantage of a reflecting telescope over a refracting telescope?
qa.e: Mirrors reflect all wavelengths equally.

qa.q: A telescope of magnifying power 25 has a tube length of 104 cm in normal adjustment. What is the focal length of its objective (in cm)?
qa.e: fo = 25fe and fo + fe = 104, so 26fe = 104, fe = 4 cm, fo = 100 cm.

qa.q: The objective of telescope A has twice the diameter of that of telescope B. How many times more light does A gather?
qa.e: Light gathered ∝ area ∝ D², so 2² = 4.

qa.q: In a Cassegrain reflecting telescope, the secondary mirror is
qa.e: A small convex secondary reflects light back through a hole in the concave primary.

qa.q: Who proposed the wave theory of light in 1678?
qa.e: Huygens proposed it; Newton supported a corpuscular model.

qa.q: The wavefront from a point source close by is
qa.e: Points at the same distance from a point source have the same phase.

qa.q: Light from a distant star reaching a telescope has
qa.e: A tiny portion of a very large sphere is nearly flat.

qa.q: A wavefront is a surface on which all points
qa.e: Constant phase defines a wavefront.

qa.q: The direction of energy flow of a light wave is
qa.e: Rays, along which energy flows, are normal to wavefronts.

qa.q: Which experiment established the wave nature of light in 1801?
qa.e: Interference fringes are a clear wave effect.

qa.q: When does ray optics give correct results?
qa.a: When the wavelength of light is very small compared with the size of objects and apertures
qa.e: Then diffraction effects are negligible.

qa.q: The wave theory predicts that the speed of light in water compared with air is
qa.e: v = c/n with n > 1; this was confirmed by experiment, ruling against the simple corpuscular model.

qa.q: According to Huygens principle, the new wavefront is
qa.a: the forward envelope of the secondary wavelets
qa.e: The common tangent in the forward direction forms the new wavefront.

qa.q: Why is there no backward-travelling wave in Huygens' construction?
qa.a: The amplitude of the secondary wavelets in the backward direction is zero
qa.e: A more detailed theory shows backward amplitude vanishes.

qa.q: Using Huygens construction for reflection at a plane surface, we can prove that
qa.a: the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection
qa.e: Congruent triangles in the construction give i = r.

qa.q: A plane wavefront passes through a convex lens. The emerging wavefront is
qa.a: spherical and converging to the focus
qa.e: The central part is delayed more by thicker glass, curving the wavefront.

qa.q: A plane wavefront falls on a concave mirror. The reflected wavefront is
qa.e: A concave mirror focuses a plane wave.

qa.q: Why does a plane wavefront passing through a thin prism get tilted?
qa.a: The part passing through the thicker base is delayed more than the part near the apex
qa.e: Light is slower in glass; more glass means more delay.

qa.q: In Huygens' principle, the secondary wavelets in a uniform medium travel with
qa.a: the same speed as the original wave
qa.e: They are part of the same wave in the same medium.

qa.q: Assertion (A): A lens forms an image because all rays from an object point reach the image point in equal times. Reason (R): Light travels slower in glass, so the thicker central part of a convex lens delays the central rays. Choose the correct option.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
qa.e: Extra glass in the middle compensates for the shorter geometrical path, equalising travel times.

qa.q: Light of wavelength 450 nm in vacuum enters glass of refractive index 1.5. What is its wavelength in glass (in nm)?
Light of frequency 6 × 10¹⁴ Hz enters water. What is its frequency in water (in units of 10¹⁴ Hz)?
qa.e: Frequency does not change on refraction.

qa.q: The speed of light in a medium is 2 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹. What is its refractive index?
By Huygens construction, Snell's law is
qa.e: The wavelet distances v₁τ and v₂τ give this ratio.

qa.q: When a wavefront goes from a denser to a rarer medium at an angle greater than the critical angle,
qa.a: no refracted wavefront forms and the light is totally reflected
qa.e: sin r would have to exceed 1, which is impossible.

qa.q: Light enters a medium where its speed is 2.4 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹ from air. If sin i = 0.5, what is sin r? (c = 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹)
qa.e: sin r = sin i × v₂/v₁ = 0.5 × 2.4/3 = 0.4.

qa.q: Why does light bend towards the normal when entering a denser medium, in the wave picture?
qa.a: The part of the wavefront that enters first slows down, turning the wavefront
qa.e: The slower side lags, rotating the wavefront towards the normal.

qa.q: A ray goes from glass (v = 2 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹) into air (v = 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹). What is sin ic?
qa.e: sin ic = v₁/v₂ = 2/3 ≈ 0.67.

qa.q: Two coherent waves each of intensity I₀ meet in phase. What is the resultant intensity (in units of I₀)?
qa.e: I = 4I₀ cos²0 = 4I₀.

qa.q: Two coherent sources of equal intensity I₀ produce interference. What is the intensity at a point where the phase difference is π (in units of I₀)?
qa.e: cos²(π/2) = 0.

qa.q: Two coherent waves of intensity I₀ meet with phase difference π/2. What is the resultant intensity (in units of I₀)?
qa.e: I = 4I₀ cos²(π/4) = 4I₀ × ½ = 2I₀.

qa.q: Light from two independent sodium lamps does not produce a steady interference pattern because
qa.a: their phase difference changes rapidly and randomly
qa.e: Independent sources are incoherent.

qa.q: For constructive interference, the path difference must be
qa.e: Waves arrive in phase when the path difference is a whole number of wavelengths.

qa.q: At a point, two coherent waves have a path difference of 2.5λ. The point is
qa.e: 2.5λ = (2 + ½)λ is the destructive condition.

qa.q: Two incoherent sources each of intensity I₀ illuminate a screen. The average intensity is (in units of I₀)
qa.e: Without a steady phase relation, intensities simply add.

qa.q: Assertion (A): In interference, the energy missing from dark fringes appears in bright fringes. Reason (R): The average intensity over the pattern equals the sum of individual intensities. Choose the correct option.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
qa.e: I varies between 0 and 4I₀ with average 2I₀, so energy is conserved and redistributed.

qa.q: In a double-slit experiment, λ = 500 nm, d = 0.2 mm and D = 1.2 m. What is the fringe width (in mm)?
The fringe width in a YDSE is 0.8 mm. How far from the central bright fringe is the 4th bright fringe (in mm)?
qa.e: x₄ = 4β = 3.2 mm.

qa.q: With β = 0.8 mm, where is the 2nd dark fringe from the centre (in mm)?
qa.e: Dark fringes at (n + ½)β, with the 2nd dark fringe at n = 1: 1.5 × 0.8 = 1.2 mm.

qa.q: Why did Young pass light from one source through two slits instead of using two lamps?
qa.a: Two slits lit by one source act as coherent sources
qa.e: The slits share the same wavefront, so their phase difference stays constant.

qa.q: The path difference at a point on the screen at height x in YDSE is approximately
qa.e: From geometry with D ≫ d, S₂P - S₁P ≈ xd/D.

qa.q: In YDSE, light of 600 nm gives a fringe width of 1.2 mm with D = 1 m. What is the slit separation (in mm)?
The central fringe in YDSE is bright because
qa.a: the path difference there is zero, so the waves arrive in phase
qa.e: Zero path difference gives constructive interference.

qa.q: The fringes in Young's double-slit experiment are
qa.e: β = λD/d is constant for small angles.

qa.q: A YDSE in air has β = 1.2 mm. What is β when it is immersed in water (n = 4/3) (in mm)?
The wavelength used in a YDSE is changed from 600 nm to 400 nm. The fringe width changes from 1.5 mm to (in mm)
The screen is moved from 1 m to 1.5 m from the slits. The fringe width changes from 0.4 mm to (in mm)
In a YDSE with d = 0.25 mm and D = 1 m, the distance between the central fringe and the 5th bright fringe is 10 mm. What is the wavelength (in nm)?
In a YDSE using white light, the fringe closest to the central white fringe on either side is
qa.e: Shorter wavelength gives smaller β, so violet fringes are nearest.

qa.q: Two coherent waves of intensity I₀ each meet with path difference λ/4. What is the intensity there (in units of I₀)?
qa.e: φ = 2π × ¼ = π/2. I = 4I₀ cos²(π/4) = 2I₀.

qa.q: In a YDSE, the maximum intensity is I_max. What is the intensity at a point where the path difference is λ/6?
qa.e: φ = π/3. I = I_max cos²(π/6) = I_max × 3/4.

qa.q: Assertion (A): The total light energy reaching the screen in YDSE is unchanged by interference. Reason (R): Interference only redistributes energy between bright and dark fringes. Choose the correct option.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
qa.e: Energy conservation holds; interference changes where energy goes, not how much.

qa.q: Light of wavelength 500 nm passes through a slit of width 0.1 mm. What is the width of the central maximum on a screen 2 m away (in mm)?
For a single slit of width a, the first minimum occurs at
qa.e: The slit divides into two halves whose contributions cancel.

qa.q: The width of the central maximum in single-slit diffraction is 4 mm. If the slit width is doubled, the new width is (in mm)
qa.e: Width ∝ 1/a.

qa.q: The angular width of the central maximum for λ = 600 nm and a = 0.6 mm is (in mrad)
qa.e: Angular width = 2λ/a = 2 × 600 × 10⁻⁹/6 × 10⁻⁴ = 2 × 10⁻³ rad.

qa.q: Diffraction of light is noticeable only when
qa.a: the size of the aperture or obstacle is comparable to the wavelength
qa.e: λ for light is tiny (~500 nm), so only small apertures show it clearly.

qa.q: In single-slit diffraction, the secondary maxima are
qa.a: much less intense than the central maximum
qa.e: Intensity falls rapidly away from the centre.

qa.q: Light of wavelength 600 nm forms a diffraction pattern whose first minimum is at θ = 30°. What is the slit width (in µm)? (sin 30° = 0.5)
Why do we hear sound around corners but cannot see around them?
qa.a: Sound wavelengths (metres) are comparable to doorways; light wavelengths (~500 nm) are far smaller
qa.e: Diffraction is significant only when wavelength is comparable to the gap.

qa.q: In a double-slit pattern, the bright fringes are
qa.e: Interference gives uniform fringes β = λD/d.

qa.q: In single-slit diffraction, compared with the secondary maxima, the central maximum is
qa.a: twice as wide and much brighter
qa.e: Its angular width is 2λ/a versus λ/a for others.

qa.q: Interference arises from superposition of waves from
qa.e: Two slits act as two coherent sources.

qa.q: In the razor-blade activity, which light source is suitable?
qa.a: A distant clear bulb with a straight filament
qa.e: A narrow, bright, distant source gives a clear pattern safely.

qa.q: In YDSE, λ = 500 nm, d = 0.5 mm and D = 1.5 m. What is the fringe width (in mm)?
A single slit of width 0.5 mm is lit by 500 nm light. What is the width of the central maximum on a screen 1.5 m away (in mm)?
In Huygens construction, a plane wavefront is incident on a plane mirror at angle i. The reflected wavefront makes an angle r with the mirror where
qa.e: Congruent triangles in the construction show equal angles.

qa.q: Two coherent sources each of intensity I₀ interfere. What is the ratio of maximum to minimum intensity?
qa.e: I_max = 4I₀ and I_min = 0 for equal intensities.

qa.q: Unpolarised light of intensity 60 W m⁻² passes through one polaroid. What is the transmitted intensity (in W m⁻²)?
qa.e: A polaroid passes half of unpolarised light.

qa.q: What does the phenomenon of polarisation prove about light?
qa.e: Only transverse waves have a direction of vibration that can be filtered.

qa.q: Why can sound waves in air not be polarised?
qa.a: They are longitudinal, vibrating along the direction of travel
qa.e: Polarisation needs vibrations perpendicular to travel.

qa.q: Two polaroids are placed with their pass axes perpendicular (crossed). Unpolarised light of intensity I₀ falls on them. The intensity after both is
qa.e: The first gives I₀/2 polarised light; the second, at 90°, blocks it.

qa.q: In the string-and-slit analogy for polarisation, a horizontal vibration reaches a vertical slit. What happens?
qa.e: Only vibrations along the slit can pass.

qa.q: A single polaroid is rotated slowly in a beam of unpolarised light. The transmitted intensity
qa.e: Unpolarised light has no preferred direction.

qa.q: Plane polarised light is light in which
qa.a: the electric field vibrates in a single plane
qa.e: Its E vector oscillates along one line perpendicular to travel.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Light passing through a polaroid has half the intensity of the incident unpolarised light. Reason (R): The polaroid passes only the component of E along its axis, and averaging over all directions gives one half. Choose the correct option.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
qa.e: The average of cos²θ over all angles is ½.

qa.q: Plane polarised light of intensity 40 W m⁻² falls on an analyser at 60° to its plane of polarisation. What is the transmitted intensity (in W m⁻²)?
Polarised light of intensity I₀ falls on an analyser at 30°. What fraction is transmitted?
Unpolarised light of intensity 32 W m⁻² passes through two polaroids whose axes are at 45°. What is the final intensity (in W m⁻²)?
qa.e: After the first: 16. After the second: 16 × cos²45° = 8.

qa.q: Unpolarised light of intensity I₀ passes through three polaroids: P₁, P₂ at 30° to P₁, and P₃ at 90° to P₁. What is the final intensity (as a fraction of I₀)?
Two polaroids are crossed. A third polaroid is inserted between them with its axis at 45°. What fraction of unpolarised light now passes?
qa.e: I₀/2 × ½ × ½ = I₀/8.

qa.q: Malus' law states that the intensity transmitted by an analyser is
qa.e: The amplitude goes as cosθ, so intensity goes as cos²θ.

qa.q: Why do polarising sunglasses reduce glare from a wet road?
qa.a: Light reflected from the road is partly polarised, and the lenses block that polarisation
qa.e: Reflected glare is largely horizontally polarised; the lenses' axis is vertical.

qa.q: At what angle should an analyser be set relative to the polariser to transmit half of the polarised light (in degrees)?
qa.e: cos²45° = ½.

qa.q: What is the minimum energy needed to remove an electron from a metal surface called?
qa.e: φ₀ is the minimum energy an electron needs to escape the surface.

qa.q: A work function of 4 eV equals how many joules (in units of 10⁻¹⁹ J)?
Who discovered the electron through experiments on cathode rays?
qa.e: Thomson showed cathode rays are negatively charged particles (1897).

qa.q: Which type of electron emission uses a very strong electric field?
qa.e: Fields of about 10⁸ V m⁻¹ can pull electrons out of a metal.

qa.q: In a vacuum tube, electrons are released by heating a filament. This is
qa.e: Heat gives electrons enough energy to overcome the work function.

qa.q: Why can free electrons not escape a metal on their own at room temperature?
qa.a: They are held back by the attraction of the positive ions near the surface
qa.e: A surface potential barrier must be overcome.

qa.q: Which metal from this list has the lowest work function?
qa.e: Alkali metals like caesium release electrons most easily.

qa.q: Thomson's and Millikan's experiments together allowed scientists to find
qa.a: the mass of the electron (from e/m and e)
qa.e: m = e/(e/m) once both e and e/m are known.

qa.q: Who first observed that ultraviolet light helps sparks pass across a gap?
qa.e: Hertz noticed this in 1887 during his EM wave experiments.

qa.q: A negatively charged zinc plate is exposed to UV light. It
qa.e: UV ejects electrons, discharging the plate.

qa.q: Below the threshold frequency, increasing the intensity of light falling on a metal
qa.e: Each photon has too little energy, however many there are.

qa.q: Which of these metals shows the photoelectric effect with visible light?
qa.e: Alkali metals have low work functions.

qa.q: In a photoelectric experiment, the photosensitive plate on which light falls is the
qa.e: Electrons are emitted from it and collected by the anode.

qa.q: Why is the photoelectric tube evacuated?
qa.a: So that emitted electrons are not stopped by collisions with gas molecules
qa.e: Electrons must travel freely from emitter to collector.

qa.q: Why is a quartz window used in the photoelectric tube?
qa.a: Quartz lets ultraviolet light through, while ordinary glass absorbs it
qa.e: Many metals need UV for emission.

qa.q: An uncharged zinc plate is exposed to ultraviolet light for some time. Its charge becomes
qa.e: It loses electrons and is left positive.

qa.q: The stopping potential for a photosensitive surface is 2.5 V. What is the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons (in units of 10⁻¹⁹ J)?
When the intensity of light (above threshold frequency) is doubled, the saturation photocurrent
qa.e: The number of photons, and hence electrons, per second doubles.

qa.q: When the intensity of light is doubled at fixed frequency, the stopping potential
qa.e: Kmax depends on frequency, not intensity.

qa.q: What is meant by saturation current?
qa.a: The maximum photocurrent, when all emitted electrons reach the collector
qa.e: Further increase in anode potential cannot increase it.

qa.q: Photoelectrons have a maximum kinetic energy of 4.8 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. What is the stopping potential (in V)?
How quickly does photoelectric emission begin after light falls on the surface?
qa.e: There is no measurable time lag even for very weak light.

qa.q: On a graph of photocurrent versus anode potential for two intensities at the same frequency, the curves
qa.a: meet the potential axis at the same stopping potential but have different saturation currents
qa.e: Same frequency means same V₀; higher intensity means higher saturation current.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Doubling the intensity of light doubles the photocurrent. Reason (R): Photocurrent depends on the number of photons striking the surface per second. Choose the correct option.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
qa.e: More photons per second eject more electrons per second.

qa.q: On a graph of stopping potential against frequency, the slope of the line is
qa.a: h/e, the same for all metals
qa.e: From eV₀ = hν - φ₀, V₀ = (h/e)ν - φ₀/e.

qa.q: The V₀-ν line for a metal cuts the frequency axis at 6 × 10¹⁴ Hz. What is the threshold frequency (in units of 10¹⁴ Hz)?
qa.e: The intercept where V₀ = 0 is ν₀.

qa.q: For that metal (ν₀ = 6 × 10¹⁴ Hz), what is the work function (in eV)? (h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C; give to 2 decimal places)
According to classical wave theory, the maximum kinetic energy of photoelectrons should depend on
qa.e: A more intense wave carries more energy, so wave theory expected faster electrons.

qa.q: Which observation could wave theory NOT explain?
qa.a: No emission below a threshold frequency, however intense the light
qa.e: Wave theory says energy builds up for any frequency.

qa.q: Two metals A and B have threshold frequencies 4 × 10¹⁴ Hz and 6 × 10¹⁴ Hz. Their V₀-ν lines are
qa.a: parallel, with B's line shifted to higher frequency
qa.e: Same slope h/e; different intercepts ν₀.

qa.q: V₀ for a metal is 1 V at ν₁ and 3 V at ν₂ = ν₁ + 5 × 10¹⁴ Hz. What is h/e (in units of 10⁻¹⁵ V s)?
qa.e: h/e = ΔV₀/Δν = 2/(5 × 10¹⁴) = 4 × 10⁻¹⁵ V s.

qa.q: According to wave theory, an electron hit by very dim light would
qa.a: need a long time to absorb enough energy before escaping
qa.e: Energy spread over the wavefront would trickle in slowly.

qa.q: Photons of energy 5 eV fall on a metal with work function 3 eV. What is the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons (in eV)?
qa.e: Kmax = hν - φ₀ = 5 - 3 = 2 eV.

qa.q: For the same case (photon energy 5 eV, φ₀ = 3 eV), what is the stopping potential (in V)?
qa.e: eV₀ = Kmax = 2 eV, so V₀ = 2 V.

qa.q: A metal has φ₀ = 2.07 eV. What is its threshold wavelength (in nm)? (hc = 1242 eV nm)
A metal has a work function of 3.315 eV. What is its threshold frequency (in units of 10¹⁴ Hz)? (h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, 1 eV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J)
Light of wavelength 400 nm falls on a metal of work function 2.1 eV. What is Kmax (in eV)? (hc = 1240 eV nm)
qa.e: Photon energy = 1240/400 = 3.1 eV. Kmax = 3.1 - 2.1 = 1 eV.

qa.q: How does Einstein's theory explain the threshold frequency?
qa.a: A photon must have energy hν at least equal to φ₀ to free an electron
qa.e: If hν < φ₀, no single photon can free an electron.

qa.q: Millikan's verification of Einstein's equation gave a value of Planck's constant from
qa.a: the slope of the stopping potential versus frequency graph
qa.e: Slope = h/e; multiplying by e gives h.

qa.q: Light of wavelength 600 nm falls on a metal of work function 2.5 eV. What happens? (hc = 1240 eV nm)
qa.a: No electrons are emitted, since the photon energy (about 2.07 eV) is less than φ₀

qa.q: Light of wavelength 248 nm falls on a metal of work function 3 eV. What is the stopping potential (in V)? (hc = 1240 eV nm)
qa.e: Photon energy = 1240/248 = 5 eV. Kmax = 2 eV, so V₀ = 2 V.

qa.q: For a metal, V₀ = 1.0 V at ν = 7 × 10¹⁴ Hz and 2.6 V at 11 × 10¹⁴ Hz. What is h (in units of 10⁻³⁴ J s)? (e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)
qa.e: h/e = 1.6/(4 × 10¹⁴) = 4 × 10⁻¹⁵ V s. h = 4 × 10⁻¹⁵ × 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 6.4 × 10⁻³⁴ J s. This experimental value is close to the accepted 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s.

qa.q: What is the energy of a photon of wavelength 500 nm (in eV)? (hc = 1240 eV nm)
The momentum of a photon of wavelength 663 nm is (in units of 10⁻²⁷ kg m s⁻¹) (h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s)
The intensity of a monochromatic beam is doubled. The energy of each photon
qa.e: Intensity depends on the number of photons; each still has hν.

qa.q: Which statement about photons is correct?
qa.a: They travel at c in vacuum and have zero rest mass
qa.e: Photons are massless and neutral.

qa.q: A metal with φ₀ = 2 eV is lit by photons of energy 2.5 eV. If the photon energy is raised to 3.5 eV, Kmax becomes how many times larger?
qa.e: Kmax goes from 0.5 eV to 1.5 eV, i.e. 3 times.

qa.q: Assertion (A): A photon has momentum even though its rest mass is zero. Reason (R): Photon momentum is p = E/c. Choose the correct option.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
qa.e: Energy and momentum are linked by p = E/c for massless particles.

qa.q: A source of 2 W emits light whose photons each have energy 4 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. How many photons does it emit per second (in units of 10¹⁸)?
A 10 W bulb emits light of wavelength 663 nm. How many photons per second (in units of 10¹⁹)? (h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, c = 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹)
Why are photons not deflected by electric or magnetic fields?
qa.e: Fields exert forces only on charged particles.

qa.q: A photon of wavelength 331.5 nm has momentum (in units of 10⁻²⁷ kg m s⁻¹)? (h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s)
In a collision between a photon and an electron, which quantities are conserved?
qa.e: These are conserved in all collisions; photon number need not be.

qa.q: Two sources emit the same power, one in red light (700 nm) and one in violet (400 nm). Which emits more photons per second?
qa.e: Red photons carry less energy each, so more are needed for the same power.

qa.q: What is the energy of a photon of wavelength 663 nm (in eV)? (h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, c = 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹, 1 eV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J)
Assertion (A): The number of photons can change in a collision. Reason (R): Photons can be absorbed or created, while energy and momentum are conserved. Choose the correct option.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
qa.e: Unlike charge, photon number is not conserved.

qa.q: What is the de Broglie wavelength of a 0.1 kg ball moving at 6.63 m s⁻¹ (in units of 10⁻³³ m)? (h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s)
An electron is accelerated through 400 V. What is its de Broglie wavelength (in nm)? (λ = 1.227/√V nm)
The momentum of a particle is doubled. Its de Broglie wavelength
qa.e: λ = h/p.

qa.q: The kinetic energy of an electron is made four times larger. Its de Broglie wavelength becomes
qa.e: λ ∝ 1/√K, so √4 = 2 and λ halves.

qa.q: Why are wave effects not observed for everyday objects like a moving car?
qa.a: Their de Broglie wavelengths are far too small to detect
qa.e: With large m, λ = h/(mv) is negligibly small.

qa.q: An electron and a proton have the same kinetic energy. Which has the longer de Broglie wavelength?
qa.e: λ = h/√(2mK); smaller mass gives longer λ.

qa.q: An electron and a proton have the same speed. The ratio λ(electron)/λ(proton) equals
qa.e: λ = h/(mv) ∝ 1/m at fixed v.

qa.q: The de Broglie wavelength of an electron through 100 V is about 0.12 nm. This is comparable to
qa.a: the spacing between atoms in a crystal
qa.e: Atomic spacings are about 0.1 nm, so crystals can diffract electrons.

qa.q: A proton (m = 1.66 × 10⁻²⁷ kg) moves at 4 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹. What is its de Broglie wavelength (in pm)? (h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s)
An electron is accelerated through 1600 V. What is its de Broglie wavelength (in nm)? (λ = 1.227/√V nm; give to 2 decimal places)
An alpha particle and a proton are accelerated through the same potential difference. What is λ(proton)/λ(alpha)? (m_α = 4m_p, q_α = 2e)
A neutron and an electron have the same de Broglie wavelength. Which statement is correct?
qa.e: λ = h/p, so equal λ means equal p.

qa.q: A particle's kinetic energy is increased from K to 9K. Its de Broglie wavelength becomes
A photon and an electron both have a de Broglie wavelength of 0.62 nm. What is the energy of the photon (in eV)? (hc = 1240 eV nm)
The de Broglie wavelength of an electron is 0.2 nm. If it is accelerated so that its momentum doubles, its new wavelength is (in nm)
Electrons with λ = 0.1 nm are used in a microscope instead of light of 500 nm. Roughly how many times smaller details can they resolve?
qa.e: Resolution scales with wavelength: 500/0.1 = 5000.

qa.q: In Thomson's model of the atom,
qa.a: positive charge is spread uniformly, with electrons embedded in it
qa.e: This is the 'plum pudding' or watermelon picture.

qa.q: Which observation in the Geiger-Marsden experiment led to the idea of a nucleus?
qa.a: A few alpha particles were scattered through very large angles
qa.e: Only a concentrated positive charge can turn alpha particles back.

qa.q: What did most alpha particles do on striking the gold foil?
qa.a: They passed through with little or no deflection
qa.e: Most of the atom is empty space.

qa.q: Why was a very thin gold foil used?
qa.a: So that each alpha particle would be scattered by at most one nucleus
qa.e: Thin foil minimises multiple scattering events.

qa.q: The nucleus is smaller than the atom by a factor of about
qa.e: Atomic size ~10⁻¹⁰ m, nuclear size ~10⁻¹⁵ to 10⁻¹⁴ m.

qa.q: Why could Thomson's model not explain large-angle scattering of alpha particles?
qa.a: Spread-out positive charge cannot produce a strong enough force to turn an alpha particle back
qa.e: A diffuse charge gives only small deflections.

qa.q: How were the scattered alpha particles detected in the experiment?
qa.a: By flashes of light on a zinc sulphide screen seen through a microscope
qa.e: Each alpha hit produces a tiny scintillation on ZnS.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Most of the volume of an atom is empty space. Reason (R): Most alpha particles pass through a thin metal foil without deflection. Choose the correct option.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
qa.e: The experimental fact (R) is the evidence for the conclusion (A).

qa.q: What is the impact parameter for a head-on collision of an alpha particle with a nucleus?
qa.e: The line of motion passes through the nucleus.

qa.q: An alpha particle with a large impact parameter
qa.a: is scattered through a small angle
qa.e: Far from the nucleus, the Coulomb force is weak.

qa.q: A 9 MeV alpha particle approaches a nucleus of Z = 45 head-on. What is the distance of closest approach (in fm)? (k = 9 × 10⁹ N m² C⁻², e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)
If the kinetic energy of the alpha particle is doubled, the distance of closest approach
At the distance of closest approach in a head-on collision, the alpha particle's kinetic energy is
qa.a: zero; it has all become potential energy
qa.e: It momentarily stops before being pushed back.

qa.q: What does the distance of closest approach tell us about the nucleus?
qa.a: It gives an upper limit to the size of the nucleus
qa.e: The nucleus must be smaller than d for the Coulomb law to hold up to that distance.

qa.q: For the same alpha energy, the distance of closest approach for a nucleus with twice the charge is
qa.e: d ∝ Z.

qa.q: An alpha particle approaches a nucleus with a small impact parameter. Its scattering angle is
qa.e: Close approach means strong repulsion and large deflection.

qa.q: The total energy of an electron in a circular orbit of radius r around a proton is
qa.e: E = K + U = e²/(8πε₀r) - e²/(4πε₀r).

qa.q: For an electron in orbit, if the total energy is -3.4 eV, what is its kinetic energy (in eV)?
With E = -3.4 eV, what is the potential energy (in eV)?
What does the negative total energy of an orbiting electron tell us?
qa.a: It is bound to the nucleus and energy is needed to free it
qa.e: Zero energy corresponds to a free electron at rest at infinity.

qa.q: According to classical electromagnetic theory, an electron orbiting a nucleus should
qa.a: radiate energy and spiral into the nucleus
qa.e: An accelerating charge radiates and loses energy.

qa.q: Which observation could Rutherford's model not explain?
qa.a: The sharp line spectra of atoms
qa.e: A spiralling electron would emit a continuous spectrum.

qa.q: In Rutherford's model, which force provides the centripetal force on the electron?
qa.e: Coulomb attraction keeps the electron in orbit.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Rutherford's model cannot explain the stability of atoms. Reason (R): An accelerated charge radiates energy according to classical theory. Choose the correct option.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
qa.e: A circling electron is accelerated, so it would lose energy and collapse.

qa.q: An emission line spectrum consists of
qa.a: bright lines at specific wavelengths on a dark background
qa.e: Excited atoms emit at characteristic wavelengths.

qa.q: When white light passes through cool hydrogen gas, the transmitted spectrum shows
qa.a: dark lines at the wavelengths hydrogen emits
qa.e: Atoms absorb the same wavelengths they emit.

qa.q: Why are atomic spectra called the 'fingerprints' of elements?
qa.a: Each element has a unique, characteristic set of spectral lines
qa.e: No two elements share the same line pattern.

qa.q: The dark lines in the spectrum of sunlight are due to
qa.a: absorption of particular wavelengths by gases in the Sun's outer atmosphere
qa.e: Cooler gases above the hot surface absorb characteristic lines.

qa.q: A spectrum with bright lines at certain wavelengths is produced by
qa.a: a gas of atoms excited by heating or an electric discharge
qa.e: Isolated atoms in a gas emit line spectra.

qa.q: Which element was first discovered by studying the spectrum of the Sun?
qa.e: Its lines were seen in the solar spectrum before it was found on Earth.

qa.q: The emission line of an element is at 486 nm. At what wavelength will its absorption line appear (in nm)?
qa.e: Emission and absorption lines coincide.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Line spectra provide evidence that atomic energy levels are discrete. Reason (R): Only photons with energies equal to differences between levels are emitted or absorbed. Choose the correct option.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
qa.e: Discrete level differences give discrete photon energies and sharp lines.

qa.q: What is the radius of the second Bohr orbit of hydrogen (in Å)? (a₀ = 0.53 Å)
The ratio of the radius of the 3rd orbit to the radius of the 2nd orbit of hydrogen is
The speed of the electron in the first Bohr orbit is about 2.2 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹. What is it in the 4th orbit (in units of 10⁵ m s⁻¹)?
Bohr's quantisation condition for angular momentum is
qa.e: Angular momentum is an integral multiple of h/2π.

qa.q: The angular momentum of an electron in the 3rd orbit is (in units of h/2π)
qa.e: L = nh/2π with n = 3.

qa.q: According to Bohr, when does an atom emit radiation?
qa.a: When an electron jumps from a higher-energy orbit to a lower one
qa.e: Photon energy hν = Ei - Ef.

qa.q: Bohr's first postulate, that electrons in stationary orbits do not radiate, contradicts
qa.e: Classically, any accelerated charge must radiate.

qa.q: How does the radius of a Bohr orbit vary with the principal quantum number n?
qa.e: rn = n²a₀.

qa.q: What is the energy of the electron in the n = 5 state of hydrogen (in eV)?
How much energy is needed to excite a hydrogen atom from n = 1 to n = 3 (in eV)?
What is the ionisation energy of a hydrogen atom in its ground state (in eV)?
qa.e: Energy needed to take the electron from -13.6 eV to 0 is 13.6 eV.

qa.q: A hydrogen atom is in the n = 2 state. What minimum energy will ionise it (in eV)?
The ratio of energies E₁ : E₂ for hydrogen is
qa.e: En ∝ 1/n², so E₁/E₂ = 4.

qa.q: What evidence did the Franck-Hertz experiment provide?
qa.a: Atoms absorb energy only in discrete amounts, so energy levels are quantised
qa.e: Electron currents dropped at definite accelerating voltages.

qa.q: An electron in hydrogen has total energy -3.4 eV. What is its kinetic energy (in eV)?
qa.e: K = -E.

qa.q: A hydrogen atom in the ground state absorbs a photon of 12.75 eV. To which level does the electron rise?
What is the energy of the photon emitted when the electron in hydrogen falls from n = 2 to n = 1 (in eV)?
What is the wavelength of that photon (10.2 eV) (in nm)? (hc = 1240 eV nm)
qa.e: λ = 1240/10.2 ≈ 121.6 nm, in the ultraviolet.

qa.q: An electron in hydrogen falls from n = 4 to n = 2. What is the photon energy (in eV)?
For the transition n = 4 → n = 2 (2.55 eV), what is the wavelength (in nm)? (hc = 1240 eV nm)
qa.e: λ = 1240/2.55 ≈ 486.3 nm, a blue-green line.

qa.q: Which transition in hydrogen emits a photon of the longest wavelength among these?
qa.e: It has the smallest energy gap (1.89 eV), so the longest λ.

qa.q: A hydrogen atom absorbs light and its electron goes from n = 2 to n = 3. The photon absorbed has the same wavelength as the photon emitted in the transition
qa.e: Absorption and emission between the same levels involve equal energies.

qa.q: The Rydberg formula for hydrogen is
qa.e: Here nf < ni for emission.

qa.q: Using R = 1.1 × 10⁷ m⁻¹, what is the wavelength of the n = 2 to n = 1 line (in nm)? (give to 2 decimal places)
According to de Broglie, how many electron wavelengths fit around the circumference of the 2nd Bohr orbit?
qa.e: 2πr = nλ with n = 2.

qa.q: de Broglie's standing-wave condition 2πr = nλ leads to
qa.a: Bohr's quantisation of angular momentum, mvr = nh/2π
qa.e: Substituting λ = h/(mv) gives mvr = nh/2π.

qa.q: How many spectral lines can be emitted when hydrogen atoms excited to n = 6 return to the ground state?
Which atom or ion can the Bohr model describe well?
qa.e: Bohr's model works for one-electron, hydrogen-like systems.

qa.q: Which of these is a limitation of Bohr's model?
qa.a: It cannot explain the relative intensities of spectral lines
qa.e: It gives line positions but not their brightness.

qa.q: The ratio of the radii of the 1st and 3rd Bohr orbits of hydrogen is
qa.e: r ∝ n².

qa.q: The ratio E₂/E₄ for hydrogen energy levels is

Assertion (A): Only certain orbits are allowed in Bohr's model. Reason (R): Only orbits whose circumference is a whole number of de Broglie wavelengths can hold a standing wave. Choose the correct option.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
qa.e: The standing-wave condition picks out exactly the allowed orbits.

qa.q: 1 atomic mass unit is defined as
qa.a: 1/12 of the mass of a carbon-12 atom
qa.e: This is the modern definition.

qa.q: What is 1 u in kilograms (approximately)?
An element has two isotopes: 60% of mass 10 u and 40% of mass 11 u. What is its average atomic mass (in u)?
Why is the atomic mass of chlorine 35.47 u and not a whole number?
qa.a: Natural chlorine is a mixture of isotopes of different masses
qa.e: A weighted average of 35 u and 37 u isotopes gives 35.47 u.

qa.q: The radius of a nucleus is of the order of
qa.e: Nuclei are a few femtometres across.

qa.q: What fraction of the mass of an atom lies in its nucleus?
qa.e: Protons and neutrons are about 1836 times heavier than electrons.

qa.q: Which instrument is used to measure atomic masses precisely?
qa.e: It separates ions by their mass-to-charge ratio.

qa.q: A ratio of atomic size to nuclear size of about 10⁴ means that if the nucleus were 1 cm across, the atom would be about
How many neutrons are there in ²⁷₁₃Al?
Who discovered the neutron, and in which year?
qa.e: Chadwick identified the neutral radiation from alpha-bombarded beryllium.

qa.q: Nuclides with the same atomic number but different mass numbers are called
qa.e: Same Z, different N.

qa.q: ¹⁴₆C and ¹⁴₇N are
qa.e: Same A = 14, different Z.

qa.q: Which pair are isotones?
qa.e: Both have N = 118.

qa.q: In the experiment that discovered the neutron, which element was bombarded with alpha particles?
qa.e: Beryllium gave out the penetrating neutral radiation.

qa.q: How many nucleons are in ⁵⁶₂₆Fe?
qa.e: A = 56 is the total number of protons and neutrons.

qa.q: Why does a neutron, though uncharged, count towards the mass number?
qa.a: Mass number counts all nucleons, protons and neutrons, each of mass about 1 u
qa.e: A = Z + N.

qa.q: What is the radius of a nucleus with A = 64 (in fm)? (R₀ = 1.2 fm)
The ratio of the radii of nuclei with A = 27 and A = 125 is
Why is nuclear density nearly the same for all nuclei?
qa.a: Both the mass and the volume of a nucleus are proportional to A
qa.e: Density = mass/volume, and A cancels.

qa.q: The nuclear density is about
qa.e: Roughly 10¹⁴ times the density of water.

qa.q: A nucleus has a radius of 6 fm. What is its mass number? (R₀ = 1.2 fm)
If the mass number of a nucleus is made 8 times larger, its radius becomes
The volume of a nucleus is proportional to
qa.e: V ∝ R³ ∝ A.

qa.q: Roughly how many times denser is nuclear matter than water?
What is the energy equivalent of 1 g of matter (in units of 10¹³ J)? (c = 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹)
A mass defect of 0.01 u corresponds to a binding energy of (in MeV)
Find the binding energy of ⁴He: m(¹H) = 1.007825 u, mn = 1.008665 u, m(⁴He) = 4.002603 u (in MeV, to 2 decimal places). (1 u = 931.5 MeV)
The mass defect of a nucleus is defined as
qa.a: total mass of separate nucleons minus mass of the nucleus
qa.e: ΔM = [Zmp + Nmn] - M.

qa.q: Binding energy of a nucleus is
qa.a: the energy needed to separate it completely into its protons and neutrons
qa.e: Eb = ΔMc².

qa.q: What energy is released when 2 kg of matter is fully converted into energy (in units of 10¹⁷ J)? (c = 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹)
A nucleus has a mass defect of 0.1 u. What is its binding energy (in MeV)?

Assertion (A): The mass of a nucleus is less than the sum of the masses of its nucleons. Reason (R): Energy is released when nucleons bind, and this energy carries away mass according to E = mc². Choose the correct option.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
qa.e: The released binding energy corresponds to the mass defect.

qa.q: A nucleus with A = 20 has a binding energy of 160 MeV. What is its binding energy per nucleon (in MeV)?
Near which mass number does the binding energy per nucleon curve reach its peak?
qa.e: Iron-56 region has the highest Ebn (about 8.75 MeV).

qa.q: Which nucleus is the most stable?
qa.e: It has the highest binding energy per nucleon.

qa.q: What does the nearly constant binding energy per nucleon for 30 < A < 170 suggest?
qa.a: The nuclear force is short-range and saturates
qa.e: Each nucleon interacts only with its nearest neighbours.

qa.q: Find Ebn for ¹⁶O, given its mass defect 0.13708 u (in MeV, to 2 decimal places). (1 u = 931.5 MeV)
Why does fission of a heavy nucleus release energy?
qa.a: The products have a higher binding energy per nucleon than the original nucleus
qa.e: Moving towards the peak of the curve releases energy.

qa.q: A ⁴He nucleus has a total binding energy of 28.3 MeV. What is its binding energy per nucleon (in MeV)?
Assertion (A): Fusion of light nuclei releases energy. Reason (R): The binding energy per nucleon increases as light nuclei combine into heavier ones (up to A ≈ 56). Choose the correct option.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
qa.e: Products are more tightly bound, so mass is lost and energy released.

qa.q: Which property best describes the nuclear force?
qa.a: Strong, short-range and nearly charge independent
qa.e: These three features summarise the nuclear force.

qa.q: Below roughly what separation does the nuclear force between nucleons become repulsive (in fm)?
qa.e: The potential minimum is near 0.8 fm.

qa.q: The nuclear force between a neutron and a proton compared with that between two protons is
qa.e: Charge independence: n-p ≈ p-p ≈ n-n.

qa.q: Why does a nucleus not fly apart due to the repulsion between protons?
qa.a: The attractive nuclear force is much stronger than the Coulomb repulsion at those distances
qa.e: The strong nuclear force overcomes the Coulomb repulsion.

qa.q: Two nucleons are 10 fm apart. The nuclear force between them is
qa.e: Beyond a few fm, the nuclear force falls almost to zero.

qa.q: In the potential energy versus separation graph for two nucleons, the region to the left of the minimum (smaller r) corresponds to
qa.e: U rises steeply as r decreases, so the force pushes them apart.

qa.q: Why is there no simple formula for the nuclear force like Coulomb's law?
qa.a: It is complicated: strongly attractive at a few fm, repulsive at shorter distances and quickly vanishing beyond
qa.e: Its behaviour changes sharply with distance.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Nuclear density is nearly constant for all nuclei. Reason (R): The nuclear force is short-range and saturates, so each nucleon interacts only with its neighbours. Choose the correct option.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
qa.e: Saturation means nucleons pack at a fixed spacing, giving constant density.

qa.q: About how much energy is released in one fission of ²³⁵U (in MeV)?
qa.e: Each fission releases about 200 MeV.

qa.q: Complete the reaction: ²³⁵₉₂U + ¹₀n → ¹⁴⁴₅₆Ba + ⁸⁹₃₆Kr + x ¹₀n. What is x?
qa.e: Mass numbers: 236 = 144 + 89 + x, so x = 3.

qa.q: Energy per reaction in a typical chemical reaction compared with a nuclear reaction is
qa.e: eV versus MeV.

qa.q: How many fissions per second are needed to produce 1 W of power? (200 MeV per fission, 1 MeV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹³ J; answer in units of 10¹⁰)
qa.e: Energy per fission = 200 × 1.6 × 10⁻¹³ = 3.2 × 10⁻¹¹ J. Fissions per second = 1/3.2 × 10⁻¹¹ ≈ 3.125 × 10¹⁰.

qa.q: What makes a chain reaction possible in fission?
qa.a: Each fission releases more neutrons, which can cause further fissions
qa.e: 2 or 3 neutrons per fission can sustain the chain.

qa.q: A ²³⁵U nucleus fissions and releases 0.2 u of mass as energy. How much energy is released (in MeV)?
In which form is most of the energy of fission released?
qa.a: Kinetic energy of the fission fragments
qa.e: The two charged fragments fly apart at high speed.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Uncontrolled chain reactions release energy explosively. Reason (R): In each step the number of fissions multiplies because each fission releases more than one neutron. Choose the correct option.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
qa.e: Without control, fissions grow exponentially in a tiny fraction of a second.

qa.q: Why does fusion require very high temperatures?
qa.a: Nuclei need very high kinetic energy to overcome their Coulomb repulsion and come close enough to fuse
qa.e: Only at millions of kelvin do nuclei move fast enough.

qa.q: In the proton-proton cycle in the Sun, how many protons are effectively combined to form one ⁴He nucleus?
qa.e: Net: 4 ¹H → ⁴He + 2e⁺ + 2ν + energy.

qa.q: A fusion reaction converts 0.0189 u of mass into energy. What is the Q-value (in MeV, to 2 decimal places)? (1 u = 931.5 MeV)
Find the Q-value of ²H + ³H → ⁴He + n: m(²H) = 2.014102 u, m(³H) = 3.016049 u, m(⁴He) = 4.002603 u, mn = 1.008665 u (in MeV, to 2 decimal places).
A positive Q-value for a nuclear reaction means
qa.a: energy is released (the products have less total mass)
qa.e: Q = (initial mass - final mass)c² > 0.

qa.q: What is the main challenge in building a controlled fusion reactor?
qa.a: Confining an extremely hot plasma long enough for fusion to occur
qa.e: No material wall can hold plasma at millions of kelvin; magnetic confinement is used.

qa.q: Which international project, with India as a partner, is building an experimental fusion reactor?
qa.e: ITER in France aims to demonstrate fusion power.

qa.q: The Sun releases about 26.7 MeV per helium nucleus formed. If about 9 × 10³⁷ helium nuclei form each second, what is its power (in units of 10²⁶ W)? (1 MeV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹³ J)
qa.e: P = 9 × 10³⁷ × 26.7 × 1.6 × 10⁻¹³ ≈ 3.84 × 10²⁶ W, close to the Sun's measured output.

qa.q: Which is an elemental semiconductor?
qa.e: Si and Ge are the elemental semiconductors.

qa.q: A material has a resistivity of 10⁻⁷ Ω m. It is most likely a
qa.e: Metals have ρ from about 10⁻² to 10⁻⁸ Ω m.

qa.q: Which is an advantage of semiconductor devices over vacuum tubes?
qa.a: They are small, need low power and have no heated filament
qa.e: Solid-state devices are compact and efficient.

qa.q: Gallium arsenide (GaAs) is an example of
qa.e: It is made of two elements, Ga and As.

qa.q: The resistivity range of semiconductors is roughly
qa.e: Between metals and insulators.

qa.q: In a vacuum tube, electrons are supplied by
qa.e: Thermionic emission from a heated cathode.

qa.q: Which is an organic semiconductor?
qa.e: Some organic molecules and polymers behave as semiconductors.

qa.q: Roughly how many orders of magnitude separate the resistivity of a typical insulator (10¹⁵ Ω m) from that of a metal (10⁻⁸ Ω m)?
The energy gap of an insulator is typically
qa.e: Large Eg keeps electrons out of the conduction band.

qa.q: The energy gap of silicon at room temperature is about (in eV)
qa.e: Si ≈ 1.1 eV; Ge ≈ 0.7 eV.

qa.q: In a metal, the valence and conduction bands
qa.a: overlap, or the conduction band is partly filled
qa.e: Electrons can move into nearby empty states easily.

qa.q: Why do energy bands form in solids?
qa.a: Atomic energy levels of neighbouring atoms overlap and split into many closely spaced levels
qa.e: Interaction between many atoms broadens each level into a band.

qa.q: A material has an energy gap of 0.7 eV. It is most likely
qa.e: Ge has Eg ≈ 0.7 eV.

qa.q: The band that holds the electrons responsible for conduction in a semiconductor is the
qa.e: Electrons excited to the conduction band move freely.

qa.q: Diamond has an energy gap of about 6 eV. Diamond is
qa.e: Eg > 3 eV.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Semiconductors conduct a little at room temperature. Reason (R): Their energy gap is small enough for some electrons to be thermally excited to the conduction band. Choose the correct option.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
qa.e: A small Eg lets thermal energy promote some electrons.

qa.q: In an intrinsic semiconductor,
qa.a: the number of free electrons equals the number of holes
qa.e: ne = nh = ni because they form in pairs.

qa.q: How many covalent bonds does each silicon atom form in a silicon crystal?
qa.e: Silicon has four valence electrons and bonds with four neighbours.

qa.q: A hole in a semiconductor is
qa.a: a vacancy left by a missing electron in a bond, acting as a positive charge
qa.e: It moves as neighbouring electrons fill it.

qa.q: At absolute zero temperature, a pure semiconductor
qa.e: All bonds are intact; there are no free carriers.

qa.q: In an intrinsic semiconductor, electrons give a current of 3 mA and holes 1 mA. What is the total current (in mA)?
qa.e: I = Ie + Ih = 4 mA.

qa.q: When the temperature of an intrinsic semiconductor rises, its conductivity
qa.e: More bonds break, creating more electron-hole pairs.

qa.q: A pure silicon sample has ni = 1.5 × 10¹⁶ m⁻³. What is its hole concentration (in units of 10¹⁶ m⁻³)?
qa.e: nh = ni for an intrinsic semiconductor.

qa.q: Under an applied electric field in a semiconductor, holes move
qa.a: in the direction of the field
qa.e: They behave like positive charges.

qa.q: Silicon doped with boron becomes
qa.a: p-type, with holes as majority carriers
qa.e: Boron is trivalent, an acceptor.

qa.q: Which impurity makes germanium n-type?
qa.e: Antimony is pentavalent, a donor.

qa.q: In a p-type semiconductor, the minority carriers are
qa.e: Holes are majority; electrons minority.

qa.q: Where does the donor energy level lie in an n-type semiconductor?
qa.a: Just below the bottom of the conduction band
qa.e: A small energy frees the donor electron into the conduction band.

qa.q: A pentavalent impurity atom in silicon forms how many covalent bonds?
qa.e: Four electrons bond with Si neighbours; the fifth is loosely bound.

qa.q: An n-type semiconductor is
qa.e: Each donor atom that gives an electron becomes a positive ion; the total charge is zero.

qa.q: Why does doping greatly increase the conductivity of a semiconductor?
qa.a: Each dopant atom contributes a charge carrier, adding far more carriers than are thermally produced
qa.e: Even a tiny fraction of dopant atoms supplies many carriers compared with ni.

qa.q: Assertion (A): Indium-doped silicon is p-type. Reason (R): Indium is trivalent and creates a hole by accepting an electron from a neighbouring bond. Choose the correct option.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
qa.e: A missing bond electron creates a hole, the majority carrier.

qa.q: Silicon with ni = 1.5 × 10¹⁶ m⁻³ is doped so that ne = 4.5 × 10²² m⁻³. What is nh (in units of 10⁹ m⁻³)?
The law of mass action for semiconductors states that
qa.e: This holds in thermal equilibrium.

qa.q: Germanium with ni = 2 × 10¹⁹ m⁻³ is doped with acceptors so that nh = 4 × 10²³ m⁻³. What is ne (in units of 10¹⁵ m⁻³)?
qa.e: ne = ni²/nh = 4 × 10³⁸/4 × 10²³ = 10¹⁵ m⁻³.

qa.q: When donor impurities are added to an intrinsic semiconductor, the hole concentration
qa.e: nh = ni²/ne; more electrons means fewer holes.

qa.q: A semiconductor has ne = 10²² m⁻³ and nh = 10¹⁰ m⁻³. What type is it?
qa.e: Electrons are the majority carriers.

qa.q: For that semiconductor (ne = 10²² m⁻³, nh = 10¹⁰ m⁻³), what is ni (in units of 10¹⁶ m⁻³)?
qa.e: ni = √(ne nh) = √(10³²) = 10¹⁶ m⁻³.

qa.q: A full-wave rectifier is fed with 50 Hz AC. What is the frequency of its output ripple (in Hz)?
qa.e: Both half-cycles give pulses, so there are 100 pulses per second.

qa.q: Which statement is correct for a p-type semiconductor in equilibrium?
qa.a: nh ≫ ne and ne × nh = ni²
qa.e: Holes dominate, and the mass action product is unchanged.

qa.q: The depletion region of a p-n junction contains
qa.a: immobile charged ions and no free charge carriers
qa.e: Carriers near the junction have diffused away, leaving fixed ions.

qa.q: Diffusion current across a p-n junction is caused by
qa.a: majority carriers moving from higher to lower concentration
qa.e: Electrons go n → p and holes p → n by diffusion.

qa.q: The barrier potential of a silicon p-n junction is about (in V)
The direction of the electric field in the depletion region is
qa.a: from the n-side to the p-side
qa.e: Positive donor ions are on the n-side, negative acceptor ions on the p-side.

qa.q: Drift current across a p-n junction is caused by
qa.a: minority carriers moved by the junction's electric field
qa.e: The junction field sweeps minority carriers across.

qa.q: In an unbiased p-n junction at equilibrium, the net current is
qa.a: zero, as drift and diffusion currents cancel
qa.e: No external source means no net flow.

qa.q: What is the barrier potential of a germanium junction, approximately (in V)?
qa.e: Germanium has a lower barrier than silicon.

qa.q: Assertion (A): A depletion layer forms at a p-n junction. Reason (R): Diffusing electrons and holes recombine and leave behind uncovered immobile ions. Choose the correct option.
qa.a: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
qa.e: The region near the junction is depleted of carriers but holds fixed ions.

qa.q: A p-n junction diode is forward biased when
qa.a: its p-side is connected to the positive terminal of the battery
qa.e: This lowers the barrier.

qa.q: In forward bias, the width of the depletion layer
qa.e: The applied voltage opposes the barrier.

qa.q: The small current in a reverse-biased diode is mainly due to
qa.e: The field favours drift of minority carriers.

qa.q: For a silicon diode, the forward current becomes significant when the applied voltage exceeds about (in V)
qa.e: This is the cut-in (knee) voltage for Si.

qa.q: In reverse bias, below breakdown, the reverse current
qa.a: is very small and nearly independent of voltage
qa.e: Only a few minority carriers are available.

qa.q: The diode symbol's arrow points
qa.a: from the p-side (anode) to the n-side (cathode), the direction of forward current
qa.e: It shows conventional current direction in forward bias.

qa.q: What happens at the reverse breakdown voltage of a diode?
qa.e: A large field causes a sharp rise in current.

qa.q: In reverse bias, the potential barrier
qa.e: The applied voltage adds to the barrier.

qa.q: On a diode's forward curve, current increases from 20 mA to 40 mA as voltage increases from 0.75 V to 0.8 V. What is the dynamic resistance (in Ω)?
Dynamic resistance of a diode is defined as
qa.a: ΔV/ΔI at a point on the characteristic
qa.e: It is the inverse slope of the V-I curve.

qa.q: In the forward characteristic of a silicon diode, the current is very small until about
qa.a: 0.7 V, after which it rises steeply
qa.e: The threshold (knee) voltage for Si is about 0.7 V.

qa.q: Why is a microammeter used to measure current in the reverse-bias part of the experiment?
qa.a: Reverse current is very small, of the order of µA
qa.e: A milliammeter would show almost no deflection.

qa.q: A diode's reverse current changes from 1 µA to 1.2 µA when reverse voltage changes from 5 V to 25 V. What is the reverse dynamic resistance (in MΩ)?
Why is a resistor connected in series with the diode when plotting its forward characteristic?
qa.a: To limit the current and protect the diode from damage
qa.e: Above threshold, current rises very fast and can overheat the diode.

qa.q: A steeper slope of the forward V-I curve (I against V) at a point means the dynamic resistance there is
qa.e: rd = ΔV/ΔI is the inverse of the slope.

qa.q: Which feature of the V-I characteristic shows that a diode is a non-ohmic device?
qa.a: The curve is non-linear and different in forward and reverse directions
qa.e: Ohmic devices give a straight line, symmetric for both directions.

qa.q: A half-wave rectifier is fed with 50 Hz AC. What is the output frequency (in Hz)?
qa.e: One output pulse per input cycle.

qa.q: A full-wave rectifier is connected to a 60 Hz supply. What is its output frequency (in Hz)?
qa.e: Two pulses per cycle: 2 × 60 = 120 Hz.

qa.q: In a full-wave rectifier with a centre-tap transformer, how many diodes are used?
qa.e: Each diode conducts during alternate half-cycles.

qa.q: Why is a capacitor connected across the load in a rectifier circuit?
qa.a: To smooth the pulsating DC by charging at peaks and discharging between them
qa.e: It reduces ripple in the output.

qa.q: What is the main advantage of a full-wave rectifier over a half-wave rectifier?
qa.a: It uses both half-cycles, giving more output and less ripple
qa.e: No half-cycle is wasted.

qa.q: Which change reduces the ripple in a capacitor-filtered rectifier?
qa.e: A larger C (and RL) discharges more slowly between peaks.

qa.q: A rectifier works because a diode
qa.e: Forward bias conducts; reverse bias blocks.

qa.q: In a half-wave rectifier, the output during the half-cycles when the diode is reverse biased is
qa.e: The diode blocks current, so no voltage appears across the load.
